subtopic_detail: HIV post-exposure prophylaxis: ASHM 3-drug regimen
stem:
A 27-year-old intern sustains a hollow-bore needlestick injury while cannulating a patient known to have HIV with a detectable viral load of 42,000 copies/mL on an incomplete antiretroviral regimen. The exposure occurred 90 minutes ago. She squeezed the site, washed with soap and water, and presented immediately to the emergency department.

She is fit, on no regular medications, and has no personal history of hepatitis B or C. She is not pregnant, sexually active with one long-term partner using barrier contraception, and her last HIV test six months ago was negative. Baseline bloods including HIV serology, hepatitis serology, syphilis, renal function and pregnancy test are being drawn now.

The source patient is confirmed HIV-positive with resistance testing showing wild-type virus fully sensitive to first-line antiretrovirals. She reports no allergies. Local infectious diseases has been notified.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits.
data_table.Examination: Small puncture wound left index finger, minimal bleeding, no other injuries.
data_table.Investigations: Baseline HIV, hepatitis B/C, syphilis serology and pregnancy test collected; eGFR >90 mL/min/1.73m^2.
data_table.Medications: Nil regular. No known drug allergies.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate post-exposure prophylaxis to commence now?

options.text: Zidovudine plus lamivudine twice daily for 28 days
options.rationale: Zidovudine-lamivudine is a two-drug regimen from earlier ASHM guidance and is no longer first-line PEP because of inferior potency, resistance concerns and zidovudine's marrow and gastrointestinal toxicity. Current ASHM PEP guidelines mandate a three-drug regimen for all significant exposures (Source: ASHM National PEP Guidelines).

options.text: Efavirenz plus zidovudine-lamivudine daily for 28 days
options.rationale: Efavirenz-based PEP is no longer preferred because of central nervous system side effects, teratogenicity concerns in the first trimester and lower tolerability, all of which reduce PEP completion rates. Integrase inhibitor-based regimens are now the standard third agent (Source: ASHM National PEP Guidelines).

options.text: Tenofovir disoproxil-emtricitabine daily for 28 days without a third agent
options.rationale: Two-NRTI PEP is inadequate when the source is confirmed HIV-positive with detectable viraemia; adding an integrase inhibitor as the third drug is mandatory. Two-drug PEP is not endorsed for any exposure category in the current ASHM guidance (Source: ASHM National PEP Guidelines).

options.text: Tenofovir disoproxil-emtricitabine plus dolutegravir daily for 28 days
options.rationale: The ASHM National PEP Guidelines recommend a 28-day course of tenofovir disoproxil fumarate 300 mg plus emtricitabine 200 mg once daily combined with dolutegravir 50 mg once daily as first-line PEP after a significant occupational exposure to a known HIV-positive source with detectable viraemia. Commencement within 72 hours is essential, with the greatest efficacy inside four hours (Source: ASHM National PEP Guidelines).

options.text: Await baseline source patient viral load and defer any prophylaxis for 48 hours
options.rationale: PEP efficacy declines rapidly with delay and must be commenced within 72 hours, ideally within four hours of exposure. The source viral load is already known to be detectable and the exposure is high risk; deferring treatment risks failure of prophylaxis (Source: ASHM National PEP Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Occupational hollow-bore needlestick from a known HIV-positive source with detectable viraemia is a high-risk exposure. ASHM recommends a 28-day three-drug regimen of tenofovir disoproxil-emtricitabine plus dolutegravir, started as soon as possible and always within 72 hours (Source: ASHM National PEP Guidelines).
key_points: PEP within 72 hours, ideally under 4 hours
Three-drug regimen mandatory for high-risk exposures
TDF-FTC + dolutegravir is first-line per ASHM
Baseline HIV, hepatitis B/C, renal function and pregnancy test required
explanation.pearls: Follow-up HIV serology at 6 and 12 weeks (fourth-generation assay); hepatitis B booster or immunoglobulin if not immune.

subtopic_detail: PJP primary prophylaxis at CD4 threshold
stem:
A 44-year-old man is newly diagnosed with HIV during a sexual health screen after a new partner tested positive. He is asymptomatic, has never taken antiretrovirals and has no prior AIDS-defining illness. He works full time and has no fevers, cough, weight loss or oral candidiasis.

On examination he looks well. Chest is clear and there is no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. There is no oral thrush and no skin lesions. His BMI is 26 kg/m^2 and there are no signs of wasting.

Initial staging bloods return the same day. Full blood count, renal function and liver function are within normal limits. CD4 count is 148 cells/microL, HIV RNA 84,000 copies/mL, HLA-B*5701 negative, hepatitis B and C serology negative, toxoplasma IgG negative, syphilis EIA negative. He has no sulfa drug allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits.
data_table.Examination: Well, no oral thrush, chest clear, no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly.
data_table.Investigations: CD4 148 cells/microL, HIV RNA 84,000 copies/mL, toxoplasma IgG negative, HLA-B*5701 negative, hepatitis B/C negative, eGFR >90 mL/min/1.73m^2.

lead_in: In addition to commencing antiretroviral therapy, what is the most appropriate opportunistic infection prophylaxis?

options.text: Azithromycin 1200 mg orally once weekly
options.rationale: Azithromycin prophylaxis is indicated for disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex when the CD4 count falls below 50 cells/microL. His CD4 of 148 is well above that threshold and does not warrant MAC prophylaxis (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

options.text: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg orally daily
options.rationale: The ASHM HIV Management Guidelines and Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic recommend PJP primary prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole once the CD4 count falls below 200 cells/microL. His CD4 is 148 so prophylaxis is indicated. The same regimen also covers toxoplasmosis, which becomes relevant if CD4 falls below 100 and toxoplasma IgG is positive (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

options.text: Valganciclovir 900 mg orally daily
options.rationale: Primary CMV prophylaxis is not routinely recommended in HIV even at very low CD4 counts because of toxicity, cost and lack of survival benefit. CMV disease is managed pre-emptively with retinal screening and treatment when disease is diagnosed, not with universal prophylaxis (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

options.text: Fluconazole 200 mg orally weekly for cryptococcal prophylaxis
options.rationale: Routine primary prophylaxis against cryptococcosis is not recommended in Australian practice; instead, cryptococcal antigen screening is offered when the CD4 count falls below 100 in high-prevalence settings, with pre-emptive fluconazole only if the antigen is positive (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

options.text: No opportunistic infection prophylaxis is required at this stage
options.rationale: His CD4 count of 148 crosses the well-established PJP prophylaxis threshold of 200 cells/microL, so withholding prophylaxis exposes him to a preventable AIDS-defining pneumonia while awaiting immune reconstitution on antiretroviral therapy (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Primary PJP prophylaxis in HIV is triggered by CD4 count below 200 cells/microL (or oropharyngeal candidiasis or an AIDS-defining illness). Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is first-line and also covers toxoplasmosis at CD4 counts below 100 in IgG-positive patients (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).
key_points: PJP prophylaxis threshold: CD4 <200 cells/microL
Toxoplasma prophylaxis: CD4 <100 AND toxoplasma IgG positive
MAC prophylaxis: CD4 <50 (with azithromycin)
TMP-SMX 160/800 mg daily is first-line PJP prophylaxis
explanation.pearls: Prophylaxis can be stopped once CD4 rises above 200 for at least three months on suppressive ART.

subtopic_detail: Acute HIV seroconversion illness recognition
stem:
A 24-year-old man presents to his general practitioner with a 10-day history of fevers, sore throat, myalgias and a diffuse maculopapular rash on his trunk. He reports condomless receptive anal intercourse with a new male partner four weeks ago. He has no known chronic illnesses and takes no regular medications.

On examination he is febrile at 38.4 degrees C with cervical, axillary and inguinal lymphadenopathy. His oropharynx is erythematous with small ulcerative lesions on the palate. He has a non-blanching-in-parts maculopapular rash across his trunk. Chest, cardiovascular and abdominal examinations are otherwise unremarkable. He is not taking any recent antibiotics.

His general practitioner suspects an acute viral illness and considers whether standard HIV serology alone will be sufficient. A monospot test is negative and Epstein-Barr virus IgM is pending.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4 C, HR 96, BP 118/72, RR 16, SpO2 99 percent room air.
data_table.Examination: Generalised lymphadenopathy, palatal ulcers, diffuse maculopapular truncal rash.
data_table.Investigations: Monospot negative; EBV IgM pending. FBC, LFTs, UEC pending.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial HIV investigation?

options.text: HIV Western blot as a standalone confirmatory test
options.rationale: Western blot is confirmatory only, insensitive in the seroconversion window, and has been replaced in the ASHM testing algorithm by combination antigen-antibody assays with supplemental testing. It is not used as an initial diagnostic test (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Policy).

options.text: Third-generation HIV antibody-only test with repeat in three months
options.rationale: Third-generation antibody-only assays detect IgG only and will typically miss the earliest phase of infection when only p24 antigen and RNA are present. Deferring diagnosis for three months delays antiretroviral therapy and secondary prevention counselling (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Policy).

options.text: Fourth-generation HIV antigen-antibody assay together with HIV RNA viral load
options.rationale: Acute HIV seroconversion classically presents with fever, pharyngitis, generalised lymphadenopathy, maculopapular rash and mucocutaneous ulceration inside the first six weeks of exposure. A fourth-generation antigen-antibody assay detects p24 antigen from around day 14 to 21 but antibody may still be negative; adding HIV RNA closes the window because viraemia peaks at very high levels during acute infection. ASHM recommends combined antigen-antibody testing plus HIV RNA whenever acute HIV is suspected (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Policy).

options.text: Rapid point-of-care HIV antibody-only test with no other assays
options.rationale: Most point-of-care rapid tests detect antibody only and have a longer window period than laboratory fourth-generation assays. A negative rapid test in an acutely symptomatic patient with high pre-test probability cannot exclude acute HIV (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Policy).

options.text: CD4 lymphocyte count as the sole initial diagnostic test
options.rationale: CD4 count is a staging and prognostic tool, not a diagnostic assay. It can be transiently depressed during acute infection but cannot distinguish HIV from other causes of lymphopenia (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Acute HIV seroconversion illness presents as a mononucleosis-like syndrome with fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, rash and mucocutaneous ulcers. Diagnosis requires a fourth-generation HIV antigen-antibody assay plus HIV RNA to cover the antibody-window period (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Policy).
key_points: Seroconversion syndrome: fever, rash, pharyngitis, generalised lymphadenopathy, oral ulcers
Window period is closed earliest by combined p24 antigen-antibody plus HIV RNA
Rapid antibody-only tests can miss acute infection
Very high viral load during acute infection drives transmission risk
explanation.pearls: Consider syphilis, secondary EBV/CMV mononucleosis and acute hepatitis in the differential; test broadly.

subtopic_detail: Advanced HIV with CD4 <50: MAC evaluation and prophylaxis
stem:
A 51-year-old man with HIV, previously lost to follow up for four years, re-presents with six weeks of fevers, night sweats, drenching sweats and 8 kg unintentional weight loss. He is not on antiretroviral therapy. He denies cough or shortness of breath and has not travelled recently.

On examination he is thin with temporal wasting. Temperature 38.2 degrees C, pulse rate 104, blood pressure 108/68, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98 percent on room air. There is oral candidiasis but no pulmonary crackles. The abdomen is soft with tender hepatomegaly to 4 cm below the costal margin. There is no focal lymphadenopathy or meningism.

Investigations return today: CD4 count 32 cells/microL, HIV RNA 380,000 copies/mL, haemoglobin 92 g/L (135-175), alkaline phosphatase 480 U/L (30-110), gamma-GT 210 U/L (5-50), bilirubin within normal limits, chest x-ray clear, blood cultures still pending. Cryptococcal antigen is negative and tuberculin gamma-release assay is negative. Sputum acid-fast smear is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.2 C, HR 104, BP 108/68, RR 18, SpO2 98 percent room air.
data_table.Examination: Cachectic, oral thrush, tender hepatomegaly 4 cm, chest clear.
data_table.Investigations: CD4 32 cells/microL, HIV RNA 380,000 copies/mL, Hb 92 g/L (135-175), ALP 480 U/L (30-110), GGT 210 U/L (5-50), CXR clear, cryptococcal antigen negative, QuantiFERON negative, sputum AFB smear negative.
data_table.Medications: Nil. Not on antiretrovirals for four years.

lead_in: In addition to starting antiretroviral therapy and PJP prophylaxis, what is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence azithromycin 1200 mg orally weekly for MAC primary prophylaxis without further investigation
options.rationale: Starting azithromycin prophylaxis before excluding active disseminated MAC risks selecting for macrolide resistance if occult MAC bacteraemia is present. Fever, wasting, anaemia and a cholestatic hepatitis picture at CD4 32 are highly suggestive of disseminated MAC, and blood mycobacterial cultures must be sent first (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

options.text: Add oral fluconazole 400 mg daily empirically for suspected disseminated cryptococcosis
options.rationale: Cryptococcal antigen is negative, effectively excluding cryptococcal disease as the driver of his current presentation. Empirical fluconazole is not warranted and adds hepatotoxicity to an already deranged liver enzyme picture (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

options.text: Empirical four-drug antituberculous therapy pending culture results
options.rationale: QuantiFERON is negative, sputum smear is negative and there is no pulmonary infiltrate; empirical RIPE therapy is not indicated and would delay recognition of MAC. Antituberculous therapy also has significant interactions with antiretrovirals that require careful selection (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

options.text: Start valganciclovir empirically for suspected CMV disease
options.rationale: CMV disease at CD4 below 50 typically causes retinitis, colitis or oesophagitis rather than a cholestatic hepatitis-and-wasting picture. Empirical valganciclovir carries substantial marrow toxicity and should not be initiated without evidence of end-organ CMV disease (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

options.text: Send mycobacterial blood cultures before considering MAC prophylaxis or treatment
options.rationale: At CD4 below 50 with fevers, wasting, anaemia and a cholestatic liver enzyme picture, disseminated MAC is the leading opportunistic infection. Mycobacterial blood cultures are the diagnostic test of choice and must be collected before empirical azithromycin because monotherapy of active disease drives macrolide resistance. Confirmed disseminated MAC is then treated with clarithromycin or azithromycin plus ethambutol, not with prophylactic monotherapy (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

explanation.summary: In advanced HIV with CD4 below 50, disseminated MAC classically presents with fever, weight loss, anaemia and a cholestatic hepatitis picture. Mycobacterial blood cultures must be sent before empirical macrolide therapy because macrolide monotherapy of active disease drives resistance (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).
key_points: MAC prophylaxis threshold: CD4 <50 with azithromycin 1200 mg weekly
Rule out active disseminated MAC before commencing prophylaxis
Disseminated MAC treatment: clarithromycin (or azithromycin) plus ethambutol
Cholestatic ALP/GGT with wasting at low CD4 = think MAC
explanation.pearls: Prompt ART is still indicated; delaying ART for MAC treatment increases mortality more than IRIS risk.

subtopic_detail: AIDS-defining CNS lesion: toxoplasmosis vs primary CNS lymphoma
stem:
A 39-year-old woman with poorly adherent HIV presents with a two-week history of progressive right-sided weakness, headaches and one episode of a witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure. She stopped her antiretrovirals six months ago and has not been engaged in specialist care.

On examination she is afebrile with right hemiparesis, right-sided pronator drift and mild expressive dysphasia. There is no meningism, papilloedema or rash. Cardiorespiratory and abdominal examinations are unremarkable.

CD4 count is 42 cells/microL, HIV RNA 220,000 copies/mL, toxoplasma IgG positive, cryptococcal antigen negative and syphilis serology negative. She is not on any PJP or toxoplasmosis prophylaxis. MRI brain with contrast shows two ring-enhancing lesions, one in the left basal ganglia and one at the grey-white junction of the right frontal lobe, each with surrounding oedema. She has no sulfa allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits.
data_table.Examination: Right hemiparesis, right pronator drift, mild expressive dysphasia, no meningism.
data_table.Investigations: CD4 42 cells/microL, HIV RNA 220,000 copies/mL, toxoplasma IgG positive, cryptococcal antigen negative, MRI brain: two ring-enhancing lesions with oedema.
data_table.Medications: Nil currently. No PJP/toxo prophylaxis. No sulfa allergy.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Empirical sulfadiazine, pyrimethamine and folinic acid, reassessed at 10 to 14 days
options.rationale: Multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions in advanced HIV with CD4 below 100 and positive toxoplasma IgG have a pre-test probability of cerebral toxoplasmosis of over 80 per cent. ASHM and Therapeutic Guidelines recommend empirical sulfadiazine plus pyrimethamine plus folinic acid, with clinical and radiological reassessment at 10 to 14 days; failure to respond prompts biopsy to exclude primary CNS lymphoma (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

options.text: Proceed directly to stereotactic brain biopsy before commencing any antimicrobial therapy
options.rationale: Biopsy is reserved for atypical presentations, toxoplasma IgG negative patients, single lesions with high suspicion for lymphoma on thallium SPECT or MRS, or failure of a 10 to 14 day empirical trial. In a typical multi-lesion IgG-positive presentation, empirical therapy is standard practice and biopsy is second-line (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

options.text: Commence liposomal amphotericin B and flucytosine induction
options.rationale: Amphotericin plus flucytosine is induction therapy for cryptococcal meningoencephalitis. Cryptococcal antigen is negative and imaging does not suggest cryptococcoma, making this empirical treatment inappropriate (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

options.text: Start high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone before any antimicrobial therapy
options.rationale: Empirical corticosteroids can shrink CNS lymphoma temporarily and confound both imaging and biopsy interpretation. They should be avoided unless there is impending herniation from mass effect. Even then dexamethasone rather than methylprednisolone is preferred, and it is added to, not instead of, antimicrobial therapy (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

options.text: Immediate whole-brain radiotherapy for presumed primary CNS lymphoma
options.rationale: Primary CNS lymphoma typically presents as a single periventricular lesion in EBV-driven disease and requires histological confirmation before radiotherapy. Two lesions in a toxoplasma-IgG-positive patient favour toxoplasmosis; empirical radiotherapy without diagnosis is inappropriate (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions in a toxoplasma-IgG-positive patient with CD4 below 100 are treated empirically for cerebral toxoplasmosis using sulfadiazine, pyrimethamine and folinic acid. Clinical and radiological response is assessed at 10 to 14 days; non-responders undergo biopsy for primary CNS lymphoma (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).
key_points: Toxoplasmosis risk: CD4 <100 with positive toxoplasma IgG
Empirical treatment before biopsy is standard for typical presentations
Sulfadiazine + pyrimethamine + folinic acid is first-line
Non-response by 14 days triggers biopsy for CNS lymphoma
explanation.pearls: TMP-SMX-based regimens provide both PJP and toxoplasmosis prophylaxis in CD4-below-100 patients with positive toxoplasma IgG.

subtopic_detail: Initial ART regimen selection per ASHM 2024
stem:
A 32-year-old woman is newly diagnosed with HIV during antenatal-planning bloods; she is not currently pregnant but plans to conceive within the next six months with her HIV-negative male partner. She has no prior antiretroviral exposure and is otherwise well.

On examination she is well with a BMI of 24 kg/m^2. There is no oral candidiasis, no lymphadenopathy and no skin lesions. Cardiovascular, respiratory and abdominal examinations are unremarkable.

Baseline investigations show CD4 count 460 cells/microL, HIV RNA 68,000 copies/mL, HLA-B*5701 negative, hepatitis B surface antigen negative with immune serology (positive surface antibody), hepatitis C antibody negative, syphilis serology negative and rubella immune. Renal function, liver function and lipids are within normal limits. She has no known drug allergies and takes no regular medications. She has been counselled about U=U (undetectable equals untransmittable) and preconception planning.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits.
data_table.Examination: Well, no oral thrush, no lymphadenopathy.
data_table.Investigations: CD4 460 cells/microL, HIV RNA 68,000 copies/mL, HLA-B*5701 negative, HBsAg negative (immune), HCV negative, eGFR >90 mL/min/1.73m^2, LFTs and lipids within normal limits.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial antiretroviral regimen?

options.text: Zidovudine, lamivudine and nevirapine three times daily
options.rationale: Zidovudine-lamivudine-nevirapine is an obsolete first-line regimen with significant marrow, hepatic and hypersensitivity toxicity, and higher pill and dosing burden. It is no longer recommended by ASHM outside historic resource-limited contexts (Source: ASHM Antiretroviral Guidelines).

options.text: Efavirenz with tenofovir disoproxil and emtricitabine as a single daily tablet
options.rationale: Efavirenz-based regimens are no longer preferred first-line in Australian guidance because of central nervous system adverse effects, historical first-trimester teratogenicity concerns and inferior tolerability compared with integrase inhibitor regimens. They are reserved as alternatives when preferred regimens are contraindicated (Source: ASHM Antiretroviral Guidelines).

options.text: Ritonavir-boosted atazanavir with tenofovir disoproxil and emtricitabine
options.rationale: Boosted protease inhibitor regimens are second-line in current ASHM guidance; they carry a higher pill burden, more drug interactions and a hyperbilirubinaemia signal, and are outperformed by integrase inhibitor regimens for tolerability and viral suppression rates (Source: ASHM Antiretroviral Guidelines).

options.text: Bictegravir with tenofovir alafenamide and emtricitabine as a single daily tablet
options.rationale: ASHM 2024 preferred first-line antiretroviral regimens for treatment-naive adults are integrase strand transfer inhibitor based; bictegravir with tenofovir alafenamide and emtricitabine as a single-tablet regimen is a preferred option, with strong efficacy, low interaction profile, favourable pregnancy safety data (once conception occurs) and durable virological suppression suitable for a patient planning imminent conception (Source: ASHM Antiretroviral Guidelines).

options.text: Long-acting injectable cabotegravir and rilpivirine every two months as initial therapy
options.rationale: Long-acting injectable cabotegravir with rilpivirine is approved as a switch option for patients already virologically suppressed on oral therapy, not for treatment initiation. It requires prior confirmed sensitivity and suppression, and is not appropriate as first-line initiation (Source: ASHM Antiretroviral Guidelines).

explanation.summary: ASHM 2024 preferred first-line antiretroviral therapy is an integrase inhibitor combined with two nucleoside/tide backbone drugs, most commonly bictegravir-tenofovir alafenamide-emtricitabine or dolutegravir-based combinations. These deliver rapid, durable viral suppression with a favourable side effect and interaction profile (Source: ASHM Antiretroviral Guidelines).
key_points: First-line: integrase inhibitor + 2 NRTI backbone
Bictegravir-TAF-FTC is a preferred single-tablet regimen
Efavirenz and boosted PIs are alternatives, not first-line
Long-acting injectables are switch options, not initiation
explanation.pearls: U=U: sustained undetectable viral load eliminates sexual transmission and supports safe conception planning.

subtopic_detail: Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) after ART initiation
stem:
A 46-year-old man was diagnosed with HIV three weeks ago after presenting with a two-month history of low-grade fevers, weight loss and a productive cough. Chest imaging at that presentation showed patchy right upper lobe changes; QuantiFERON was positive and a sputum GeneXpert confirmed rifampicin-sensitive Mycobacterium tuberculosis. He was commenced on isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol two weeks ago, and integrase inhibitor based antiretroviral therapy was started one week ago at his baseline CD4 count of 48 cells/microL and HIV RNA of 620,000 copies/mL.

He now re-presents with worsening fevers to 39.1 degrees C, new painful right supraclavicular and cervical lymphadenopathy, increased cough and pleuritic chest pain. Chest x-ray shows enlarging right upper lobe consolidation and new right paratracheal lymphadenopathy compared with imaging from three weeks ago. He is adherent with both regimens and denies missed doses.

Repeat sputum acid-fast smear is negative and there is no evidence of drug-resistant tuberculosis on repeat susceptibility testing. Blood cultures are negative to date. He is haemodynamically stable, saturating 96 percent on room air.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.1 C, HR 108, BP 122/78, RR 22, SpO2 96 percent room air.
data_table.Examination: Tender right supraclavicular and cervical lymphadenopathy, right basal crackles.
data_table.Investigations: CXR: enlarging RUL consolidation, new right paratracheal nodes. Sputum AFB smear negative. Blood cultures negative. Susceptibility unchanged.
data_table.Medications: RIPE therapy day 14. INSTI-based ART day 7. Adherent.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management step?

options.text: Stop antiretroviral therapy and continue antituberculous therapy alone
options.rationale: Interrupting antiretroviral therapy during paradoxical IRIS worsens outcomes by allowing HIV replication to rebound, delays immune recovery and does not resolve the inflammatory reaction; ASHM guidance is to continue both therapies wherever clinically feasible (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

options.text: Change antituberculous therapy to a second-line regimen for suspected multi-drug resistant tuberculosis
options.rationale: Repeat susceptibility testing confirms ongoing drug sensitivity and there is no microbiological failure. The worsening clinical picture reflects immune reconstitution against persisting antigen, not treatment failure, so second-line antituberculous drugs are inappropriate (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

options.text: Continue both regimens and commence prednisolone 1.5 mg/kg daily for two weeks with a taper
options.rationale: This is paradoxical tuberculosis-associated IRIS: worsening lymphadenopathy, fevers and radiographic disease within weeks of starting antiretroviral therapy at low CD4 count, with excluded treatment failure and no drug resistance. Both antituberculous therapy and antiretroviral therapy should continue, and moderate-to-severe symptomatic IRIS is treated with prednisolone approximately 1.5 mg/kg daily for two weeks followed by a taper, supported by the Meintjes randomised controlled trial and endorsed by ASHM (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

options.text: Add broad-spectrum intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam for presumed bacterial superinfection
options.rationale: There is no clinical, radiographic or microbiological evidence of bacterial superinfection; he is haemodynamically stable, has no consolidation pattern of bacterial pneumonia and blood cultures are negative. Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics add toxicity without addressing the underlying inflammatory driver (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Excisional biopsy of the enlarged supraclavicular node before any further treatment change
options.rationale: Excisional biopsy is not the first step in a patient with a confirmed tuberculosis diagnosis and typical timeline for paradoxical IRIS. Biopsy is reserved for atypical presentations or diagnostic uncertainty regarding lymphoma or a resistant organism, neither of which applies here (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Paradoxical tuberculosis-associated IRIS occurs when antiretroviral therapy is started in the setting of very low CD4 counts and pre-existing opportunistic infection, producing worsening clinical or radiographic features despite microbiological response. Management is to continue both therapies and add corticosteroids for moderate-to-severe cases, per the Meintjes trial and ASHM guidance (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).
key_points: IRIS risk highest with CD4 <100 and rapid viral load fall
Continue both antituberculous therapy and antiretroviral therapy
Exclude treatment failure and drug resistance first
Prednisolone 1.5 mg/kg daily for 2 weeks then taper (Meintjes trial)
explanation.pearls: Cryptococcal IRIS mandates delaying ART by 4-6 weeks after antifungal induction to reduce fatal CNS inflammation.

subtopic_detail: PrEP eligibility and baseline monitoring per ASHM
stem:
A 29-year-old man attends a sexual health clinic requesting HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis. He is HIV negative and has had condomless receptive anal intercourse with multiple male partners over the last six months, including one partner recently diagnosed with rectal gonorrhoea. He describes occasional crystal methamphetamine use in sexual contexts.

He is otherwise well with no significant medical history and takes no regular medications. He mentions that four days ago he had a condom failure with an anonymous partner of unknown HIV status. He denies any current fevers, rash, sore throat or lymphadenopathy.

On examination he looks well with normal vital signs. There is no oral thrush, no lymphadenopathy and no rash. Baseline point-of-care fourth-generation HIV antigen-antibody test is negative today. Serum creatinine drawn last week was 78 micromol/L (60-110) with an eGFR greater than 90 mL/min/1.73m^2. Hepatitis B surface antigen was negative with immune surface antibody, and hepatitis C antibody was negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits.
data_table.Examination: Well, no oral thrush, no lymphadenopathy, no rash.
data_table.Investigations: Point-of-care 4th-gen HIV Ag/Ab negative today; creatinine 78 micromol/L (60-110), eGFR >90 mL/min/1.73m^2; HBsAg negative (immune); HCV negative.
data_table.Medications: Nil regular. No known drug allergies.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence a 28-day PEP course now, then transition to daily PrEP once repeat HIV serology at four weeks is negative
options.rationale: The condom failure four days ago is outside the 72-hour PEP window, so PEP cannot be started for that exposure; instead, the priority is to exclude occult acute HIV before commencing PrEP. Given his high-risk profile and imminent PrEP eligibility, ASHM guidance is to defer daily PrEP until acute HIV is excluded with a fourth-generation antigen-antibody test plus HIV RNA at follow-up, then commence tenofovir disoproxil-emtricitabine PrEP with three-monthly HIV, renal function and STI monitoring. In this scenario, restarting the described sequence with PEP first is not appropriate given the timing; the safest actionable pathway is to bridge to PrEP after HIV exclusion (Source: ASHM PrEP Guidelines).

options.text: Commence daily tenofovir disoproxil-emtricitabine PrEP today and arrange three-monthly review
options.rationale: Starting standard daily PrEP without addressing the condom failure four days ago risks converting an unrecognised acute HIV infection into a PrEP-induced integrase or NRTI resistance selection scenario, because a two-drug regimen is inadequate to suppress established infection. The exposure four days ago is within the 72-hour PEP window boundary and must be evaluated first (Source: ASHM PrEP Guidelines).

options.text: Send fourth-generation HIV antigen-antibody test plus HIV RNA today and defer PrEP until results confirm HIV-negative status
options.rationale: Sending baseline HIV RNA plus fourth-generation testing is appropriate, but this option omits the crucial actionable component of scheduling explicit PrEP commencement once results confirm HIV-negative status, and does not address the ongoing high-risk behaviour in the interim. It is a diagnostic step rather than a management plan (Source: ASHM PrEP Guidelines).

options.text: Recommend consistent condom use and STI screening only, without offering PrEP given his methamphetamine use
options.rationale: Methamphetamine use in sexual contexts is a marker of higher HIV acquisition risk and an indication for PrEP rather than a contraindication. Withholding PrEP because of substance use is not supported by ASHM guidance and reinforces stigma (Source: ASHM PrEP Guidelines).

options.text: Commence on-demand event-driven PrEP dosing (2-1-1) as first-line strategy without further HIV testing
options.rationale: Event-driven 2-1-1 dosing is only supported for men who have sex with men where sexual events are predictable, and still requires baseline HIV, renal and hepatitis testing to exclude acute HIV and renal impairment before commencement. Skipping baseline HIV testing risks PrEP-induced resistance if occult acute HIV is present (Source: ASHM PrEP Guidelines).

explanation.summary: PrEP is indicated for high-risk sexual exposure and requires baseline HIV, renal function and hepatitis serology before initiation. A recent exposure inside or just outside the 72-hour PEP window requires acute HIV exclusion before starting a two-drug PrEP regimen, because starting PrEP during unrecognised acute HIV selects for resistance (Source: ASHM PrEP Guidelines).
key_points: PrEP: TDF-FTC daily or event-driven 2-1-1 for MSM
Baseline: HIV Ag/Ab (+/- RNA), renal function, hepatitis B/C, STIs
Exclude acute HIV before starting to avoid resistance
Three-monthly HIV, renal function and STI monitoring on PrEP
explanation.pearls: PEP window is 72 hours from exposure; beyond that, focus shifts to acute HIV exclusion and bridging to PrEP.

subtopic_detail: Uncomplicated cystitis in a non-pregnant woman
stem:
A 28-year-old woman presents to a suburban general practice with two days of dysuria, urinary frequency and suprapubic discomfort. She has never had a urinary tract infection before, is not sexually active in the past three months and takes no regular medications. She uses reliable contraception, her last menstrual period was 10 days ago, and a bedside urine beta-hCG is negative. She has no fever, flank pain, vomiting or vaginal discharge.

Examination reveals a comfortable woman with mild suprapubic tenderness. Bedside urinalysis is positive for nitrites and leucocyte esterase, negative for blood. She reports no penicillin, sulfonamide or nitrofuran allergy, and her estimated GFR at a recent workplace medical was above 60 mL/min/1.73m^2.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 76, BP 118/72, RR 14, SpO2 99 percent room air, T 36.8 C.
data_table.Examination: Mild suprapubic tenderness, no flank tenderness, no vaginal discharge on external inspection.
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis nitrites positive, leucocyte esterase positive, blood negative. Urine beta-hCG negative.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical oral antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Amoxicillin 500 mg orally every 8 hours for 5 days
options.rationale: Amoxicillin monotherapy is not recommended empirically for uncomplicated cystitis in Australia because of high E. coli resistance rates. It is only appropriate when susceptibility is confirmed on culture (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook - Amoxicillin).

options.text: Cefalexin 500 mg orally every 12 hours for 5 days
options.rationale: Cefalexin is an eTG alternative when first-line agents are unsuitable, not the primary choice for uncomplicated cystitis. It has broader ecological impact and is preferred in pregnancy rather than in non-pregnant women with normal renal function (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute cystitis).

options.text: Trimethoprim 300 mg orally once daily for 3 days
options.rationale: eTG lists trimethoprim 300 mg orally, daily for 3 days as a first-line option for acute cystitis in non-pregnant women with normal renal function, alongside nitrofurantoin 100 mg orally 6-hourly for 5 days. Either agent is acceptable first-line; local resistance patterns and tolerability guide the choice (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute cystitis).

options.text: Ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally every 12 hours for 3 days
options.rationale: Fluoroquinolones are reserved for complicated infections or resistant organisms in Australia and are not first-line for uncomplicated cystitis because of collateral resistance and tendinopathy or QT risk. Reflexive fluoroquinolone use is a labelled anti-pattern (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute cystitis).

options.text: Nitrofurantoin 100 mg orally every 6 hours for 3 days
options.rationale: Nitrofurantoin is a first-line agent but the eTG duration for acute uncomplicated cystitis is 5 days, not 3. A 3-day course underdoses the regimen and risks early recurrence (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute cystitis).

explanation.summary: Uncomplicated cystitis in non-pregnant women with normal renal function is treated empirically with a short course of trimethoprim (3 days) or nitrofurantoin (5 days) per eTG. Culture is not required for a first uncomplicated episode with a classic presentation. Cefalexin and beta-lactams are second-line or reserved for pregnancy. Fluoroquinolones are avoided outside complicated infections.
key_points: Trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 3 days OR nitrofurantoin 100 mg 6-hourly for 5 days are eTG first-line.
Amoxicillin is inadequate empirically due to E. coli resistance in Australia.
Fluoroquinolones are reserved for complicated or resistant infection.
Nitrofurantoin duration is 5 days, not 3 - a common prescribing error.
explanation.pearls: Nitrofurantoin needs eGFR above 45 mL/min/1.73m^2 to concentrate in urine adequately; below that, switch to trimethoprim or cefalexin.

sources.label: RACGP - Urinary tract infection in adults

subtopic_detail: Acute pyelonephritis - oral versus IV thresholds
stem:
A 34-year-old woman presents to a metropolitan emergency department with 24 hours of right flank pain, rigors and vomiting on a background of two days of dysuria and frequency. She is not pregnant (urine beta-hCG negative), has no structural urinary tract abnormality, no indwelling catheter and no recent antibiotic exposure. She has taken oral fluids overnight and passed urine twice this morning.

On examination she is uncomfortable but alert and cooperative. There is right renal angle tenderness and no suprapubic mass. Vitals: HR 102, BP 118/74, RR 18, SpO2 98 percent room air, T 38.6 C. Bedside bloods show WCC 14.2 x10^9/L, CRP 96 mg/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L (baseline 72), lactate 1.4 mmol/L. Blood and urine cultures have been sent. She has no vomiting since arrival, tolerated 200 mL of oral fluid and has no allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 102, BP 118/74, RR 18, SpO2 98 percent, T 38.6 C.
data_table.Examination: Right renal angle tenderness, no suprapubic mass, no vaginal discharge.
data_table.Investigations: WCC 14.2 x10^9/L, CRP 96 mg/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L (baseline 72), lactate 1.4 mmol/L, urinalysis nitrites and leucocytes positive.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: IV ceftriaxone 1 g daily plus IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg loading
options.rationale: Dual IV therapy is unnecessary when she is haemodynamically stable, tolerating oral fluids and without sepsis criteria. eTG reserves combination IV beta-lactam plus aminoglycoside for severe sepsis, septic shock or failed initial therapy (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute pyelonephritis).

options.text: IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg single dose then oral trimethoprim 300 mg daily
options.rationale: eTG recommends a single loading dose of IV gentamicin (4 to 7 mg/kg IBW) followed by oral step-down for non-severe pyelonephritis in patients able to tolerate oral therapy. Trimethoprim 300 mg daily for a total 10-14 day course is a listed oral option pending susceptibilities (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute pyelonephritis).

options.text: Oral nitrofurantoin 100 mg every 6 hours for 14 days total
options.rationale: Nitrofurantoin does not achieve adequate tissue concentrations in renal parenchyma and is contraindicated in pyelonephritis. Its use is restricted to lower urinary tract infection (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook - Nitrofurantoin).

options.text: Oral cefalexin 500 mg every 6 hours for 14 days total
options.rationale: Oral cefalexin has inadequate serum concentrations for empirical pyelonephritis therapy and is not an eTG first-line option. Cefalexin is reserved for cystitis in pregnancy, not pyelonephritis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute pyelonephritis).

options.text: Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg every 12 hours for 7 to 10 days
options.rationale: Oral ciprofloxacin is an eTG alternative when aminoglycosides are contraindicated, but is not first-line given Australian E. coli fluoroquinolone resistance and adverse effect profile. Reserve for confirmed susceptibility or beta-lactam contraindication (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute pyelonephritis).

explanation.summary: eTG stratifies pyelonephritis by severity. Non-severe cases who tolerate oral fluids and are haemodynamically stable receive a single IV gentamicin loading dose plus early oral step-down (trimethoprim, amoxicillin-clavulanate, or cefalexin depending on culture) for a total 10-14 days. Severe sepsis, pregnancy, obstruction or failed oral therapy triggers full IV therapy and admission.
key_points: Single-dose gentamicin plus oral step-down is the eTG default for non-severe pyelonephritis.
Nitrofurantoin is contraindicated - inadequate tissue penetration.
Oral cefalexin monotherapy is not recommended for pyelonephritis.
Total course is 10-14 days, longer than cystitis.
explanation.pearls: Gentamicin dosing uses ideal body weight (or dose-adjusted weight if BMI over 30) at 4-7 mg/kg; a single loading dose rarely requires level monitoring.

subtopic_detail: Catheter-associated bacteriuria - when to treat
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 78-year-old man on the rehabilitation ward six weeks after a right total hip replacement. He has an indwelling urinary catheter placed intraoperatively for peri-operative retention that has remained in situ due to ongoing voiding trials.

The nursing team sent a routine mid-stream catheter specimen this morning that has just returned: greater than 10^5 CFU/mL Escherichia coli, sensitive to trimethoprim, amoxicillin-clavulanate and cefalexin. He is afebrile, feels well, is eating and mobilising with physiotherapy, and has no suprapubic pain, flank tenderness, delirium or new confusion. Vital signs are within normal limits and his most recent bloods 48 hours ago showed WCC 7.1 x10^9/L, CRP 8 mg/L and creatinine 82 micromol/L (baseline 78). His trial of void is planned for tomorrow morning.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits.
data_table.Examination: Well, afebrile, no suprapubic or flank tenderness, no delirium.
data_table.Investigations: Catheter urine culture E. coli greater than 10^5 CFU/mL sensitive to trimethoprim, cefalexin, augmentin. WCC 7.1 x10^9/L, CRP 8 mg/L 48 h ago.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence oral trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 7 days empirically
options.rationale: Treating asymptomatic catheter-associated bacteriuria promotes resistance and Clostridioides difficile infection without altering outcomes. eTG explicitly recommends against antibiotic treatment in this scenario (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Catheter-associated UTI).

options.text: Commence oral cefalexin 500 mg 12-hourly for 5 days empirically
options.rationale: Any antibiotic prescription for asymptomatic catheter bacteriuria is inappropriate. Choice of agent does not change the recommendation - no treatment is indicated (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Catheter-associated UTI).

options.text: Change the catheter and commence trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 7 days
options.rationale: Neither empirical antibiotics nor routine catheter change is indicated for asymptomatic bacteriuria. Catheter change without symptoms simply reseeds the bladder with new organisms (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Catheter-associated UTI).

options.text: No antibiotics and proceed with the planned trial of void tomorrow
options.rationale: Asymptomatic catheter-associated bacteriuria in a patient without local or systemic symptoms should not be treated with antibiotics. Repeat culture is also not indicated and simply generates more positive results. Proceed with catheter removal as planned (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Catheter-associated UTI).

options.text: Send blood cultures and start IV ceftriaxone 1 g daily pending sensitivities
options.rationale: Blood cultures and IV antibiotics are reserved for suspected sepsis or systemic infection. He has no fever, tachycardia, hypotension, delirium or raised inflammatory markers (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Catheter-associated UTI).

explanation.summary: Catheter-associated bacteriuria is almost universal after several days of catheterisation, but is not itself an indication for treatment. eTG and IDSA guidance treat only symptomatic CAUTI, defined by new fever, suprapubic or flank pain, delirium in older adults, rigors, or clinical sepsis. Antibiotics for asymptomatic bacteriuria drive resistance and C. difficile without benefit. Exceptions are pregnancy and immediately before urological procedures with mucosal trauma.
key_points: Do not routinely culture catheter urine in asymptomatic patients.
Treat only symptomatic CAUTI (fever, suprapubic or flank pain, delirium, sepsis).
Remove or replace long-standing catheters when symptomatic CAUTI is diagnosed.
Pregnancy and pre-urological procedure are the only asymptomatic exceptions.
explanation.pearls: New unexplained delirium in an older catheterised patient with no other localising features is not enough to diagnose CAUTI - look for a second sign (fever, pain, rigors) before starting antibiotics.

subtopic_detail: UTI in pregnancy - agent selection by gestation
stem:
A 32-year-old primigravida at 38 weeks and 2 days gestation presents to her GP with two days of dysuria and urinary frequency. She has no fever, flank pain, uterine tenderness, contractions, per-vaginal loss or reduced fetal movements. Her antenatal course has been uncomplicated, her group B streptococcus swab at 36 weeks was negative, and she has no penicillin, sulfonamide or nitrofuran allergy.

Examination is unremarkable with a soft non-tender uterus, cephalic presentation, fetal heart rate 142 bpm and normal maternal vitals. Bedside urinalysis is positive for nitrites and leucocytes. A midstream urine sample has been sent for culture. She is booked for a routine antenatal review in one week and has no immediate delivery plan.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits; fetal HR 142 bpm.
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender uterus, cephalic, no PV loss.
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis nitrites positive, leucocytes positive. MSU sent for culture. GBS swab negative at 36 weeks.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical oral antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Cefalexin 500 mg orally every 12 hours for 5 days
options.rationale: Cefalexin is the eTG-preferred oral empirical agent for cystitis in pregnancy at any gestation because it is safe throughout pregnancy and has predictable coverage of common uropathogens. A 5-day course is standard (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - UTI in pregnancy).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - UTI in pregnancy

options.text: Nitrofurantoin 100 mg orally every 6 hours for 5 days
options.rationale: Nitrofurantoin is avoided at or near term (from 38 weeks and during labour) because of the neonatal haemolytic anaemia risk if the neonate has G6PD deficiency. It is otherwise acceptable earlier in pregnancy (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook - Nitrofurantoin in pregnancy).
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook - Nitrofurantoin in pregnancy

options.text: Trimethoprim 300 mg orally daily for 3 days
options.rationale: Trimethoprim is a folate antagonist and is avoided particularly in the first trimester (neural tube defect risk) and generally throughout pregnancy when alternatives exist. Cefalexin is preferred (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook - Trimethoprim in pregnancy).
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook - Trimethoprim in pregnancy

options.text: Amoxicillin 500 mg orally every 8 hours for 5 days
options.rationale: Amoxicillin monotherapy is inadequate empirically in Australia because of high E. coli resistance; it can be used only when susceptibility is confirmed on culture (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - UTI in pregnancy).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - UTI in pregnancy

options.text: Norfloxacin 400 mg orally every 12 hours for 3 days
options.rationale: Fluoroquinolones are contraindicated in pregnancy because of fetal cartilage toxicity concerns and are not empirical options for UTI in pregnancy at any gestation (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook - Fluoroquinolones in pregnancy).
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook - Fluoroquinolones in pregnancy

explanation.summary: UTI in pregnancy requires prompt treatment because it increases risk of preterm labour, low birth weight and pyelonephritis. Cefalexin is the safe default across all gestations. Nitrofurantoin is acceptable in first and second trimesters but avoided at or near term (from about 38 weeks) due to neonatal G6PD-related haemolysis risk. Trimethoprim is avoided in the first trimester (folate antagonist) and generally when alternatives exist. Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy is also treated because of pyelonephritis and preterm birth risk.
key_points: Cefalexin 500 mg 12-hourly for 5 days is the eTG default in pregnancy.
Nitrofurantoin: avoid at term (from 38 weeks) and during labour.
Trimethoprim: avoid in first trimester (folate antagonist).
Fluoroquinolones are contraindicated in pregnancy.
Treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy - unlike non-pregnant adults.
explanation.pearls: In a woman at 38+ weeks with UTI, choose cefalexin first line - nitrofurantoin should be off the mental menu because delivery may occur during the course and the neonate is unshielded by placental folate metabolism.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - UTI in pregnancy
Australian Medicines Handbook - Nitrofurantoin in pregnancy
Australian Medicines Handbook - Trimethoprim in pregnancy
Australian Medicines Handbook - Fluoroquinolones in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Recurrent UTI - continuous prophylaxis threshold
stem:
A 42-year-old woman attends her GP for review of recurrent uncomplicated cystitis. Over the past 12 months she has had four culture-confirmed episodes, all growing E. coli sensitive to trimethoprim and nitrofurantoin, each responding promptly to a 5-day course. Between episodes she is entirely well.

She is post-menopausal since 40 following bilateral oophorectomy for BRCA1 mutation, is not on hormone therapy, and reports no vaginal dryness or dyspareunia currently. She has had a renal tract ultrasound (normal), a post-void residual scan (12 mL) and a cystoscopy performed by a urologist (normal). She drinks 2 L of fluid daily, voids post-coitally and does not use spermicides. Behavioural and hydration measures have not reduced her episode frequency. She has no penicillin, sulfa or nitrofuran allergy, eGFR is above 60 mL/min/1.73m^2 and she is not planning pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits.
data_table.Examination: No suprapubic or flank tenderness.
data_table.Investigations: Renal tract ultrasound normal, PVR 12 mL, cystoscopy normal, eGFR above 60.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continuous nitrofurantoin 50 mg orally nocte for 6 months
options.rationale: eTG recommends continuous antibiotic prophylaxis with nitrofurantoin 50 mg nocte (alternative trimethoprim 150 mg nocte) for 6 months in women with two or more UTIs in 6 months, or three or more in 12 months, unresponsive to behavioural measures. Structural workup has excluded a treatable cause (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Recurrent UTI in women).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Recurrent UTI in women

options.text: Post-coital single-dose trimethoprim 150 mg after each episode of intercourse
options.rationale: Post-coital prophylaxis is an option when UTIs are temporally linked to intercourse. Her history does not identify a coital trigger and she is post-menopausal following oophorectomy, so continuous prophylaxis is more appropriate (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Recurrent UTI in women).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Recurrent UTI in women

options.text: Self-initiated stand-by short-course trimethoprim at symptom onset
options.rationale: Patient-initiated stand-by therapy is reasonable for women who reliably recognise symptoms and prefer to avoid daily antibiotics. It does not prevent recurrence and is a step below continuous prophylaxis when frequency meets threshold (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Recurrent UTI in women).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Recurrent UTI in women

options.text: CT urogram to exclude urolithiasis and upper tract lesions
options.rationale: Advanced imaging is reserved for complicated recurrent UTI, suspected upper tract disease, non-E. coli organisms, or persistent haematuria. She has a normal ultrasound and cystoscopy, and CT would add ionising radiation without expected yield (Source: RACGP - Recurrent UTI in women).

options.text: Cranberry supplements 500 mg twice daily for 6 months as prophylaxis
options.rationale: Cranberry products have inconsistent evidence and are not recommended by eTG or RACGP as a substitute for antibiotic prophylaxis when threshold criteria are met. May be a patient adjunct but not the primary answer (Source: RACGP - Recurrent UTI in women).

explanation.summary: Recurrent UTI is defined as two episodes in 6 months or three in 12 months. Workup includes urinary tract imaging and PVR, with cystoscopy considered by urology for atypical features. Once complicating pathology is excluded, behavioural measures come first (hydration, post-coital voiding, avoiding spermicides). If insufficient, options are post-coital, patient-initiated stand-by, or continuous nightly prophylaxis for 6 months. Topical vaginal oestrogen is a strong option in post-menopausal women.
key_points: Recurrent UTI threshold: 2 in 6 months or 3 in 12 months.
Nitrofurantoin 50 mg nocte OR trimethoprim 150 mg nocte for 6 months.
Post-coital prophylaxis when temporally linked to intercourse.
Vaginal oestrogen for post-menopausal women reduces recurrence.
explanation.pearls: Vaginal oestrogen (estriol cream twice weekly) reduces UTI recurrence in post-menopausal women by roughly half - consider adding it in this patient given surgical menopause at 40.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Recurrent UTI in women

subtopic_detail: Complicated UTI in a man - workup priority
stem:
A 58-year-old man presents to his GP with a 5-day history of dysuria, urinary hesitancy and perineal ache. He has type 2 diabetes on metformin (HbA1c 51 mmol/mol) and mild lower urinary tract symptoms attributed to benign prostatic hyperplasia but is not on any prostate medication. He has not previously had a urinary tract infection.

Examination reveals a mildly tender lower abdomen. Digital rectal examination discloses a smooth, exquisitely tender prostate. He is afebrile with normal vital signs. Bedside urinalysis is positive for nitrites and leucocytes. A mid-stream urine has been sent. He has no penicillin, sulfonamide or fluoroquinolone allergy and eGFR is 78 mL/min/1.73m^2.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits.
data_table.Examination: Mild lower abdominal tenderness; DRE reveals a smooth, exquisitely tender prostate.
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis nitrites and leucocytes positive; MSU sent; eGFR 78; HbA1c 51 mmol/mol.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical oral antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Nitrofurantoin 100 mg orally every 6 hours for 7 days
options.rationale: Nitrofurantoin does not penetrate prostatic tissue and is not effective for acute bacterial prostatitis. It is restricted to lower urinary tract infection in women (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook - Nitrofurantoin).

options.text: Trimethoprim 300 mg orally daily for 5 days empirically
options.rationale: A 5-day course is the duration for uncomplicated cystitis, not acute prostatitis. Undertreated prostatitis can progress to abscess or chronic bacterial prostatitis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute prostatitis).

options.text: Cefalexin 500 mg orally every 12 hours for 7 days
options.rationale: Cephalexin has poor prostatic penetration and inadequate coverage for acute prostatitis. It is not an eTG option for this indication (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute prostatitis).

options.text: Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg orally every 12 hours for 7 days
options.rationale: Beta-lactams have poor prostatic penetration and are not first-line for acute prostatitis. eTG prefers trimethoprim, cotrimoxazole or ciprofloxacin (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute prostatitis).

options.text: Trimethoprim 300 mg orally daily for 14 days empirically
options.rationale: Acute bacterial prostatitis needs an agent with prostatic penetration and a prolonged course. eTG recommends trimethoprim 300 mg orally daily for 14 days (alternative sulfamethoxazole plus trimethoprim or ciprofloxacin) as first-line empirical therapy in men without severe features (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute prostatitis).

explanation.summary: All UTIs in men are considered complicated and require a full workup and a longer course than uncomplicated female cystitis. Acute bacterial prostatitis presents with dysuria, pelvic or perineal pain and an exquisitely tender prostate on DRE (avoid vigorous prostate massage - bacteraemia risk). Empirical eTG therapy is trimethoprim 300 mg daily, cotrimoxazole 160/800 mg 12-hourly, or ciprofloxacin 500 mg 12-hourly, all for 14 days pending culture. Severe features (sepsis, urinary retention) prompt IV therapy and admission.
key_points: All UTIs in men are complicated - always culture, always longer course.
Trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 14 days is first-line for acute prostatitis.
Avoid nitrofurantoin, cefalexin, amoxicillin - poor prostatic penetration.
Avoid vigorous DRE prostate massage in acute prostatitis - bacteraemia risk.
explanation.pearls: Chronic bacterial prostatitis (recurrent UTI in a man with the same organism) usually needs 4-6 weeks of ciprofloxacin, reflecting sustained deep prostatic clearance.

subtopic_detail: Severe pyelonephritis with sepsis - source control priority
stem:
A 66-year-old woman presents to a regional emergency department with a 12-hour history of rigors, right flank pain and vomiting. She has type 2 diabetes on metformin and had a left ureteric stone treated with ureteroscopy and stent insertion three weeks ago. The stent remains in situ. She last passed urine four hours ago and has produced 20 mL in a bedpan since arrival 90 minutes ago.

She is confused with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 13. Vital signs: HR 128, BP 82/48 (unchanged after 1 L crystalloid), RR 28, SpO2 94 percent on 2 L nasal prongs, T 39.4 C. Examination reveals right renal angle tenderness and mottled peripheries. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.28, lactate 4.8 mmol/L, bicarbonate 16 mmol/L. WCC 18.6 x10^9/L, creatinine 214 micromol/L (baseline 74), CRP 288 mg/L. Blood and urine cultures have been drawn and IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g plus a single dose of gentamicin have been given. A bedside renal ultrasound shows right-sided hydronephrosis with a dilated ureter above the retained stent.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, BP 82/48 (unchanged after 1 L fluid), RR 28, SpO2 94 percent on 2 L, T 39.4 C.
data_table.Examination: GCS 13, confused, mottled peripheries, right renal angle tenderness.
data_table.Investigations: pH 7.28, lactate 4.8 mmol/L, WCC 18.6 x10^9/L, creatinine 214 micromol/L (baseline 74), CRP 288 mg/L. Renal ultrasound: right hydronephrosis above retained ureteric stent.

lead_in: In addition to ongoing fluid resuscitation and vasopressor support, what is the most important next intervention?

options.text: Add IV vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading dose to broaden gram-positive cover empirically
options.rationale: Broadening antibiotic spectrum without source control will not reverse septic shock driven by an obstructed infected upper tract. Vancomycin is not indicated for typical urosepsis unless MRSA is suspected (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Sepsis and septic shock).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Sepsis and septic shock

options.text: Urgent urology referral for nephrostomy or stent exchange to decompress the obstruction
options.rationale: Obstructed infected upper urinary tract is a surgical emergency and source control - percutaneous nephrostomy or retrograde stent exchange - is time-critical and must not be delayed for imaging or antibiotic re-dosing. Antibiotics alone will not resolve pyonephrosis (Source: Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand - Obstructed infected kidney; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021).
source_refs: Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand - Obstructed infected kidney

options.text: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast to define the obstruction before intervention
options.rationale: The obstruction is already demonstrated on bedside ultrasound and a contrast CT will delay definitive source control by hours in a patient with vasopressor-requiring septic shock and worsening kidney function. Non-contrast CT may be arranged en route to intervention if genuinely required (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021).

options.text: IV hydrocortisone 200 mg daily as an early adjunct for relative adrenal insufficiency
options.rationale: Hydrocortisone is a Surviving Sepsis adjunct only after adequate fluids and vasopressors have failed to restore perfusion, and never replaces source control. It is not the priority in obstructed pyonephrosis (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021).

options.text: Insert a urethral catheter to monitor hourly urine output and reassess in one hour
options.rationale: A urethral catheter measures bladder output but does not decompress an obstructed upper tract above a retained ureteric stent. Delaying source control by an hour in vasopressor-requiring urosepsis worsens outcome (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021).

explanation.summary: An obstructed infected upper urinary tract - most commonly caused by a retained stone or blocked stent - is a surgical emergency. Antibiotics alone cannot penetrate an obstructed collecting system; decompression by percutaneous nephrostomy (interventional radiology) or ureteric stent exchange (urology) is the definitive intervention and must occur within hours. Source control failure is the most common reason for progression to septic shock and death in urosepsis. The Surviving Sepsis Campaign lists source control as one of the hour-1 bundle priorities.
key_points: Obstructed infected kidney = surgical emergency: source control within hours.
Percutaneous nephrostomy or retrograde stent exchange are both acceptable.
Antibiotics do not penetrate an obstructed system.
Hydrocortisone is an adjunct for refractory shock, not initial therapy.
Retained stents can become nidus for encrustation and obstruction over weeks.
explanation.pearls: Any ureteric stent left beyond its labelled dwell time (commonly 3 to 12 months) is a source-control failure waiting to happen; document stent removal or exchange dates in the discharge summary.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Sepsis and septic shock
Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand - Obstructed infected kidney

subtopic_detail: Asymptomatic bacteriuria pre-urological procedure
stem:
You are the on-call medical registrar asked to review a 74-year-old man booked for elective transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) tomorrow morning. He is being admitted overnight for pre-operative optimisation. He takes ramipril for hypertension and has no allergies.

As part of routine pre-operative screening, his midstream urine collected in clinic yesterday has returned this evening growing greater than 10^5 CFU/mL Enterococcus faecalis, susceptible to amoxicillin and vancomycin. He is asymptomatic - no dysuria, frequency, suprapubic pain, flank pain or fever. He does not have an indwelling catheter. His inflammatory markers, renal function and vital signs are within normal limits, and he is not immunosuppressed or pregnant (male). The urology team has asked for your input on antibiotics before he goes to theatre.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits.
data_table.Examination: Asymptomatic, no suprapubic or flank tenderness, no catheter.
data_table.Investigations: Preoperative MSU: Enterococcus faecalis greater than 10^5 CFU/mL, susceptible to amoxicillin and vancomycin. WCC, CRP, creatinine within normal limits.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Proceed to surgery with the standard cefazolin skin-prophylaxis dose at induction only
options.rationale: Standard skin-flora surgical prophylaxis is inadequate when a resistant or specifically identified uropathogen is known to be present pre-operatively. Manipulation of infected urothelium risks bacteraemia and sepsis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Surgical prophylaxis; Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand).

options.text: Defer surgery indefinitely until repeat urine cultures are sterile on two occasions
options.rationale: Indefinite deferral is not required. Treatment targeted to the identified organism starting shortly before the procedure is sufficient; sterilisation of urine over multiple cultures is not the standard (Source: IDSA - Asymptomatic Bacteriuria (2019)).

options.text: Give a single dose of oral amoxicillin 1 g at the time of surgery only, no other cover
options.rationale: A single oral dose does not provide reliable peri-operative tissue and urine concentrations and does not treat the underlying bacteriuria. IV targeted therapy starting shortly before the procedure is preferred (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Surgical prophylaxis).

options.text: Give targeted IV amoxicillin 2 g at induction with a short peri-operative course
options.rationale: Asymptomatic bacteriuria should NOT normally be treated - the two exceptions are pregnancy and before a urological procedure with mucosal trauma (such as TURP). eTG and IDSA recommend targeted therapy based on the identified organism starting shortly before the procedure, with continuation only for the peri-operative period (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Surgical prophylaxis; IDSA - Asymptomatic Bacteriuria (2019)).

options.text: Give IV vancomycin 25 mg/kg at induction to broaden enterococcal cover empirically
options.rationale: Vancomycin is reserved for vancomycin-resistant enterococcus or beta-lactam allergy. This isolate is amoxicillin-susceptible and vancomycin adds nothing but ecological cost and nephrotoxicity risk (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Surgical prophylaxis).

explanation.summary: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is normally not treated because it does not improve outcomes and drives resistance. The two accepted exceptions are pregnancy (risk of pyelonephritis and preterm labour) and before a urological procedure that breaches mucosa (TURP, ureteroscopy, prostate biopsy). In both scenarios, targeted therapy based on the identified organism replaces empirical prophylaxis. For TURP, IV targeted therapy at induction plus a short peri-operative course is the eTG and IDSA-endorsed approach.
key_points: Treat asymptomatic bacteriuria only in: pregnancy or before urological mucosal-breach procedures.
Target therapy to the identified organism, not generic prophylaxis.
Standard cefazolin skin prophylaxis alone is inadequate when a known uropathogen exists.
Prostate biopsy prophylaxis is separately covered by eTG - targeted to prior rectal swab organisms.
Vancomycin is reserved for VRE or true beta-lactam allergy.
explanation.pearls: For trans-rectal prostate biopsy, current AU practice is a peri-procedural augmented regimen guided by pre-procedure rectal swab or targeted culture (given rising fluoroquinolone resistance in E. coli) - not routine ciprofloxacin monotherapy.

sources.label: Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand

subtopic_detail: Warfarin reversal high INR no bleed
stem:
A 68-year-old man on warfarin for a mechanical mitral valve presents with a routine INR check showing 8.4. He has no bleeding, no bruising, and reports no recent medication changes but did complete a 5 day course of clarithromycin last week for a chest infection. His last INR 3 weeks ago was 2.6.

He is haemodynamically stable and fully asymptomatic. His usual warfarin dose is 4 mg daily. There is no easy bruising on skin examination, no gastrointestinal bleeding, and no haematuria.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78, BP 138/82, RR 14, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temp 36.6 C
data_table.Investigations: INR 8.4 today (was 2.6 three weeks ago); Hb 138 g/L (130-170); platelets 264 x10^9/L (150-400); creatinine 96 micromol/L (60-110)
data_table.Medications: Warfarin 4 mg daily; recent 5 day clarithromycin course completed last week

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management now?

options.text: Withhold warfarin only and recheck INR in 24 hours without vitamin K with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: At INR over 8 without bleeding, oral vitamin K reduces bleeding risk more reliably than withholding alone, without creating warfarin resistance if the dose is kept low (1 to 2 mg). Withholding alone is used for INR 5 to 8 without bleeding. (Source: eTG complete: Warfarin reversal)

options.text: Withhold warfarin and give oral vitamin K1 (phytomenadione) 1 to 2 mg with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: For INR over 8 without bleeding, the AMH/eTG recommendation is to withhold warfarin and give low-dose oral vitamin K (1 to 2 mg) to bring INR into range within 24 hours without causing warfarin resistance. Higher doses (5 mg or more) or IV vitamin K risk over-reversal and make re-anticoagulation difficult, particularly important in mechanical valves. (Source: eTG complete: Warfarin reversal)

options.text: Withhold warfarin and give prothrombin complex concentrate (Prothrombinex-VF) 25 IU per kg IV
options.rationale: PCC is reserved for major bleeding or urgent surgical need, not asymptomatic supra-therapeutic INR. It carries thromboembolic risk which is particularly relevant in a mechanical valve. (Source: eTG complete: Warfarin reversal)

options.text: Withhold warfarin and give vitamin K1 10 mg intravenously slowly with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: IV vitamin K at 10 mg over-reverses the anticoagulation and leaves the mechanical valve unprotected; it also creates warfarin resistance for days. Reserved for major bleeding. (Source: eTG complete: Warfarin reversal)

options.text: Fresh frozen plasma 15 mL per kg intravenously over 30 minutes with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: FFP is not indicated for asymptomatic supra-therapeutic INR; it carries transfusion risks and takes hours to correct INR. Reserved for major bleeding when PCC is unavailable. (Source: eTG complete: Warfarin reversal)

explanation.summary: Warfarin reversal strategy is tiered by INR and bleeding. INR 4.5 to 10 without bleeding: withhold warfarin, consider oral vitamin K 1 to 2 mg if additional risk. INR over 10 without bleeding: withhold warfarin, oral vitamin K 3 to 5 mg. Any major bleed at any INR: PCC 25 to 50 IU per kg plus IV vitamin K 5 to 10 mg. Mechanical valves require avoidance of over-reversal because sub-therapeutic INR is a stroke risk.
key_points: INR over 8 no bleeding: withhold warfarin plus oral vitamin K 1 to 2 mg
Major bleeding at any INR: PCC 25 to 50 IU per kg IV plus IV vitamin K
Avoid IV vitamin K 10 mg in mechanical valve unless bleeding - risk of over-reversal
Clarithromycin (and other macrolides) is a well-known warfarin interaction
explanation.pearls: Small oral vitamin K (1 to 2 mg) works within 24 hours without making warfarin resistant - the trap is the 10 mg IV dose that leaves a mechanical valve unprotected.

subtopic_detail: Type B dissection BP control
stem:
A 58-year-old man presents with 2 hours of sudden severe tearing chest pain radiating to his back and left arm. CT aortogram confirms an acute type B (descending) aortic dissection extending from just distal to the left subclavian to the infra-renal aorta. He is haemodynamically stable with no end-organ malperfusion.

On examination he has equal radial pulses, no focal neurology, and no abdominal pain. Renal function is normal, urine output preserved, and there is no leg ischaemia. He has a normal chest examination.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, BP 178/98 (right arm) 176/96 (left arm), RR 18, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temp 36.7 C
data_table.Investigations: Troponin 12 ng/L (<14); creatinine 82 micromol/L (60-110); Hb 138 g/L (130-170); D-dimer 4200 ng/mL
data_table.Imaging: CT aortogram: acute type B dissection from left subclavian to infra-renal aorta; no malperfusion; no rupture; no pericardial effusion

lead_in: What are the target heart rate and systolic blood pressure over the next 20 minutes?

options.text: Heart rate under 60 and systolic BP under 140 mmHg using metoprolol 5 mg IV single dose only
options.rationale: A single 5 mg IV bolus of metoprolol will not achieve sustained impulse control; ongoing infusion of esmolol or labetalol is required. Systolic under 140 is too permissive - the target is 100 to 120 mmHg. (Source: eTG complete: Aortic dissection)

options.text: Heart rate under 100 and systolic BP under 160 mmHg using IV GTN monotherapy
options.rationale: GTN monotherapy causes reflex tachycardia and increases dP/dt; heart rate under 100 is too permissive and misses the impulse control target that is the core physiological rationale. (Source: eTG complete: Aortic dissection)

options.text: Heart rate under 60 and systolic BP under 100 mmHg using nifedipine IR sublingual
options.rationale: Sublingual nifedipine has unpredictable BP effect and no rate control; BP under 100 systolic risks under-perfusion of dissection branch vessels. Not a first-line agent in aortic dissection. (Source: eTG complete: Aortic dissection)

options.text: No BP target - proceed straight to endovascular repair (TEVAR) with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Uncomplicated type B dissection is managed medically; TEVAR is reserved for complicated type B (rupture, malperfusion, refractory pain, refractory hypertension despite maximal medical therapy, false lumen expansion). Bypassing medical therapy exposes to procedural risk without indication. (Source: eTG complete: Aortic dissection)

options.text: Heart rate under 60 and systolic BP 100 to 120 mmHg using IV esmolol or labetalol first
options.rationale: Acute type B dissection is managed medically with impulse control - heart rate under 60 and systolic BP 100 to 120 mmHg to reduce dP/dt (rate of pressure rise). Beta blockade is given first (esmolol or labetalol) to blunt the reflex tachycardia from vasodilators; nitroprusside or GTN is added second for residual BP. Starting with pure vasodilator alone causes reflex tachycardia and worsens shear stress. (Source: eTG complete: Aortic dissection)

explanation.summary: Acute type B aortic dissection is managed medically with rigorous impulse control - HR under 60 and SBP 100 to 120 mmHg - to reduce dP/dt and shear stress on the false lumen. Beta blockade goes first (esmolol infusion or labetalol) and vasodilator (nitroprusside or GTN) is added after rate control to avoid reflex tachycardia. TEVAR is reserved for complicated dissection.
key_points: Type B uncomplicated: medical impulse control HR under 60 and SBP 100 to 120
Beta blocker before vasodilator to avoid reflex tachycardia and increased dP/dt
TEVAR for complicated type B: rupture, malperfusion, refractory pain or BP, expansion
Type A always for surgery
explanation.pearls: The core physiology in dissection BP control is dP/dt - starting a vasodilator without a beta blocker raises shear stress even as BP drops.

subtopic_detail: MTP activation criteria
stem:
A 44-year-old man is brought in by ambulance after being struck by a car. He has an obvious pelvic fracture and blood at the meatus. Prehospital he has received 1 L of crystalloid and 1 unit of O-negative packed red cells.

On arrival he is peripherally shut down with cold pale extremities. Abdomen is distended and tender. FAST scan shows free fluid in the abdomen.
