Ongoing bleeding is estimated at 250 mL per 5 minutes based on his chest drain and pelvic external stabiliser output. His last recorded systolic pressure was 78 despite ongoing resuscitation.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, BP 78/44, RR 32, SpO2 96 percent on non-rebreather, temp 35.2 C
data_table.Investigations: Hb 68 g/L (130-170); platelets 92 x10^9/L (150-400); INR 1.8 (0.9-1.2); fibrinogen 1.4 g/L (2-4); pH 7.18, base excess -12, lactate 9.4 mmol/L, ionised calcium 0.92 mmol/L (1.10-1.30)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Withhold platelets until count drops below 50 x10^9/L and give red cells only
options.rationale: In active haemorrhage MTP uses empiric 1:1:1 including platelets; waiting for the count to drop below 50 accepts avoidable dilutional coagulopathy and worsens outcome. (Source: NBA Massive Transfusion Protocol template)

options.text: Transfuse further packed red cells only until Hb is over 100, then reassess coagulation
options.rationale: Isolated red cell transfusion without FFP, platelets and cryoprecipitate creates a dilutional coagulopathy on top of the trauma-induced coagulopathy. The 1:1:1 ratio is the AU standard for major haemorrhage in trauma. (Source: NBA Massive Transfusion Protocol template)

options.text: Prothrombin complex concentrate (Prothrombinex-VF) 50 IU per kg IV as the first blood product
options.rationale: PCC is reserved for warfarin reversal or bleeding on DOAC (specific to factor Xa inhibitor bleeding); it is not standard in trauma-induced coagulopathy where FFP and cryoprecipitate are preferred and target multiple factor deficiencies. (Source: NBA Massive Transfusion Protocol template)

options.text: Activate the massive transfusion protocol with 1:1:1 packed red cells, FFP, and platelets
options.rationale: He meets ABC score and shock-index criteria for MTP activation: ongoing haemorrhage, shock, coagulopathy (INR 1.8, low fibrinogen, thrombocytopenia), acidosis and hypocalcaemia. NBA guideline for MTP is 1:1:1 red cells : FFP : platelets, with early cryoprecipitate for fibrinogen under 1.5, TXA within 3 hours of injury, and IV calcium for hypocalcaemia from citrate. (Source: NBA Massive Transfusion Protocol template)

options.text: Recombinant factor VIIa 90 mcg per kg IV as first-line for uncontrolled haemorrhage
options.rationale: Recombinant VIIa is a last-resort agent with thromboembolic risk; it is not first-line and never a substitute for balanced blood product resuscitation. NBA guidance restricts it to specialist decision. (Source: NBA Massive Transfusion Protocol template)

explanation.summary: Trauma major haemorrhage triggers MTP - 1:1:1 red cells : FFP : platelets with early cryoprecipitate for fibrinogen under 1.5, TXA 1 g IV within 3 hours (repeat at 8 h), and IV calcium for citrate-related hypocalcaemia. Isolated red cell transfusion creates dilutional coagulopathy; VIIa is a last-resort agent, not a first choice.
key_points: MTP triggers: ABC score, shock index over 1, ongoing haemorrhage, coagulopathy
Balanced ratio 1:1:1 red cells : FFP : platelets
Cryoprecipitate for fibrinogen under 1.5 g/L; TXA within 3 h
IV calcium for citrate-induced hypocalcaemia during large transfusion
explanation.pearls: Hypocalcaemia from citrate is under-recognised in massive transfusion - give calcium empirically after 4 units of blood or if ionised calcium is under 1.1.

sources.label: CRASH-2 trial for TXA in trauma

subtopic_detail: Necrotising fasciitis vs cellulitis
stem:
A 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents to your ED with 24 hours of pain out of proportion to physical findings in his right calf. The skin over the area looks like mild cellulitis with faint erythema. He is systemically unwell.

On examination there is faint erythema over the medial calf, exquisite tenderness on light palpation extending well beyond the area of erythema, a small area of dusky skin at the medial malleolus, and reduced sensation over the medial ankle. There is no wound of entry visible. Pedal pulses are palpable.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 122, BP 96/58, RR 26, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temp 38.7 C
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22.4 x10^9/L (4-11); CRP 260 mg/L (<5); sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145); glucose 16.8 mmol/L; creatinine 168 micromol/L (60-110); Hb 118 g/L (130-170); lactate 4.2 mmol/L
data_table.Imaging: Bedside soft tissue ultrasound shows fascial thickening and small gas bubbles

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: IV flucloxacillin 2 g every 6 hours and elevate the limb, review at 4 hours
options.rationale: Flucloxacillin monotherapy under-covers gram-negative and anaerobic organisms in necrotising fasciitis; waiting 4 hours delays the required surgical control that dominates mortality reduction. Cellulitis is not the diagnosis here. (Source: eTG complete: Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections)
source_refs: eTG complete: Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections

options.text: Urgent surgical exploration with debridement plus empirical IV meropenem plus clindamycin
options.rationale: Necrotising fasciitis requires urgent surgical debridement within 6 hours - the pain-out-of-proportion, dusky skin, reduced sensation (nerve necrosis), high LRINEC score, and fascial gas on ultrasound are all supportive. Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics per eTG include meropenem plus clindamycin (for exotoxin suppression) plus vancomycin (for MRSA cover). Antibiotics do not substitute for surgical control. (Source: eTG complete: Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections)
source_refs: eTG complete: Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections

options.text: IV ceftriaxone plus metronidazole and MRI to confirm before considering surgery
options.rationale: MRI delays surgery in a time-critical infection where clinical and bedside imaging findings are already diagnostic; every hour of delay increases mortality. Ceftriaxone plus metronidazole is not the AU empirical regimen for necrotising fasciitis. (Source: eTG complete: Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections)
source_refs: eTG complete: Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections

options.text: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy first, then antibiotics and involve senior review
options.rationale: Hyperbaric oxygen is an adjunct after surgical debridement and antibiotics have been initiated; it is not the first-line intervention and is not universally recommended. Delay for HBO would be catastrophic. (Source: eTG complete: Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections)
source_refs: eTG complete: Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections

options.text: Bedside incision and drainage at the point of maximal tenderness and admission for observation
options.rationale: Bedside I and D does not achieve the wide operative debridement required and may worsen sepsis by opening the plane without full source control. Definitive theatre-based debridement is mandatory. (Source: eTG complete: Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections)
source_refs: eTG complete: Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections

explanation.summary: Necrotising soft tissue infection kills through delay - the surgical debridement window is 6 hours. Clues that shift the diagnosis from cellulitis are pain-out-of-proportion, tenderness beyond erythema, dusky skin, sensory loss (nerve necrosis), high LRINEC, and fascial gas or fluid on imaging. Empirical antibiotics per eTG are meropenem plus clindamycin plus vancomycin.
key_points: Pain out of proportion, sensory loss, and dusky skin are the necrotising red flags
LRINEC 6 or more is intermediate risk; 8 or more is high risk
Surgical debridement within 6 hours is the mortality lever, not the antibiotic
AU empirical regimen: meropenem plus clindamycin plus vancomycin
explanation.pearls: The LRINEC score misses about a third of confirmed cases - if the clinical picture screams necrotising, do not let a low score reassure you.

sources.label: eTG complete: Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections

subtopic_detail: Type A dissection surgical
stem:
A 46-year-old man with a family history of connective tissue disease presents with sudden tearing chest pain radiating between the shoulder blades. He is normotensive but pale and diaphoretic. CT aortogram shows an intimal flap involving the ascending aorta extending into the descending aorta with a small pericardial effusion measuring 8 mm.

On examination his right radial pulse is diminished compared to the left and there is a diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge. He has no focal neurology and no leg ischaemia. Bedside echocardiogram shows no tamponade physiology but confirms the pericardial fluid.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 108, BP 118/68 (right arm) 138/80 (left arm), RR 22, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temp 36.9 C
data_table.Investigations: Troponin 12 ng/L (<14); creatinine 88 micromol/L (60-110); Hb 132 g/L (130-170); D-dimer 6800 ng/mL
data_table.Imaging: CT aortogram: intimal flap from just above aortic root into descending aorta; 8 mm pericardial effusion; no rupture; visible root involvement
data_table.Echo: Aortic regurgitation moderate; pericardial fluid 8 mm without tamponade

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Immediate cardiothoracic surgical repair of the ascending aorta with cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Involvement of the ascending aorta (Stanford type A) is a surgical emergency because of risk of proximal extension into pericardium (tamponade), coronary arteries (MI) and aortic regurgitation. Perioperative medical management still requires impulse control - HR under 60 and SBP 100 to 120 mmHg via beta blockade first. Delaying for medical management alone is not sufficient for type A. (Source: eTG complete: Aortic dissection)

options.text: Medical management with IV labetalol and IV nitroprusside targeting SBP 100 to 120 mmHg
options.rationale: Medical management alone is the strategy for uncomplicated type B (descending), not for type A (ascending). Type A has 1 percent per hour mortality without surgery. Delaying repair for medical control alone would be fatal. (Source: eTG complete: Aortic dissection)

options.text: Thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) as first-line with cardiac monitoring in place
options.rationale: TEVAR is used for descending aortic dissection (type B) with complications. It cannot address the ascending aorta or the root without special hybrid procedures; open surgical repair is the standard for type A. (Source: eTG complete: Aortic dissection)

options.text: Emergency pericardiocentesis and admit to CCU on IV nitrate infusion with cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: There is no tamponade physiology so pericardiocentesis is not indicated; pericardiocentesis in a dissecting aorta can worsen bleeding into the pericardium by relieving tamponade tamponade. Nitrate infusion without beta blockade would worsen dP/dt. (Source: eTG complete: Aortic dissection)

options.text: Aspirin 300 mg plus ticagrelor 180 mg for presumed acute coronary syndrome
options.rationale: Antiplatelet loading is contraindicated in aortic dissection - it increases bleeding risk into the false lumen and pericardium. Troponin is not elevated and imaging shows a dissection, not ACS. (Source: eTG complete: Aortic dissection)

explanation.summary: Type A aortic dissection involves the ascending aorta and is a surgical emergency because of proximal extension into pericardium, coronaries and aortic valve. Untreated mortality is 1 percent per hour; open surgical repair is life-saving. Perioperative medical management still targets HR under 60 and SBP 100 to 120 mmHg via beta blockade first. Type B (descending only) is managed medically unless complicated.
key_points: Stanford type A: involves ascending aorta - open surgical repair
Stanford type B: descending only - medical impulse control, TEVAR if complicated
Medical impulse control still applies pre-op for both: HR under 60, SBP 100 to 120
Antiplatelets and pericardiocentesis are contraindicated in a dissecting aorta
explanation.pearls: Even in type A the pre-theatre plan is beta blockade first - vasodilator alone would raise dP/dt and worsen the tear before the surgeon arrives.

subtopic_detail: Sepsis hour-1 bundle
stem:
A 74-year-old woman is admitted from a nursing home with 24 hours of confusion, fever and reduced urine output. She has a chronic indwelling urinary catheter for outlet obstruction. She is on metformin for diabetes and no other regular medications.

On examination she is drowsy, has warm peripheries with a wide pulse pressure, and mottling of her thighs. Her catheter bag has cloudy foul-smelling urine. Chest is clear and abdomen is soft with suprapubic tenderness. She weighs approximately 60 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118 sinus tachycardia, BP 88/38, RR 26, SpO2 96 percent on 2 L nasal prongs, temp 39.4 C
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22.6 x10^9/L (4-11); CRP 320 mg/L (<5); creatinine 218 micromol/L (baseline 78; 60-110); urea 18 mmol/L (2.5-7.5); lactate 4.6 mmol/L (<2); glucose 12.4 mmol/L; VBG pH 7.28; procalcitonin pending
data_table.Catheter urine: Cloudy foul-smelling; leucocyte esterase positive; nitrite positive; microscopy pending

lead_in: What is the correct sequence of actions in the first hour?

options.text: IV normal saline 30 mL per kg over 3 hours, wait for cultures before antibiotics
options.rationale: Antibiotic delay in septic shock is associated with increased mortality (up to 7 percent per hour). Cultures should not gate antibiotic timing - obtain cultures but give antibiotics within an hour of recognition. (Source: eTG complete: Sepsis and septic shock)
source_refs: eTG complete: Sepsis and septic shock

options.text: Blood cultures, arterial or venous lactate, then IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g
options.rationale: The Surviving Sepsis one-hour bundle applied in AU practice: obtain cultures before antibiotics (do not delay antibiotics more than 45 min), broad-spectrum antibiotics targeted to source (piperacillin-tazobactam plus gentamicin for urinary sepsis with sepsis physiology per eTG), 30 mL per kg crystalloid, lactate measurement, and noradrenaline if MAP under 65 after fluid resuscitation. Source control via catheter change is part of care. (Source: eTG complete: Sepsis and septic shock)
source_refs: eTG complete: Sepsis and septic shock

options.text: Empirical IV ceftriaxone 1 g plus oral metronidazole and 500 mL saline bolus, review in 6 hours
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone plus metronidazole under-covers Pseudomonas and enterococci in a catheter-associated urinary sepsis from a nursing home; oral metronidazole in a hypotensive patient is unpredictable in absorption. Fluid volume of 500 mL is insufficient; 30 mL per kg (about 1.8 L for 60 kg) is the initial target. (Source: eTG complete: Sepsis and septic shock)
source_refs: eTG complete: Sepsis and septic shock

options.text: Vasopressor infusion first via peripheral IV, then antibiotics, then cultures
options.rationale: Vasopressor before adequate fluid resuscitation is generally inappropriate; noradrenaline is added when MAP remains under 65 after fluid resuscitation. Skipping cultures forfeits pathogen data used to narrow therapy. (Source: eTG complete: Sepsis and septic shock)
source_refs: eTG complete: Sepsis and septic shock

options.text: Broad-spectrum antibiotics alone (piperacillin-tazobactam) without cultures, IV fluids or vasopressor
options.rationale: Antibiotic monotherapy without fluid resuscitation and cultures loses the physiological rescue components of the bundle. The AU one-hour bundle demands cultures, lactate, fluids, antibiotics, and vasopressor as a coordinated set. (Source: eTG complete: Sepsis and septic shock)
source_refs: eTG complete: Sepsis and septic shock

explanation.summary: AU sepsis management uses the one-hour bundle: obtain cultures without delaying antibiotics past 45 min, give broad-spectrum antibiotics matched to source, measure lactate, start 30 mL per kg crystalloid, and add noradrenaline if MAP under 65 after fluid. For catheter-associated urinary sepsis with shock, eTG recommends piperacillin-tazobactam plus gentamicin (single-dose aminoglycoside to cover Pseudomonas and gram-negatives). Source control includes catheter change.
key_points: One-hour bundle: cultures, lactate, antibiotics, fluid 30 mL per kg, vasopressor if MAP under 65 after fluid
Do not delay antibiotics for cultures past 45 min - each hour of delay increases mortality
Catheter-associated urosepsis with shock: piperacillin-tazobactam plus single-dose gentamicin
Source control (catheter change) is part of care, not optional
explanation.pearls: Antibiotic timing dominates mortality in septic shock - the target is under 45 minutes for the first dose.

sources.label: eTG complete: Sepsis and septic shock

subtopic_detail: LV free wall rupture post-MI
stem:
A 68-year-old woman who presented 6 days ago with an anterior STEMI treated with primary PCI is on the coronary care unit. She has been mobilising well since day 3. At 4 am the nurse calls you because she suddenly becomes short of breath and hypotensive.

On arrival she looks unwell, has muffled heart sounds and is peripherally shut down. Jugular venous pressure is grossly elevated with y-descent absent. Bedside echocardiogram shows a large pericardial effusion with right ventricular diastolic collapse. There is no new ST-segment shift on ECG and CXR shows a modest widening of the cardiac silhouette compared with the film from 24 hours ago.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, BP 68/40, RR 30, SpO2 92 percent on 15 L non-rebreather, temp 36.9 C
data_table.Investigations: Troponin 8200 ng/L (on downtrend from admission peak 45 000); Hb 96 g/L (was 118 yesterday); creatinine 108 micromol/L; INR 1.1; lactate 5.8 mmol/L; ECG anterior Q waves, no new ST shift
data_table.Medications: Aspirin 100 mg; ticagrelor 90 mg BD; atorvastatin 80 mg; ramipril 5 mg; bisoprolol 5 mg
data_table.Echo: Large pericardial effusion with RV diastolic collapse; regional wall motion abnormalities consistent with old anterior infarct; no ventricular septal defect visualised

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management?

options.text: Recurrent stent thrombosis - repeat coronary angiography and PCI and repeat as clinically indicated
options.rationale: Recurrent stent thrombosis presents with new ST elevation and rising troponin; her troponin is on downtrend and ECG shows no new ST shift. The tamponade physiology and falling Hb identify a mechanical complication rather than acute reinfarction. (Source: eTG complete: Post-MI mechanical complications)

options.text: Dressler syndrome - high dose aspirin and NSAIDs with colchicine, admit for observation and involve senior review
options.rationale: Dressler syndrome typically occurs 2 to 6 weeks post-MI with pleuritic chest pain, low-grade fever, small pericardial effusion without tamponade, and inflammatory markers up. This patient has tamponade physiology, falling Hb and is 6 days post-MI, which fits free wall rupture rather than post-cardiac injury pericarditis. (Source: eTG complete: Post-MI mechanical complications)

options.text: Post-MI ventricular septal defect - emergency surgery after intra-aortic balloon pump insertion
options.rationale: Post-MI VSD produces a new pan-systolic murmur with left-to-right shunt on echo colour flow, not a pericardial effusion with tamponade. Falling Hb into the pericardial space is not the VSD pattern. (Source: eTG complete: Post-MI mechanical complications)

options.text: Papillary muscle rupture - emergency mitral valve surgery and repeat as clinically indicated
options.rationale: Papillary muscle rupture causes acute severe mitral regurgitation with pulmonary oedema and a new murmur but not typically a large pericardial effusion. The echo pattern here is compressive pericardial effusion, not acute MR. (Source: eTG complete: Post-MI mechanical complications)

options.text: Left ventricular free wall rupture with cardiac tamponade - emergency cardiac surgery for pericardial evacuation
options.rationale: Sub-acute LV free wall rupture typically presents 3 to 7 days post-MI with tamponade physiology (JVP up, y-descent absent, hypotension, RV diastolic collapse on echo) and a falling haemoglobin without external bleeding. Definitive treatment is emergency surgical repair; pericardiocentesis can transiently relieve tamponade but reduces the compressive haemostasis and risks accelerated rebleeding. Antiplatelet load and dual antiplatelet therapy amplify the risk. (Source: eTG complete: Post-MI mechanical complications)

explanation.summary: Sub-acute LV free wall rupture is the leading post-MI mechanical complication at day 3 to 7 in a patient with a completed transmural infarct. It presents with sudden cardiovascular collapse and tamponade physiology (JVP elevation with absent y-descent, hypotension, RV diastolic collapse), often with a falling haemoglobin as blood accumulates in the pericardium. Definitive treatment is emergency surgical repair; pericardiocentesis is a bridge only, and DAPT amplifies bleeding risk.
key_points: Free wall rupture typically day 3 to 7 post-MI; peaks in transmural infarcts
Tamponade physiology plus falling Hb without external bleeding is the fingerprint
Emergency surgical repair is definitive; pericardiocentesis is temporising
Dressler syndrome is weeks later and rarely causes tamponade
explanation.pearls: A falling Hb into a growing pericardial effusion at day 6 post-MI is the free wall rupture story - pericardiocentesis alone lets the tamponade tamponade lose its haemostatic role.

subtopic_detail: Warfarin reversal in life-threatening bleeding
stem:
A 72-year-old man on warfarin for atrial fibrillation with a CHA2DS2-VA of 4 presents to your regional emergency department with 2 hours of a sudden severe headache with vomiting and left sided weakness. He last took his warfarin 12 hours ago. He has no history of hepatic impairment. He usually runs an INR between 2.0 and 3.0.

On arrival he is GCS 12 with dysarthria, a left facial droop, and left arm 3/5 power. A non-contrast CT head confirms a 5 cm right basal ganglia intracerebral haemorrhage with 4 mm of midline shift. Blood pressure is 178/104 and haemodynamics are otherwise stable. IV access has been secured. He is nil by mouth pending neurosurgery review.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82 irregular, BP 178/104, RR 18, SpO2 98% on room air, temp 36.8 C, GCS 12
data_table.Examination: Alert to voice; dysarthria; left facial droop; left arm 3/5 power; leg 4/5; no meningism; pupils equal and reactive
data_table.Investigations: INR 3.2; APTT 42 seconds; haemoglobin 132 g/L; platelets 220 x10^9/L; fibrinogen 3.4 g/L; sodium 140 potassium 4.2 creatinine 96; CT head as described

lead_in: What is the most appropriate reversal regimen?

options.text: Vitamin K 10 milligrams intravenously alone with hourly INR monitoring for the next 4 hours before considering further reversal treatment
options.rationale: Vitamin K alone takes 6-12 hours to lower INR meaningfully and does not immediately restore clotting factors; in life-threatening bleeding, prothrombinex is needed to achieve factor replacement within minutes. Vitamin K must still be given but as an adjunct, not sole therapy. (Source: NBA Warfarin reversal guideline)

options.text: Prothrombinex-VF 50 international units per kilogram intravenously plus vitamin K 5 to 10 milligrams intravenously with repeat INR at 30 minutes
options.rationale: NBA Australian warfarin reversal for life-threatening bleeding (including intracerebral haemorrhage) is prothrombinex-VF 50 IU/kg IV (weight-banded in some protocols) plus vitamin K 5-10 mg IV, with repeat INR at 30 minutes; add fresh frozen plasma 150-300 mL if prothrombinex is unavailable or if the INR remains elevated. (Source: NBA Warfarin reversal guideline)

options.text: Fresh frozen plasma 15 millilitres per kilogram alone without prothrombinex and vitamin K 1 milligram orally with repeat INR at 6 hours
options.rationale: FFP alone requires 4-6 units for adequate factor replacement, has slower onset than prothrombinex, and carries greater volume load; prothrombinex is preferred first-line in AU practice. Oral vitamin K is not appropriate in life-threatening bleeding. (Source: NBA Warfarin reversal guideline)

options.text: Recombinant factor VIIa 90 micrograms per kilogram intravenously as the primary reversal agent given the intracranial haemorrhage
options.rationale: Recombinant factor VIIa is not in the NBA warfarin reversal pathway; it carries substantial thrombotic risk and is not indicated for warfarin reversal. Prothrombinex plus vitamin K is the AU first-line for life-threatening warfarin-related bleeding. (Source: NBA Warfarin reversal guideline)

options.text: Idarucizumab 5 grams intravenously in two 2.5 gram doses as immediate specific reversal agent for the anticoagulant effect
options.rationale: Idarucizumab is a specific dabigatran reversal agent, not warfarin. Using it for warfarin gives no reversal effect and delays appropriate prothrombinex plus vitamin K administration. (Source: NBA Warfarin reversal guideline)

explanation.summary: This is warfarin-related intracerebral haemorrhage requiring immediate reversal. The NBA Australian pathway for life-threatening bleeding on warfarin is prothrombinex-VF 50 IU/kg IV plus vitamin K 5-10 mg IV, with repeat INR at 30 minutes; FFP is added if prothrombinex is unavailable or if INR remains elevated. Vitamin K alone is too slow, FFP alone has slower onset and volume risk, recombinant factor VIIa is not indicated for warfarin, and idarucizumab is specific to dabigatran.
key_points: NBA warfarin reversal (life-threatening bleed): prothrombinex-VF 50 IU/kg IV plus vitamin K 5-10 mg IV
Repeat INR at 30 minutes and re-dose if needed
FFP is second-line or add-on, not first-line in Australia
Idarucizumab is dabigatran reversal, not warfarin
explanation.pearls: For any warfarin-related intracranial haemorrhage, prothrombinex 50 IU/kg plus vitamin K 5-10 mg IV within 30 minutes is your target; do not spend the first hour on FFP alone.

subtopic_detail: Sepsis hour-1 bundle sequencing
stem:
A 64-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease stage 3 presents to your district hospital emergency department with 2 days of increasing dysuria, frank haematuria, and 6 hours of rigors. She had a right ureteric stent placed 3 weeks ago for an obstructing stone. She has been drinking 3 litres of water daily.

On arrival she is drowsy but rousable and haemodynamically compromised. Her right renal angle is tender. There is no rash. IV access has been secured with an 18 gauge cannula. The nurse has just returned from taking blood cultures and a serum lactate. Vital signs and gas results have just come back.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, BP 84/48 (MAP 60), RR 28, SpO2 96% on room air, temp 38.9 C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable; mottled peripheries with capillary refill 4 seconds; right renal angle tender; abdomen soft; no rash
data_table.Investigations: Venous gas pH 7.28 lactate 4.6 mmol/L base excess -8; white cell count 21 x10^9/L neutrophils 18; creatinine 168 micromol/L (baseline 130); urinalysis nitrites and leucocytes positive; bedside urine microscopy pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give a 30 millilitre per kilogram Hartmann's bolus over 30 minutes and commence peripheral noradrenaline 10 micrograms per minute immediately before starting antibiotics
options.rationale: Vasopressors are added when MAP remains under 65 despite adequate fluid resuscitation, not started before antibiotics. Antibiotic priority in the first hour is paramount for shock outcomes. (Source: Surviving Sepsis 2021 / eTG Antibiotic)

options.text: Give a 30 millilitre per kilogram crystalloid bolus over 3 hours first then administer intravenous ceftriaxone 2 grams once the bolus is completed
options.rationale: Delaying antibiotics for 3 hours is inconsistent with the hour-1 bundle, which mandates antibiotics within 1 hour of shock recognition. Fluid and antibiotics run in parallel, not sequentially. Ceftriaxone monotherapy also under-covers resistant post-stent flora. (Source: Surviving Sepsis 2021 / eTG Antibiotic)

options.text: Give intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 grams plus gentamicin 5 milligrams per kilogram now followed by a 30 millilitre per kilogram crystalloid bolus over 3 hours
options.rationale: Surviving Sepsis hour-1 bundle: give broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour of septic shock recognition, and start a 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus for hypotension or lactate above 4. Piperacillin-tazobactam plus gentamicin covers Gram-negative and Gram-positive urosepsis and the resistant flora often present after a recent stent. Vasopressors are added if MAP under 65 after fluid. (Source: Surviving Sepsis 2021 / eTG Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange urgent CT KUB and defer antibiotic administration until obstruction is confirmed and urology has assessed for immediate stent revision
options.rationale: Imaging is important to identify source control needs but must not delay antibiotics or resuscitation in septic shock; antibiotics and fluids run first, imaging follows. (Source: Surviving Sepsis 2021 / eTG Antibiotic)

options.text: Give intravenous meropenem 1 gram as monotherapy and 500 millilitres of Hartmann's bolus over 30 minutes before repeat vital signs assessment at 1 hour
options.rationale: 500 mL bolus is well under the 30 mL/kg recommended for septic shock; underfluid resuscitation prolongs shock. Meropenem monotherapy is broader than typically needed for urosepsis in Australia (eTG piperacillin-tazobactam plus gentamicin is the standard). (Source: Surviving Sepsis 2021 / eTG Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: This is septic shock from urosepsis in a patient with a recent ureteric stent, complicated by acute kidney injury and lactic acidosis. The Surviving Sepsis hour-1 bundle mandates broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour of shock recognition, blood cultures before antibiotics (already taken), lactate measurement, and 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate above 4. Vasopressors are added when MAP stays under 65 after fluid resuscitation. Piperacillin-tazobactam plus gentamicin covers resistant post-stent urosepsis flora. Imaging and source control follow antibiotics and resuscitation.
key_points: Hour-1 bundle: antibiotics within 1 hour of shock recognition
30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate >4 mmol/L
Vasopressors added when MAP <65 after fluid resuscitation
Piperacillin-tazobactam plus gentamicin for post-stent urosepsis (eTG)
explanation.pearls: In septic shock, antibiotics and fluids run in parallel within the first hour; save vasopressors for after fluid, and never delay antibiotics for imaging or source control planning.

subtopic_detail: Osteoporosis first-line agent selection
stem:
A 68-year-old postmenopausal woman is referred to your general medicine outpatient clinic for review after a low-trauma right distal radius fracture 6 weeks ago after tripping on a garden hose. She takes ramipril 5 mg daily for hypertension and has no other medical history. She has no history of oesophageal disease and swallows tablets easily.

Her dual energy X-ray absorptiometry scan (DXA) at the femoral neck shows a T score of -2.9 and at lumbar spine -2.6. Her serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D is 62 nmol/L and corrected calcium is 2.32 mmol/L. Renal function is normal with an eGFR of 78 mL/min/1.73 m2. She is willing to accept an oral therapy and lives with her husband who can help her with dosing.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 72, BP 132/78, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temp 36.6 C
data_table.Examination: Alert; well healed distal radius fracture with plaster removed 2 weeks ago; no proximal myopathy or bone tenderness elsewhere; no dental disease
data_table.Investigations: DXA femoral neck T -2.9 lumbar spine T -2.6; 25-OH-vitamin D 62 nmol/L; corrected calcium 2.32 mmol/L; creatinine 68 eGFR 78; TSH 2.4 mIU/L; alkaline phosphatase 92 U/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Oral strontium ranelate 2 grams daily dissolved in water at bedtime with attention to cardiovascular risk factors and periodic cardiovascular review
options.rationale: Strontium ranelate has been withdrawn or restricted in many jurisdictions because of cardiovascular risk and has fallen out of first-line use. It is not the AU first-line for osteoporosis. (Source: Osteoporosis Australia/RACGP MSK guidelines)

options.text: Subcutaneous denosumab 60 milligrams every 6 months as first-line with strict adherence to schedule to avoid rebound bone loss on discontinuation
options.rationale: Denosumab is very effective but is not routine first-line in Australia because of the rebound vertebral fracture risk on discontinuation; PBS restriction is for patients who cannot tolerate or have contraindications to oral bisphosphonates. It is preferred second-line. (Source: Osteoporosis Australia/RACGP MSK guidelines)

options.text: Subcutaneous teriparatide 20 micrograms daily for up to 24 months as anabolic therapy given the low T score at both femoral neck and lumbar spine
options.rationale: Teriparatide is a PBS-restricted anabolic reserved for very high fracture risk (T score under -3.0 with 2 or more fractures on bisphosphonate) or for severe glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis; first-line therapy is oral alendronate for this patient. (Source: Osteoporosis Australia/RACGP MSK guidelines)

options.text: Oral alendronate 70 milligrams weekly with instructions to remain upright for 30 minutes after each dose and take vitamin D 1000 international units daily
options.rationale: For postmenopausal osteoporosis with a minimal-trauma fracture and T score under -2.5, alendronate 70 mg weekly is first-line per Australian osteoporosis guidance because it is inexpensive, PBS-listed, and has robust anti-fracture data. Take upright with water 30 minutes before food. Vitamin D and calcium sufficient at baseline. (Source: Osteoporosis Australia/RACGP MSK guidelines)

options.text: Oral raloxifene 60 milligrams daily as a selective oestrogen receptor modulator with attention to hot flushes and venous thromboembolism risk
options.rationale: Raloxifene is a second or third-line option and increases venous thromboembolism risk; it is not first-line for postmenopausal osteoporosis with a fragility fracture. Bisphosphonate is preferred first-line. (Source: Osteoporosis Australia/RACGP MSK guidelines)

explanation.summary: This is postmenopausal osteoporosis with a minimal-trauma distal radius fracture and T scores under -2.5 at the femoral neck and lumbar spine. Australian first-line pharmacotherapy is an oral bisphosphonate (alendronate 70 mg weekly), taken upright with water 30 minutes before food. Vitamin D and calcium are adequate at baseline. Denosumab is second-line due to rebound vertebral fracture risk on discontinuation; teriparatide is reserved for very high risk patients; strontium ranelate has been restricted for cardiovascular reasons; and raloxifene is a later-line SERM.
key_points: First-line for postmenopausal osteoporosis with minimal-trauma fracture: oral bisphosphonate
Take alendronate 70 mg weekly upright 30 min before food with water
Denosumab has rebound vertebral fracture risk on discontinuation
Teriparatide reserved for very high risk (T -3.0 with 2+ fractures on bisphosphonate)
explanation.pearls: For a first fragility fracture with a T score of -2.5 or worse, oral alendronate 70 mg weekly is the AU default; save denosumab for oral intolerance or contraindication.

subtopic_detail: Aortic dissection type discrimination and initial management
stem:
A 58-year-old man with a history of poorly controlled hypertension presents to your metropolitan emergency department with sudden onset of tearing interscapular chest pain radiating to his back 60 minutes ago. He is a current smoker and has a strong family history of aortic aneurysm. He denies syncope. His pulses are palpable in both radial arteries with a difference in blood pressure of 24 mmHg between arms.

On arrival he is diaphoretic and anxious. Cardiovascular examination reveals an early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge and equal bilateral chest expansion with air entry. There is no focal neurology or abdominal pain. IV access has been secured. A CT angiogram of the aorta has just returned and shows an intimal flap starting at the ascending aorta and extending distally past the arch into the descending thoracic aorta and abdominal aorta beyond the coeliac axis, without extension into the coronary ostia or a pericardial effusion.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 102, BP 176/98 right arm and 152/86 left arm, RR 22, SpO2 96% on room air, temp 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic; anxious; early diastolic murmur at left sternal edge; equal bilateral chest expansion; abdomen soft; distal pulses palpable and equal
data_table.Investigations: 12-lead ECG shows LV hypertrophy without ischaemic change; troponin negative; chest X-ray widened mediastinum; CT aortogram as described in stem

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous esmolol infusion titrated to heart rate under 60 followed by intravenous sodium nitroprusside to systolic under 120 mmHg with cardiothoracic referral
options.rationale: This is a Stanford type A dissection (starts in ascending aorta) and is a surgical emergency; medical management aims to reduce shear stress with beta-blockade FIRST to lower dP/dt, then a vasodilator to bring systolic BP to about 100-120 mmHg while awaiting operative repair. Nitroprusside without prior beta-blockade risks reflex tachycardia worsening shear stress. Aortic root repair is definitive. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular: Aortic dissection)

options.text: Intravenous labetalol 20 milligrams bolus and admit under vascular for medical management alone as this is a Stanford type B dissection amenable to conservative therapy
options.rationale: The flap starts in the ascending aorta making this Stanford type A, not type B. Type A dissection is a surgical emergency (30 percent mortality per day untreated) not amenable to medical management alone. Labetalol is appropriate but the disposition is theatre, not conservative admission. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular: Aortic dissection)

options.text: Thrombolysis with tenecteplase weight-based dosing intravenously for presumed anterior STEMI with new murmur suggestive of papillary muscle rupture
options.rationale: Thrombolysis in aortic dissection is catastrophic (accelerates the dissection and causes tamponade or exsanguination). The tearing pain radiating to the back plus widened mediastinum plus BP asymmetry point to dissection not STEMI, and the ECG is not diagnostic of STEMI. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular: Aortic dissection)

options.text: Intravenous morphine and oral aspirin 300 milligrams then clopidogrel 300 milligrams with admission to coronary care unit for further workup and troponin trending
options.rationale: Aspirin plus clopidogrel dual antiplatelet therapy in aortic dissection worsens haemorrhage and delays operative repair. Anticoagulation and antiplatelet loading are contraindicated. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular: Aortic dissection)

options.text: Intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion titrated to systolic blood pressure under 140 with intravenous furosemide 40 milligrams for the diastolic murmur suggestive of acute aortic regurgitation
options.rationale: Nitrate without beta-blockade causes reflex tachycardia and worsens dissection propagation; the priority is beta-blockade first (esmolol or labetalol) then a vasodilator. Furosemide is not indicated in dissection unless overt pulmonary oedema is present. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular: Aortic dissection)

explanation.summary: This is Stanford type A aortic dissection (flap starts in the ascending aorta) with aortic regurgitation and BP asymmetry. Type A is a surgical emergency with mortality of 1 percent per hour untreated. Medical bridging aims to reduce shear stress: beta-blocker FIRST (esmolol infusion to HR under 60) to lower dP/dt, then a vasodilator (nitroprusside or GTN) to bring systolic BP to 100-120 mmHg while cardiothoracic surgery is arranged. Vasodilator alone causes reflex tachycardia and worsens propagation. Antiplatelet loading, thrombolysis, and diuretic-first strategies are all incorrect and harmful.
key_points: Type A dissection = surgical emergency; type B usually medical
Medical bridging: beta-blocker first (HR <60), then vasodilator (SBP 100-120)
Antiplatelet loading and thrombolysis are contraindicated
Vasodilator without beta-blockade causes reflex tachycardia and propagation
explanation.pearls: In aortic dissection, always beta-block BEFORE giving nitroprusside; giving nitroprusside first causes reflex tachycardia that extends the flap.

subtopic_detail: Necrotising fasciitis recognition and management
stem:
A 55-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and obesity presents to your regional emergency department with 24 hours of increasing right calf pain that has become disproportionate to the clinical findings. He recalled scratching his leg on garden wire 4 days ago. His pain has escalated despite oral paracetamol and now feels excruciating on light touch.

On examination there is a small area of erythema on the anterior right calf with hazy dusky discoloration extending beyond the erythematous border and a single haemorrhagic bulla. Sensation over the affected area is reduced. He has palpable pedal pulses and no obvious crepitus. He is drowsy and diaphoretic with cool peripheries. IV access has been secured and initial resuscitation has commenced with fluids and cultures drawn.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, BP 96/58 (MAP 71), RR 26, SpO2 96% on room air, temp 38.6 C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable; cool peripheries with capillary refill 3 seconds; right calf with area of erythema, dusky discoloration beyond the erythematous border, one haemorrhagic bulla, reduced sensation, no crepitus; palpable pedal pulses; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 22 x10^9/L; sodium 132 potassium 4.4 creatinine 148 (baseline 90) urea 12; glucose 18.2 mmol/L; venous gas pH 7.28 lactate 4.4; CRP 380 mg/L; haemoglobin 128 g/L; LRINEC score 8

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the lower limb to confirm gas in the tissue planes before any surgical review is arranged
options.rationale: Imaging is helpful when the diagnosis is uncertain but should NEVER delay surgical review or theatre when clinical features and LRINEC are strongly suggestive; absence of gas on imaging does NOT exclude nec fasc. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Necrotising fasciitis)

options.text: Intravenous flucloxacillin 2 grams 6 hourly and mark the erythema border with observation for 4 hours before deciding on surgical review or escalation
options.rationale: Flucloxacillin monotherapy under-covers polymicrobial necrotising fasciitis and does not suppress streptococcal toxin production. Watching and waiting is fatal in nec fasc; the LRINEC of 8 and clinical picture mandate immediate surgery. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Necrotising fasciitis)

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 grams and elevate the limb with strict bed rest for cellulitis treatment while awaiting orthopaedic surgical review the next morning
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone monotherapy is insufficient for nec fasc and treating this as cellulitis with elective review delays theatre. Overnight delay in a septic nec fasc patient is fatal. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Necrotising fasciitis)

options.text: Immediate surgical review with plan for urgent theatre debridement plus intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam plus vancomycin plus clindamycin as empirical antibiotic cover
options.rationale: This is necrotising fasciitis (pain out of proportion, hazy dusky discoloration beyond erythema, haemorrhagic bulla, sensory loss, LRINEC 8) with sepsis. Definitive management is EARLY surgical debridement in theatre alongside broad empirical antibiotics including clindamycin for toxin suppression. Piperacillin-tazobactam plus vancomycin plus clindamycin is the standard eTG Australian empirical regimen. Every hour of delay to surgery raises mortality. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Necrotising fasciitis)

options.text: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy with 100 percent oxygen at 2.4 atmospheres for 90 minutes as adjunctive treatment before the first surgical debridement is performed
options.rationale: Hyperbaric oxygen may be an adjunct AFTER surgical debridement and antibiotics; it does NOT replace or precede surgery. Delaying debridement to arrange HBO is contraindicated. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Necrotising fasciitis)

explanation.summary: This is necrotising fasciitis with sepsis (pain out of proportion, dusky discoloration beyond erythema, haemorrhagic bulla, sensory loss, LRINEC 8). Management is IMMEDIATE surgical debridement plus broad empirical antibiotics including clindamycin for streptococcal toxin suppression. The eTG empirical regimen is piperacillin-tazobactam plus vancomycin (for MRSA) plus clindamycin. Every hour of delay to surgery raises mortality; imaging should not delay theatre when clinical features are strong. HBO is an adjunct at best, not a substitute for surgery.
key_points: Nec fasc clinical clues: pain out of proportion, dusky discoloration beyond erythema, bullae, sensory loss
LRINEC score >=8 is high probability
Empirical antibiotics: piperacillin-tazobactam + vancomycin + clindamycin (toxin suppression)
Immediate surgical debridement is the cornerstone; imaging must not delay theatre
explanation.pearls: In suspected nec fasc, activate theatre before finalising imaging; the LRINEC and clinical picture are enough, and every hour of delay adds mortality.

sources.label: ANZAS surgical guidelines: Necrotising soft tissue infection

subtopic_detail: Adult anaphylaxis refractory to first-line adrenaline
stem:
A 62-year-old woman with severe rheumatoid arthritis attends an infusion suite for her scheduled infliximab infusion. She takes metoprolol 100 mg twice daily for chronic atrial fibrillation with a controlled rate. Within 10 minutes of starting the infusion she develops generalised urticaria, wheeze, and hypotension.

The infusion has been stopped, she has been laid flat, and she has received one dose of intramuscular adrenaline 500 micrograms into the anterolateral thigh. Five minutes later she remains hypotensive with persistent wheeze and hoarse voice. She has just received a second dose of intramuscular adrenaline 500 micrograms. She has IV access with two large-bore cannulae. She has been given 1 litre of Hartmann's solution over the last 5 minutes and is on 6 L/min via Hudson mask.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82, BP 82/48 (MAP 60), RR 28, SpO2 92% on 6 L/min via Hudson mask, temp 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Generalised urticaria; audible wheeze; hoarse voice; cool peripheries with capillary refill 3 seconds; alert
data_table.Investigations: Venous gas pH 7.30 lactate 3.4 mmol/L; ECG shows atrial fibrillation with a controlled ventricular response at 82

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Third intramuscular adrenaline 500 micrograms and continue 500 millilitre crystalloid boluses to a maximum of 4 litres before considering additional agents
options.rationale: After two IM doses without response, ASCIA advises escalating to IV adrenaline infusion rather than a third IM. Continuing crystalloid without escalation of adrenaline delays effective treatment. (Source: ASCIA anaphylaxis guidelines)

options.text: Commence intravenous adrenaline infusion titrated to blood pressure and heart rate, and give intravenous glucagon 1 to 2 milligrams for beta-blocker mediated adrenaline resistance
options.rationale: After two IM adrenaline doses without adequate response, ASCIA recommends IV adrenaline infusion. In a patient on beta-blockers who is failing to respond, IV glucagon 1-2 mg (which acts on cAMP independent of beta-adrenergic receptors) is the standard adjunct to overcome beta-blocker resistance. (Source: ASCIA anaphylaxis guidelines)

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 200 milligrams and intravenous chlorpheniramine 10 milligrams as the primary treatment while the current adrenaline effect is assessed
options.rationale: Steroids and antihistamines are adjuncts and do not treat the acute cardiovascular collapse; they should not delay escalation to IV adrenaline in refractory anaphylaxis. (Source: ASCIA anaphylaxis guidelines)

options.text: Intravenous noradrenaline 10 micrograms per minute infusion as first-line vasopressor for refractory anaphylaxis with continued crystalloid at 250 millilitres per hour
options.rationale: Noradrenaline can be used as adjunct for refractory anaphylactic shock unresponsive to adrenaline, but IV adrenaline infusion is the first escalation after IM failure. Skipping adrenaline for noradrenaline is not standard. (Source: ASCIA anaphylaxis guidelines)

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 millilitres of 1:1000 with hydrocortisone 200 milligrams IV and salbutamol 5 milligrams nebuliser as combined therapy for airway symptoms
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline treats upper airway oedema but does not treat systemic anaphylactic shock; salbutamol and hydrocortisone are adjuncts. None of these address the beta-blocker-mediated adrenaline resistance that is the barrier here. (Source: ASCIA anaphylaxis guidelines)

explanation.summary: This is anaphylaxis refractory to two IM adrenaline doses in a patient on chronic beta-blocker therapy. ASCIA escalates to IV adrenaline infusion titrated to response after two IM doses fail. When beta-blocker mediated adrenaline resistance is suspected, IV glucagon 1-2 mg is the standard adjunct because it increases cAMP independent of beta-adrenergic receptors. Steroids, antihistamines, nebulised adrenaline, and noradrenaline all have supporting or adjunct roles but do not replace escalation of adrenaline and glucagon in this scenario.
key_points: After 2 IM adrenaline doses without response: IV adrenaline infusion
Beta-blocker on board: give IV glucagon 1-2 mg for adrenaline resistance
Steroids and antihistamines are adjuncts, not primary treatment
Noradrenaline is a later add-on for refractory shock unresponsive to adrenaline
explanation.pearls: In an anaphylactic patient on beta-blockers not responding to IM adrenaline, IV glucagon 1-2 mg alongside IV adrenaline infusion is the way to unlock the beta-adrenergic blockade.

subtopic_detail: Tumour lysis syndrome prophylaxis choice
stem:
A 42-year-old man newly diagnosed with Burkitt lymphoma is admitted to your haematology ward for CODOX-M induction chemotherapy. He has bulky abdominal disease, a serum lactate dehydrogenase over four times the upper limit of normal, and a white cell count of 68 x10^9/L. He is of African heritage and has no known glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency; his G6PD screen has just returned as normal.

His serum uric acid is 0.55 mmol/L, corrected calcium 2.28 mmol/L, phosphate 1.6 mmol/L, potassium 4.8 mmol/L, and creatinine 108 micromol/L. He has received 3 litres of intravenous Hartmann's solution over the last 12 hours and his urine output has been 100 mL per hour. Chemotherapy is planned to start within the next 12 hours. He weighs 72 kilograms.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, BP 118/72, RR 18, SpO2 97% on room air, temp 37.2 C
data_table.Examination: Alert; palpable bulky abdominal lymphadenopathy; hepatosplenomegaly with liver 6 cm below costal margin; no rash; no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Uric acid 0.55 mmol/L; corrected calcium 2.28 mmol/L; phosphate 1.6 mmol/L; potassium 4.8 mmol/L; creatinine 108 micromol/L; LDH 1620 U/L; white cell count 68 x10^9/L; G6PD screen normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate tumour lysis syndrome prophylaxis?

options.text: Oral allopurinol 300 milligrams daily and continue intravenous crystalloid at 3 litres per square metre per day with 4 hourly biochemistry monitoring for the first 24 hours
options.rationale: Allopurinol prevents new uric acid formation but does NOT treat the existing high uric acid; it takes 48-72 hours to lower urate meaningfully. For high-risk TLS (Burkitt with bulky disease, LDH >4 times upper limit, and baseline urate above upper limit) rasburicase is preferred as it degrades existing uric acid within hours. (Source: eviQ tumour lysis syndrome / HSANZ)

options.text: Prophylactic haemodialysis prior to induction chemotherapy with a target urea reduction ratio of 65 percent before the first dose of chemotherapy
options.rationale: Prophylactic dialysis is only indicated when established renal failure or refractory hyperkalaemia or hyperphosphataemia occurs during TLS; it is not routine prophylaxis. Rasburicase plus aggressive hydration prevents most cases from progressing to dialysis. (Source: eviQ tumour lysis syndrome / HSANZ)

options.text: Oral febuxostat 80 milligrams daily and sodium bicarbonate infusion to urinary pH above 7.5 with intravenous crystalloid at 4 litres per square metre daily
options.rationale: Febuxostat is an alternative to allopurinol but is not preferred over rasburicase for high-risk TLS. Urinary alkalinisation with bicarbonate is NO LONGER recommended because it worsens calcium phosphate precipitation and increases xanthine crystallisation. (Source: eviQ tumour lysis syndrome / HSANZ)

options.text: Intravenous rasburicase 0.2 milligrams per kilogram single dose and continue intravenous crystalloid at 3 litres per square metre per day with 4 hourly biochemistry monitoring
options.rationale: Burkitt lymphoma with bulky disease, LDH more than 4 times upper limit, and elevated baseline uric acid places this patient in the high-risk TLS category. eviQ and HSANZ pathways recommend rasburicase as first-line uric acid lowering because it converts uric acid to allantoin within hours, unlike allopurinol which only blocks new formation. G6PD deficiency (haemolysis risk) has been excluded. Hyperhydration with balanced crystalloid continues. (Source: eviQ tumour lysis syndrome / HSANZ)

options.text: Delay induction chemotherapy for 48 hours and commence oral allopurinol 300 milligrams three times daily with sodium bicarbonate infusion for urinary alkalinisation
options.rationale: Burkitt lymphoma has extremely rapid doubling time; delaying chemotherapy for prophylaxis without addressing the immediate uric acid risk is dangerous. Rasburicase allows chemotherapy to start on schedule while managing hyperuricaemia. Alkalinisation is not recommended. (Source: eviQ tumour lysis syndrome / HSANZ)

explanation.summary: This patient is high-risk for TLS (Burkitt lymphoma with bulky disease, LDH more than 4 times upper limit, and baseline uric acid above upper limit). eviQ and HSANZ recommend rasburicase (0.2 mg/kg IV as a single dose or a fixed-dose regimen) for high-risk TLS because it converts uric acid to allantoin within hours, unlike allopurinol which only blocks new formation and takes 48-72 hours. G6PD deficiency is a contraindication to rasburicase due to haemolysis risk; screening was normal here. Hyperhydration continues but urinary alkalinisation with bicarbonate is no longer recommended because it worsens calcium phosphate precipitation. Prophylactic dialysis is not routine.
key_points: High-risk TLS (Burkitt, bulky disease, LDH >4x ULN, high urate): rasburicase
Screen G6PD before rasburicase (contraindicated in deficiency)
Urinary alkalinisation with bicarbonate is NOT recommended
Allopurinol only blocks new urate formation; slow onset (48-72 hours)
explanation.pearls: For high-risk TLS in Burkitt lymphoma with a G6PD-normal patient, rasburicase 0.2 mg/kg IV drops existing urate within hours; do not waste time on allopurinol prophylaxis alone.

subtopic_detail: STEMI reperfusion PCI versus fibrinolysis
stem: A 55-year-old man presents to your regional emergency department with 90 minutes of central crushing chest pain. His ECG shows 3 mm ST elevation in the anterior leads with reciprocal changes. The nearest PCI-capable hospital is 3 hours away by road transport. Air retrieval is not available for at least 2 hours. Troponin has been sent. He has no contraindications to thrombolysis. He weighs 82 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88, BP 132/82, RR 18, SpO2 98 percent, temp 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Alert, in pain, no basal crackles, JVP not elevated, no pulmonary oedema, no new murmurs
data_table.Investigations: ECG: 3 mm ST elevation V1 to V4, reciprocal depression II, III, aVF; troponin pending; potassium 4.1; creatinine 90; INR 1.0

lead_in: What is the most appropriate reperfusion strategy?

options.text: Immediate transfer to the PCI centre for primary PCI, targeting a door-to-balloon time of 90 minutes from arrival at the receiving centre for optimal reperfusion outcomes
options.rationale: Transfer for primary PCI is only preferred when total delay to PCI is under 120 minutes from first medical contact; 3 hours by road plus door-to-balloon exceeds this window, so lytics are preferred.

options.text: Wait for the troponin result then start dual antiplatelet therapy and heparin, and admit for medical management without acute reperfusion until further test results are available
options.rationale: STEMI diagnosis is ECG-based; waiting for troponin delays reperfusion. Not offering reperfusion at all is inappropriate for STEMI within 12 hours of symptom onset in a patient without contraindications.

options.text: Intravenous streptokinase 1.5 million units over 60 minutes plus oral aspirin, then defer transfer until pain resolves and further reperfusion needs are reassessed by the retrieval team
options.rationale: Streptokinase is rarely used in Australia due to inferior patency rates and allergy risk; tenecteplase is the preferred fibrinolytic. Transfer should also occur to allow rescue PCI if reperfusion fails.

options.text: Weight-adjusted IV tenecteplase (about 40 mg) plus enoxaparin and clopidogrel now, then transfer for rescue PCI if reperfusion fails or routine early angiography 3 to 24 hours
options.rationale: When primary PCI cannot be delivered within 120 minutes of first medical contact, prehospital or in-hospital fibrinolysis with weight-adjusted tenecteplase is preferred, followed by early transfer for pharmacoinvasive PCI.

options.text: IV nitroglycerin infusion titrated to pain relief, oral aspirin and metoprolol, and admit locally for medical management until pain resolves and the troponin trajectory becomes clearer over time
options.rationale: Nitrates and beta-blockers do not reperfuse the coronary artery; reperfusion is the priority in STEMI within 12 hours of symptom onset in a patient without contraindications to thrombolysis.

explanation.summary: In STEMI, primary PCI is preferred when it can be delivered within 120 minutes of first medical contact. Beyond this window, weight-adjusted bolus tenecteplase (with enoxaparin and clopidogrel or ticagrelor as per local protocol) is given without delay, followed by early transfer to a PCI centre for rescue PCI if reperfusion fails or routine coronary angiography at 3 to 24 hours (pharmacoinvasive strategy). Waiting for troponin or omitting reperfusion is inappropriate.
key_points: Primary PCI preferred if within 120 min of first medical contact
Otherwise fibrinolysis with tenecteplase then transfer
Rescue PCI if failed reperfusion; routine angiography 3 to 24 hours
STEMI diagnosis is ECG-based; do not wait for troponin
explanation.pearls: Failed reperfusion after fibrinolysis is defined as under 50 percent ST resolution at 60 to 90 minutes, ongoing chest pain, or haemodynamic instability; these mandate immediate rescue PCI, not repeat lytics.

subtopic_detail: Community-acquired pneumonia moderate severity
stem: A 65-year-old man presents to your emergency department with 3 days of productive cough, right-sided pleuritic chest pain and fever. He has a background of well-controlled type 2 diabetes. On examination he has right lower zone crackles and bronchial breathing. Chest x-ray shows a dense right lower lobe consolidation. Confusion Assessment Method is negative. His CURB-65 score is 1 (age 65 or over, plus one additional point).

data_table.Vital signs: HR 102, BP 128/78, RR 26, SpO2 91 percent room air, temp 38.6 C
data_table.Examination: Alert, orientated, right lower zone crackles and bronchial breathing, no signs of shock
data_table.Investigations: Urea 6.2 mmol/L, WCC 18, CRP 240, sodium 138, creatinine 90; CXR right lower lobe consolidation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial antibiotic strategy?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 5 days, home management with a general practitioner review at 48 hours to reassess
options.rationale: Home management may be acceptable for very low severity (CURB-65 0 to 1 with no adverse features) but hypoxia at SpO2 91 percent and RR 26 are adverse features so hospital IV therapy is preferred.

options.text: IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 8 hours plus IV azithromycin 500 mg once daily for 7 days total, targeting broad spectrum cover for the community-acquired pneumonia observed today
options.rationale: Broad spectrum cover with anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam is reserved for severe pneumonia or specific risk factors (structural lung disease, healthcare exposure) and is not first line for moderate CAP.

options.text: IV ceftriaxone 2 g once daily plus IV vancomycin 15 mg/kg twice daily for 10 days, providing empirical MRSA cover for the community-acquired pneumonia observed today at admission
options.rationale: Vancomycin is added only when there is necrotising pneumonia, cavitation or specific MRSA risk factors; empirical addition for community-acquired pneumonia is inappropriate as first-line therapy.

options.text: Oral moxifloxacin 400 mg once daily for 5 days plus oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days, then discharge home to community with a general practitioner follow-up appointment in 2 days
options.rationale: Moxifloxacin monotherapy for CAP has QT and mycobacterial concerns; oseltamivir requires evidence of influenza; home management with hypoxia at SpO2 91 percent is not safe management.

options.text: IV benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 6 hours plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days total, then switch to oral therapy once he is clinically stable and improving
options.rationale: AU eTG for moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia requiring hospitalisation is IV benzylpenicillin plus oral doxycycline, switching to oral therapy once clinically stable, tolerating oral, and improving inflammatory markers.

explanation.summary: Moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia requiring hospital admission is treated in Australia with IV benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 6 hours plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily to cover atypicals. Once the patient is clinically stable (afebrile 24 hours, tolerating oral, improving inflammatory markers, no hypoxia), switch to oral amoxicillin 1 g TDS plus doxycycline for a total 7 day course. Broad-spectrum agents are reserved for severe disease or specific risk factors.
key_points: Moderate CAP: IV benzylpenicillin plus oral doxycycline
Switch to oral when clinically stable; total 7 days
CURB-65 useful for severity but adverse features (hypoxia, RR) also decide admission
Broad-spectrum only for severe disease or specific risk factors
explanation.pearls: IV to oral switch is safe when the patient has stable vitals for 24 hours, is tolerating oral, is haemodynamically stable, has improving CRP and WCC, and there is no pleural infection; do not wait for the CXR to clear.

subtopic_detail: Warfarin peri-procedural bridging for elective surgery
stem: A 68-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation (CHA2DS2-VASc score 4) is on warfarin with INR 2.5. She is scheduled for an elective knee arthroplasty in 7 days. She has no history of prior stroke or systemic embolism, no mechanical heart valve, and no recent (under 3 months) venous thromboembolism. She has moderate renal impairment with eGFR 45. There has been no recent bleeding.

data_table.Examination: Alert, well, ECG atrial fibrillation, no signs of embolism or bleeding
data_table.Investigations: INR 2.5, Hb 128, platelets 260, creatinine 105, eGFR 45

lead_in: What is the most appropriate peri-procedural anticoagulation plan?

options.text: Stop warfarin 5 days before surgery, no bridging heparin required, then restart warfarin 12 to 24 hours after surgery when adequate haemostasis has been achieved by the surgical team
options.rationale: For atrial fibrillation without mechanical valve, prior stroke or recent VTE, BRIDGE trial evidence shows no bridging is preferred; bridging LMWH increases bleeding without reducing stroke.

options.text: Continue warfarin at usual dose throughout the perioperative period since the bleeding risk of primary knee arthroplasty is generally acceptably low in most patients undergoing the procedure
options.rationale: Elective knee arthroplasty is a high bleeding risk procedure; warfarin must be held perioperatively to avoid intra- and postoperative bleeding requiring transfusion and reoperation.

options.text: Stop warfarin 5 days before surgery and bridge with therapeutic-dose enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily starting 3 days before the operation and continuing until the day of surgery this year
options.rationale: Full-dose bridging is reserved for very high thromboembolic risk (mechanical mitral valve, recent stroke or VTE under 3 months, CHA2DS2-VASc 7 or more); this patient does not meet those criteria.

options.text: Stop warfarin 3 days before surgery and give oral vitamin K 5 mg to accelerate INR normalisation before the procedure and cross-match blood for the operation planned to occur this week
options.rationale: Routine oral vitamin K creates warfarin resistance postoperatively, delaying re-anticoagulation; 5 days off warfarin without vitamin K reliably normalises the INR in most patients.

options.text: Switch warfarin to apixaban 5 mg twice daily starting 5 days before surgery, then hold apixaban 24 hours before the surgery scheduled for later next week and restart afterwards on advice
options.rationale: Switching between anticoagulants perioperatively adds complexity and cost without benefit, introducing a gap or overlap; simple hold of warfarin is the standard perioperative strategy.

explanation.summary: For atrial fibrillation on warfarin without mechanical valve, recent stroke, recent VTE, or CHA2DS2-VASc of 7 or more, the BRIDGE trial showed no benefit to LMWH bridging and increased bleeding risk. Stop warfarin 5 days before surgery, do not bridge, and restart warfarin 12 to 24 hours after surgery when haemostasis is achieved. Vitamin K acceleration causes postoperative warfarin resistance and should be avoided routinely.
key_points: No bridging for AF unless mechanical valve, recent stroke, recent VTE or CHA2DS2-VASc 7+
Stop warfarin 5 days pre-op
Restart warfarin 12 to 24 hours post-op when haemostasis achieved
Routine oral vitamin K causes postoperative warfarin resistance
explanation.pearls: Full-dose bridging LMWH is contraindicated within 24 hours of major surgery and is generally started 3 days before and stopped 24 hours before; prophylactic-dose LMWH can be used postoperatively for surgical VTE prophylaxis.

subtopic_detail: Hyponatraemia SIADH versus hypovolaemic differentiation
stem: A 74-year-old woman with newly diagnosed small cell lung cancer presents to your medical assessment unit with 5 days of nausea, unsteadiness and mild headache. She is on no diuretics. Her serum sodium is 118 mmol/L (baseline 138 two weeks ago), plasma osmolality 254 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 480 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 55 mmol/L. She is euvolaemic clinically. TSH and cortisol are normal. She is alert with no focal neurology.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78, BP 128/78 lying, 124/76 standing, RR 16, SpO2 97 percent, temp 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Alert, orientated, no ataxia, no focal neurology, mucous membranes moist, JVP visible at 4 cm, no oedema
data_table.Investigations: Na 118, K 4.0, urea 3.4, creatinine 60, plasma osm 254, urine osm 480, urine Na 55, TSH 1.8, cortisol 480

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Infuse 1 litre of 0.9 percent normal saline over 4 hours and reassess her sodium level after each litre until the serum sodium level reaches 130 mmol/L or above
options.rationale: Isotonic saline in SIADH can paradoxically worsen hyponatraemia because urine osmolality (480) exceeds infused osmolality; water is retained while sodium is excreted in the urine.
source_refs: European Society of Endocrinology hyponatraemia guideline

options.text: Restrict fluids to 800 mL/day with sodium and neurological monitoring twice daily, aiming to raise serum sodium by no more than 8 mmol/L per 24 hours to avoid osmotic demyelination
options.rationale: Euvolaemic hyponatraemia with concentrated urine and euvolaemia meets SIADH criteria; first-line management is fluid restriction (800 to 1000 mL/day) with monitoring and limiting correction to under 8 mmol/L per 24 hours.
source_refs: European Society of Endocrinology hyponatraemia guideline

options.text: Give 3 percent hypertonic saline 150 mL bolus over 20 minutes to rapidly correct the serum sodium above 125 mmol/L within the next 4 hours, aiming to abolish symptoms quickly today
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizures, coma, severe drowsiness); this patient has only mild symptoms and can be managed with fluid restriction first.
source_refs: European Society of Endocrinology hyponatraemia guideline

options.text: Prescribe oral demeclocycline 300 mg four times daily and continue an unrestricted oral fluid intake for maintenance, with monitoring of the serum sodium level daily on the ward round
options.rationale: Demeclocycline is now rarely used due to nephrotoxicity and slow onset; tolvaptan is preferred if pharmacotherapy is needed after fluid restriction has failed to produce an adequate response.
source_refs: European Society of Endocrinology hyponatraemia guideline

options.text: Give IV furosemide 40 mg with oral salt tablets, then correct the serum sodium with a 2 percent saline infusion titrated overnight to rise no more than 8 mmol/L in the first 24 hours
options.rationale: Furosemide plus salt tablets is a niche second-line strategy in SIADH; not first line and carries a risk of overcorrection and electrolyte disturbance without benefit over fluid restriction.
source_refs: European Society of Endocrinology hyponatraemia guideline

explanation.summary: SIADH diagnostic criteria are met with euvolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia (plasma osm below 275), inappropriately concentrated urine (urine osm above 100), and urine sodium above 30 mmol/L, with normal thyroid and adrenal function, no diuretic use and no volume depletion. First-line management is fluid restriction 800 to 1000 mL/day; hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptomatic disease. Correction is limited to under 8 mmol/L per 24 hours to prevent osmotic demyelination.
key_points: SIADH: euvolaemic, plasma osm low, urine osm > 100, urine Na > 30, normal TFTs and cortisol
First line: fluid restrict 800 to 1000 mL/day
Isotonic saline can paradoxically worsen SIADH
Correct no more than 8 mmol/L in 24 hours; hypertonic saline only for severe symptoms
explanation.pearls: If overcorrection occurs (sodium rises more than 8 mmol/L in 24 hours), stop all sodium sources, administer 5 percent dextrose IV, and consider desmopressin 2 microgram IV to prevent osmotic demyelination.

sources.label: European Society of Endocrinology hyponatraemia guideline

subtopic_detail: HHS versus DKA insulin infusion approach
stem: A 76-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on metformin and gliclazide presents to your emergency department after 5 days of polyuria and progressive drowsiness following a chest infection. His glucose is 42 mmol/L, sodium 152, potassium 4.0, urea 18, creatinine 130. Venous gas pH 7.34, bicarbonate 20, blood ketones 0.4 mmol/L. Calculated effective osmolality is 336 mOsm/kg. He is drowsy but rousable, significantly dehydrated with dry mucous membranes and reduced skin turgor.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, BP 100/60, RR 22, SpO2 96 percent, temp 37.6 C, weight 80 kg
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, GCS 13, dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, capillary refill 3 seconds, no focal neurology, chest crepitations right base
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 42, Na 152, K 4.0, urea 18, creatinine 130, VBG pH 7.34, HCO3 20, ketones 0.4, effective osm 336

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial fluid and insulin approach?

options.text: IV 0.9 percent saline 1 litre over 1 hour, then continue at 250 mL/hour and commence IV insulin infusion at 0.05 units/kg/hour immediately once serum potassium is above 3.5 mmol/L
options.rationale: HHS: give fluid first (1 L over 1 hour, reassess), start insulin low-dose 0.05 units/kg/hour and only after several hours when glucose ceases falling with fluids; rapid insulin causes cerebral oedema.
source_refs: JBDS-IP: Management of hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state

options.text: IV 0.9 percent saline 2 litres over 1 hour, commence IV insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour immediately upon admission and aim for a glucose fall of 10 mmol/L per hour with observation
options.rationale: 0.1 units/kg/hour is the DKA regimen; in HHS this rate causes too-rapid osmotic shifts leading to cerebral oedema and cardiovascular collapse. Target glucose fall in HHS is 5 mmol/L per hour.
source_refs: JBDS-IP: Management of hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state

options.text: IV 0.9 percent saline 1 litre over 1 hour, reassess volume status, then only add low-dose insulin at 0.05 units/kg/hour if glucose fails to fall by 5 mmol/L per hour with fluids alone
options.rationale: AU HHS management: aggressive but careful isotonic fluid is primary; insulin is low-dose (0.05 units/kg/hour) and delayed, only added when glucose stops falling with fluids alone, targeting 5 mmol/L fall per hour.
source_refs: JBDS-IP: Management of hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state

options.text: IV 5 percent dextrose 1 litre over 2 hours, then an IV insulin bolus of 10 units followed by a 0.1 units/kg/hour infusion, targeting a glucose of 8 mmol/L within the next 4 hours today
options.rationale: 5 percent dextrose worsens hyperglycaemia; insulin bolus is not recommended in DKA or HHS; targeting 8 mmol/L within 4 hours is far too rapid an osmolar correction for HHS management.
source_refs: JBDS-IP: Management of hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state

options.text: IV Hartmann's 500 mL over 1 hour, commence subcutaneous insulin glargine 20 units at bedtime, treat chest infection and reassess him again in the morning on the ward round after handover
options.rationale: Subcutaneous long-acting insulin has slow onset and cannot be titrated in an acutely unwell patient; IV insulin infusion (once fluid-resuscitated and if needed) is required for HHS.
source_refs: JBDS-IP: Management of hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state

explanation.summary: HHS differs from DKA in that acidosis and significant ketosis are absent, and effective osmolality is markedly raised (over 320 mOsm/kg). Management prioritises IV fluid resuscitation with 0.9 percent saline (1 L in the first hour then reassess), which alone usually reduces glucose by 5 mmol/L per hour. Insulin is started at low dose (0.05 units/kg/hour) and delayed until glucose ceases falling with fluids. Target correction is 5 mmol/L per hour fall.
key_points: HHS: acidosis absent, ketones minimal, effective osmolality > 320
Fluid resuscitation is primary; insulin low-dose and delayed
Target glucose fall 5 mmol/L per hour, not 10
Rapid osmolar correction causes cerebral oedema and haemodynamic collapse
explanation.pearls: HHS has a mortality of 15 to 20 percent compared with 1 to 5 percent for DKA; identifying and treating the precipitant (commonly infection, myocardial infarction, medication non-adherence) is crucial.

sources.label: JBDS-IP: Management of hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state

subtopic_detail: Contrast-induced nephropathy prevention
stem: A 72-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and stage 3B chronic kidney disease (eGFR 38) is booked for a CT coronary angiogram tomorrow. His usual medications are metformin, ramipril, spironolactone, atorvastatin and gliclazide. He has recently increased his frusemide because of ankle swelling. His serum creatinine has been stable and his blood pressure is well controlled. He has no history of allergy to contrast media.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 74, BP 132/80, RR 16, weight 84 kg
data_table.Examination: Alert, mild pitting ankle oedema, chest clear, JVP not raised
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 155, eGFR 38, K 4.4, Hb 128, HbA1c 7.2 percent, BNP 240

lead_in: What is the most appropriate contrast nephropathy prevention plan?

options.text: Give IV N-acetylcysteine 1200 mg twice daily for 24 hours pre-procedure and 24 hours post-procedure, and continue all of his usual medications through the procedure without dose changes
options.rationale: Recent evidence (PRESERVE trial) shows no benefit of N-acetylcysteine over placebo for contrast-induced nephropathy prevention; it is no longer recommended in contemporary practice guidelines.

options.text: Continue metformin and diuretics but withhold ramipril for 48 hours before the procedure, and no IV hydration is required for a patient with an eGFR greater than 30 mL/min/1.73m2 undergoing contrast
options.rationale: Metformin should be temporarily held from the day of contrast when eGFR is under 60 until renal function is confirmed stable 48 hours later, due to lactic acidosis risk; ACEi and diuretics are also usually held.

options.text: Prescribe oral sodium bicarbonate 3 g twice daily for 3 days before and 3 days after the procedure without other measures for prevention of contrast-induced nephropathy in this high-risk patient today
options.rationale: Sodium bicarbonate is non-superior to isotonic saline for CIN prevention (PRESERVE); IV isotonic saline hydration is the standard first-line prophylaxis in patients with additional risk factors like diabetes.

options.text: Withhold metformin, spironolactone, ramipril and frusemide from the day of procedure, IV 0.9 percent saline at 1 mL/kg/hour for 12 hours before and 12 hours after, use lowest effective iso-osmolar contrast
options.rationale: AU KHA-CARI approach for eGFR 30 to 45 with additional risk factors (diabetes, HF, ACEi, diuretics): withhold nephrotoxic and metformin drugs, provide 12-hour peri-procedural isotonic saline hydration, minimise contrast volume with iso-osmolar agent.

options.text: Cancel the CT coronary angiogram and proceed to invasive coronary angiography with a stress cardiac MRI to avoid all contrast exposure for the patient in view of his renal impairment and comorbidities
options.rationale: Invasive coronary angiography uses more contrast than CT; MRI does not replace anatomical coronary imaging. Preventive strategies allow the CT to proceed safely in most patients at risk.

explanation.summary: Contrast-induced nephropathy prevention in high-risk patients (eGFR under 45, diabetes, heart failure, ACEi/ARB/diuretics/NSAIDs) requires withholding nephrotoxic medications and temporary cessation of metformin because of lactic acidosis risk.
