IV isotonic saline at 1 mL/kg/hour is given for 12 hours before and 12 hours after the procedure. The lowest effective iso-osmolar or low-osmolar contrast volume should be used. N-acetylcysteine and sodium bicarbonate are not superior to saline hydration (PRESERVE trial 2018) and are no longer recommended.
key_points: Withhold metformin (day of contrast); recheck creatinine at 48 hours before resuming
Withhold ACEi/ARB/diuretics peri-procedure in high-risk patients
IV isotonic saline 1 mL/kg/hour 12 hours pre and post
Use lowest effective iso-osmolar contrast volume
explanation.pearls: Post-contrast acute kidney injury is now considered rarer than previously for IV studies, but the highest-risk group remains diabetics with eGFR under 30 or acute kidney injury; radiologist and cardiologist should be informed to minimise volume.

subtopic_detail: Empirical antibiotics in urosepsis with recent ESBL history
stem: A 78-year-old woman is transferred from her nursing home to your emergency department with 24 hours of confusion, fever and hypotension. She is known to have recurrent urinary tract infections and has had two admissions for ESBL Escherichia coli urosepsis in the past 6 months. On examination she is drowsy, hypotensive despite 2 litres of IV fluids, and has suprapubic tenderness. Bloods show creatinine 220 (baseline 90), lactate 3.6 and CRP 320. She is not pregnant.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, BP 88/54 (post 2 L fluids), RR 26, SpO2 96 percent, temp 39.1 C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, GCS 13, warm peripheries, capillary refill 3 seconds, suprapubic tenderness, no flank pain
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 220 (baseline 90), urea 14, lactate 3.6, WCC 22, CRP 320, urinalysis leucocytes and nitrites positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic and dosing decision?

options.text: IV amoxicillin 2 g every 6 hours plus IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg once daily until cultures return with sensitivities, with standard renal dose adjustment being applied for gentamicin in her acute kidney injury
options.rationale: Amoxicillin plus gentamicin does not reliably cover ESBL organisms; empirical cover for a patient with recent ESBL infection and septic shock must include a carbapenem for adequate empirical activity.

options.text: IV ceftriaxone 2 g once daily as empirical monotherapy, then add ampicillin only if enterococcal cover is judged required by microbiology, and continue ward-based care with hourly BP monitoring overnight
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone will not cover ESBL organisms which produce enzymes that hydrolyse third-generation cephalosporins; ward-based care is inappropriate for septic shock unresponsive to initial 2 L fluids.

options.text: IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 8 hours dose-reduced for the acute kidney injury, and continue ward-based care with hourly blood pressure monitoring and delayed reassessment in the morning ward round
options.rationale: Piperacillin-tazobactam has poor reliability in ESBL bacteraemia (MERINO trial showed higher mortality vs meropenem); ICU-level care is required for shock unresponsive to fluid resuscitation.

options.text: IV vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading then 15 mg/kg every 12 hours, plus IV metronidazole 500 mg every 8 hours for anaerobic cover, and admit her under general medicine for ongoing care and daily specialist review
options.rationale: Vancomycin plus metronidazole covers gram-positive and anaerobic infection but does not cover ESBL gram-negative pathogens driving her urosepsis, and misses the causative organism entirely today.

options.text: IV meropenem 1 g every 8 hours dose-adjusted for creatinine clearance, obtain blood and urine cultures before the first dose, and escalate to ICU for haemodynamic support and vasopressors
options.rationale: For septic shock with recent history of ESBL urosepsis, empirical carbapenem cover (meropenem) is appropriate and dose-adjusted; cultures should be taken before antibiotics if this does not delay administration beyond 45 minutes.

explanation.summary: In septic shock with a history of ESBL infection in the past 6 months, empirical antibiotic cover should include a carbapenem (meropenem 1 g every 8 hours, dose-adjusted for creatinine clearance). Piperacillin-tazobactam is inferior to meropenem for ESBL bacteraemia (MERINO trial 2018). Blood and urine cultures should be obtained before antibiotics only if this does not delay administration beyond 45 minutes. Septic shock unresponsive to 2 L of fluid warrants ICU-level care and vasopressor consideration.
key_points: ESBL history in the past 6 months: cover empirically with a carbapenem
Piperacillin-tazobactam inferior to meropenem for ESBL bacteraemia (MERINO)
Cultures before antibiotics only if no delay beyond 45 minutes
Septic shock unresponsive to 2 L fluid: escalate to ICU and vasopressors
explanation.pearls: For a patient with ESBL history but who is haemodynamically stable and not septic, oral fosfomycin 3 g single dose or oral pivmecillinam are options for uncomplicated ESBL cystitis, sparing carbapenems.

sources.label: MERINO trial: piperacillin-tazobactam vs meropenem for ESBL

subtopic_detail: Latent TB workup and treatment
stem: A 34-year-old woman migrated from Vietnam 6 months ago and attends your general practice for routine health assessment. She is well with no cough, no fever, no weight loss and no night sweats. She has never been treated for tuberculosis but recalls a household contact with active TB when she was 15. She is HIV negative and not immunosuppressed. Chest X-ray is clear. Her QFT-Plus is positive. She wishes to have children within 12 months.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Systemically well; clear chest on auscultation; no lymphadenopathy; no skin findings
data_table.Investigations: QFT-Plus positive; chest X-ray no active disease; HIV negative; HBV/HCV negative; LFTs within normal limits; not pregnant

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment offer?

options.text: Rifampicin 600 mg orally daily plus isoniazid 300 mg orally daily plus pyridoxine 25 mg orally daily for 3 months (3HR) with monthly LFT and hepatitis symptom review during treatment
options.rationale: AU CDNA and TSANZ latent TB treatment recommends 3HR (3 month rifampicin plus isoniazid) as preferred regimen due to shorter duration, better completion and equal efficacy to 6H; pyridoxine prevents peripheral neuropathy.

options.text: Isoniazid 300 mg orally daily plus pyridoxine 25 mg orally daily for 9 months (9H) as this remains the AU first-line regimen for latent TB in adults with normal baseline liver function
options.rationale: 9H is a legacy regimen; AU has moved to shorter regimens (3HR or 4R) as first-line to improve completion rates.

options.text: Rifampicin 600 mg orally daily plus pyridoxine 25 mg orally daily monotherapy for 4 months (4R) with monthly LFT monitoring and screening for drug interactions including hormonal contraception
options.rationale: 4R is an accepted alternative if isoniazid contraindicated; when both agents can be given, 3HR is preferred as shorter than 4R in AU pathways.

options.text: No treatment as latent TB is asymptomatic and treatment risk outweighs benefit in a low-transmission country like Australia, provide symptom checklist and annual review in general practice
options.rationale: Recent migration from a high-incidence country and known household contact confer a lifetime reactivation risk of 5 to 10 percent; treatment materially reduces this and is offered per AU guidance.

options.text: Repeat QFT-Plus in 6 months to confirm the positive result before commencing any treatment, as isolated QFT-Plus positivity has a false positive rate that warrants a repeat test for diagnostic certainty
options.rationale: In a person with known past exposure, single QFT-Plus positive is sufficient for LTBI diagnosis; repeat delays treatment without changing management.

explanation.summary: Latent tuberculosis infection in a person from a high-incidence country with a positive interferon-gamma release assay, clear chest X-ray and no symptoms warrants offered treatment to prevent reactivation. AU preferred regimens are 3HR (rifampicin plus isoniazid for 3 months) or 4R (rifampicin monotherapy for 4 months), with pyridoxine to prevent isoniazid neuropathy. Monthly LFT monitoring and hepatitis symptom review during treatment are standard. 9H is a legacy regimen with lower completion rates.
key_points: Positive QFT-Plus with clear XR and no symptoms = LTBI
3HR is AU preferred regimen (or 4R if isoniazid contraindicated)
Pyridoxine prevents INH peripheral neuropathy
Monthly LFTs and hepatitis symptom check during treatment
explanation.pearls: Rifampicin induces CYP3A4 and reduces efficacy of combined hormonal contraception, warfarin and many antiretrovirals; alternative contraception (copper IUD, DMPA) is planned before starting a rifampicin-containing regimen in women of reproductive age.

subtopic_detail: Cushing syndrome screening choice
stem: A 44-year-old woman presents to your general practice concerned about a 12 kg weight gain over 6 months despite unchanged diet. She has developed acne, easy bruising on her forearms and reports low mood. On examination she has central obesity, wide purple striae on her abdomen and a rounded plethoric face. Her BP is 158/94. She is not on exogenous steroids and works day shifts as an accountant with a regular sleep schedule. Fasting glucose is 8.1 mmol/L on today's finger-prick test.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82, BP 158/94, RR 14, SpO2 99 percent, temp 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Central obesity, moon facies, dorsocervical fat pad, wide purple striae on abdomen; proximal muscle weakness on rising from chair without arms; supraclavicular fullness
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 8.1 mmol/L (<7.0), HbA1c 6.8 percent (<5.7); TSH 2.1 mIU/L; UEC and calcium within normal limits; not on exogenous glucocorticoids; not pregnant

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial screening test?

options.text: Serum ACTH morning level with paired cortisol as the initial screening test, expecting an elevated ACTH to indicate pituitary Cushing and a suppressed ACTH to indicate adrenal Cushing directly
options.rationale: ACTH is used to distinguish ACTH-dependent from ACTH-independent Cushing after screening confirms hypercortisolism; not the first screen.

options.text: Overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test with a morning serum cortisol at 8 am, considering a cortisol below 50 nmol/L as an adequate response and above 50 nmol/L as an abnormal screen
options.rationale: 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test is a first-line Endocrine Society AU-endorsed screen for Cushing syndrome; morning cortisol above 50 nmol/L is abnormal and prompts confirmatory testing.

options.text: Single 8 am morning serum cortisol level, with a value above the upper limit of normal (over 550 nmol/L) considered diagnostic of Cushing syndrome and prompting immediate imaging referral
options.rationale: Single morning cortisol has poor discrimination for Cushing; loss of diurnal rhythm and failure to suppress on DST are the screening tests.

options.text: Serum aldosterone-to-renin ratio measured in the morning after 2 hours upright posture as the initial screen given the hypertension and hypokalaemia are commonly associated with primary aldosteronism
options.rationale: ARR screens for primary aldosteronism, not Cushing; her clinical features (central obesity, striae, proximal weakness, plethora) point to Cushing.

options.text: MRI pituitary with dynamic contrast enhancement as the initial investigation given the classical clinical picture is highly suggestive of pituitary adenoma causing Cushing disease in this scenario today
options.rationale: Imaging follows biochemical confirmation; up to 10 percent of the population has incidental pituitary microadenomas so pre-biochemistry MRI misleads.

explanation.summary: Suspected Cushing syndrome is screened with one of three first-line tests: overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test, 24-hour urinary free cortisol (two collections), or late-night salivary cortisol (two samples). A positive screen requires a second abnormal test from the panel to confirm hypercortisolism before proceeding to ACTH and localisation. Single morning cortisol and pituitary MRI are not initial screens because they lack specificity or lead to incidentalomas.
key_points: 1 mg overnight DST is a first-line Cushing screen
Alternatives: 24 hr UFC (x2), late-night salivary cortisol (x2)
Need two abnormal tests before diagnostic confirmation
ACTH and imaging follow biochemical confirmation, not precede it
explanation.pearls: Common causes of false-positive DST include pregnancy, oestrogen therapy (raises CBG), rifampicin (accelerates dexamethasone metabolism), depression, chronic alcohol use and severe illness; check for these before pursuing confirmatory workup on an isolated abnormal screen.

subtopic_detail: Osteoporosis initial pharmacotherapy
stem: A 68-year-old post-menopausal woman is referred to your general practice for review after a low-trauma wrist fracture 4 weeks ago from a fall from standing height. She smokes 10 cigarettes daily, drinks 3 standard drinks daily and has been on prednisolone 7.5 mg orally daily for polymyalgia rheumatica for 8 months. Her DEXA scan shows lumbar spine T-score -2.8 and femoral neck T-score -2.5. Her mother had a hip fracture at age 74. Her calcium and vitamin D are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Mildly kyphotic thoracic spine; no acute back tenderness; no visible dental disease; no active infection
data_table.Investigations: DEXA lumbar T -2.8, femoral neck T -2.5; calcium 2.36 mmol/L (2.15 to 2.55), 25-OH vitamin D 68 nmol/L (>=50), eGFR 76 mL/min/1.73 m2; PTH 3.8 pmol/L (1.6 to 7.2), TSH 2.1 mIU/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: IV zoledronic acid 5 mg once yearly infusion as first-line pharmacotherapy as she has ongoing steroid exposure, and no dental review or renal check is required as her eGFR is above 35 mL/min
options.rationale: IV zoledronate is used when oral bisphosphonates are not tolerated or absorbed; oral alendronate is first-line in AU. Dental review remains prudent before any bisphosphonate.

options.text: Denosumab 60 mg subcutaneous every 6 months as first-line pharmacotherapy without any prior bisphosphonate trial and without long-term commitment to a follow-on antiresorptive after eventual cessation
options.rationale: Denosumab is a valid option but not first-line before an oral bisphosphonate trial; and it must be followed by a bisphosphonate on cessation to prevent rebound vertebral fractures, requiring long-term planning.

options.text: Teriparatide 20 microgram subcutaneous daily for 18 months as first-line anabolic therapy given the very low T-scores and glucocorticoid use as the anabolic pathway is more effective than antiresorptive
options.rationale: Teriparatide is used after antiresorptive failure or in severe osteoporosis with vertebral fractures; not first-line, is limited on PBS to specific criteria, and has an 18 to 24 month lifetime cap.

options.text: Oral alendronate 70 mg weekly on an empty stomach with 200 mL water and remain upright for 30 minutes, calcium and vitamin D optimisation, dental review before starting, and 5-year review
options.rationale: Post-menopausal osteoporosis with prior fragility fracture is a clear indication for oral bisphosphonate; alendronate is first-line PBS-listed with dental review before initiation for MRONJ risk mitigation.

options.text: Increase oral calcium to 1500 mg daily plus vitamin D 2000 IU daily and lifestyle modification alone for 12 months, review DEXA at 12 months before considering any specific antiresorptive therapy
options.rationale: Calcium and vitamin D alone do not reduce fracture risk sufficiently in established osteoporosis after fragility fracture; pharmacotherapy is required.

explanation.summary: Post-menopausal osteoporosis with a fragility fracture, T-score <=-2.5 at hip or spine, or chronic glucocorticoid exposure warrants first-line oral bisphosphonate therapy (alendronate 70 mg weekly or risedronate 35 mg weekly) with calcium and vitamin D optimisation, dental review to reduce MRONJ risk, and 5-yearly reassessment. IV zoledronate is second-line for intolerance. Denosumab is an alternative but requires follow-on antiresorptive on cessation. Teriparatide is reserved for severe or bisphosphonate-refractory disease.
key_points: First-line pharmacotherapy: oral alendronate or risedronate
Dental review before bisphosphonate for MRONJ risk mitigation
IV zoledronate second-line if oral intolerance
Denosumab needs follow-on bisphosphonate to prevent rebound fractures
explanation.pearls: Bisphosphonate holiday after 5 years of oral therapy is considered for low-risk patients but not for those with continuing high risk (prior vertebral fracture, femoral neck T -2.5, ongoing glucocorticoid use); a repeat DEXA and clinical assessment guide the decision.

subtopic_detail: Endocarditis Duke criteria and empiric therapy
stem: A 62-year-old man presents to your emergency department with 2 weeks of intermittent fevers, night sweats and 4 kg weight loss. He had a bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement 3 months ago. On examination he has a new soft early diastolic murmur, splinter haemorrhages under two fingernails and tender nodules on the pulp of his index finger. Three sets of blood cultures drawn 1 hour apart are all positive for Streptococcus gallolyticus (bovis). Transthoracic echo shows a mobile 1.2 cm echogenic mass on the aortic prosthesis with mild aortic regurgitation.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96, BP 132/62, RR 18, SpO2 96 percent, temp 38.4 C
data_table.Examination: Splinter haemorrhages under two fingernails; tender pulp nodules on index finger (Osler nodes); new soft early diastolic aortic murmur; no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Blood cultures x3 all positive S. gallolyticus; TTE 1.2 cm mobile aortic prosthesis vegetation; mild AR; CRP 92 mg/L (<5); WCC 15 x10^9/L; creatinine 92 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management combination?

options.text: IV vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading then 15 mg/kg every 12 hours monotherapy for 6 weeks and defer any surgical review or transoesophageal echo pending clinical improvement over the next 5 to 7 days
options.rationale: Vancomycin monotherapy is not optimal for penicillin-susceptible streptococcal endocarditis and delaying TOE plus surgical consult in prosthetic valve endocarditis with regurgitation risks disease progression.

options.text: IV ceftriaxone 2 g daily monotherapy for 4 weeks and observation without cardiothoracic surgical consultation as vegetations under 2 cm rarely embolise and the mild aortic regurgitation is stable
options.rationale: Prosthetic valve endocarditis warrants combination therapy with gentamicin for 2 to 6 weeks under AU guidelines; and cardiothoracic surgical consultation is mandatory in prosthetic valve endocarditis for shared surgical decision making.

options.text: IV benzylpenicillin 2.4 g every 4 hours plus IV gentamicin 3 mg/kg daily for 6 weeks total, arrange transoesophageal echo, colonoscopy for occult colorectal malignancy and cardiothoracic surgery review
options.rationale: This meets modified Duke definite endocarditis (two major: positive typical organism and vegetation on echo); AU regimen for streptococcal PVE is benzylpenicillin plus low-dose gentamicin; S. gallolyticus mandates colonoscopy for occult colorectal cancer.

options.text: IV flucloxacillin 2 g every 4 hours plus IV rifampicin 600 mg orally twice daily for suspected staphylococcal prosthetic valve endocarditis empirically before waiting for the confirmed culture identification
options.rationale: Culture is confirmed as S. gallolyticus, not S. aureus; flucloxacillin does not cover streptococci and rifampicin is only added for staphylococcal PVE, not streptococcal.

options.text: Broad-spectrum empirical piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours pending susceptibility results, with home IV therapy commenced through the outpatient antimicrobial program once afebrile for 48 hours
options.rationale: PVE in the first 12 months post surgery does not have the microbiology of community endocarditis and needs inpatient management for at least the first 2 weeks per AU guidance; and piperacillin-tazobactam is not the streptococcal PVE regimen.

explanation.summary: Modified Duke criteria diagnose definite infective endocarditis when there are 2 major (typical organism in 2+ blood cultures, echocardiographic evidence of endocardial involvement), or 1 major plus 3 minor, or 5 minor criteria. AU regimen for streptococcal prosthetic valve endocarditis is benzylpenicillin 2.4 g IV every 4 hours plus low-dose gentamicin 3 mg/kg daily for 6 weeks. Prosthetic valve endocarditis mandates transoesophageal echocardiogram, cardiothoracic surgical review and colonoscopy for S. gallolyticus.
key_points: Modified Duke: 2 major, or 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor = definite
Streptococcal PVE: benzylpenicillin + gentamicin 6 weeks
S. gallolyticus mandates colonoscopy for occult colorectal cancer
PVE always needs TOE and cardiothoracic surgical review
explanation.pearls: Surgical indications for infective endocarditis include heart failure from valve dysfunction, uncontrolled infection despite adequate antibiotics after 5 to 7 days, large vegetations (>10 mm) with embolic phenomena and paravalvular abscess or dehiscence; early surgery in the first week improves outcomes when these are present.

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis recognition and management
stem: A 43-year-old woman with a background of Hashimoto thyroiditis on levothyroxine presents to your emergency department with 2 days of vomiting, abdominal pain and profound fatigue. She has felt increasingly weak, dizzy on standing and salt-craving over 3 months. She is otherwise on no medications. On examination she has hyperpigmentation of her palmar creases, buccal mucosa and recent surgical scar from an appendicectomy 10 years ago. Blood pressure is 78/48 mmHg. She is severely dehydrated and has never taken glucocorticoids.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, BP 78/48, RR 22, SpO2 98 percent, temp 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Hyperpigmented palmar creases, buccal mucosa, old surgical scar; dry mucous membranes; supine BP drops from 92 to 78/48 on sitting; peripherally cool; no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Na 122 mmol/L (135 to 145), K 5.8 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), glucose 3.2 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), urea 12 mmol/L, creatinine 108 micromol/L, TSH 4.8 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), VBG pH 7.32; morning cortisol pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: IV dexamethasone 4 mg stat before drawing morning cortisol and ACTH samples, IV Hartmann 1000 mL over the first hour and observe supine BP before further pharmacological intervention
options.rationale: Hartmann contains potassium which may worsen hyperkalaemia in acute adrenal crisis; and dexamethasone lacks mineralocorticoid activity so hydrocortisone is preferred.

options.text: Increase levothyroxine to 200 microgram orally daily for suspected myxoedema coma, IV normal saline 500 mL over 30 minutes and cover with ceftriaxone 2 g pending source review of infection today
options.rationale: Increasing levothyroxine before glucocorticoid replacement in adrenal insufficiency precipitates further crisis by increasing cortisol clearance; hydrocortisone must be given first.

options.text: IV insulin actrapid 5 unit and 50 mL 50 percent dextrose for hyperkalaemia, IV calcium gluconate 10 mL 10 percent for cardioprotection and IV frusemide 40 mg for potassium excretion while awaiting cortisol
options.rationale: Insulin risks worsening hypoglycaemia in a hypoglycaemic patient; the definitive treatment is hydrocortisone and saline which correct all three electrolyte and glucose derangements.

options.text: Observation with strict input output monitoring and repeat serum cortisol at 8 am the following day before commencing any glucocorticoid replacement to avoid confounding the diagnostic biochemistry today
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis is a clinical diagnosis and treatment is empirical before confirmation; delay for a morning cortisol risks death.

options.text: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat then 200 mg over 24 hours infusion, IV normal saline 1000 mL over first hour, IV 10 percent dextrose 500 mL for hypoglycaemia and hold the levothyroxine dose today
options.rationale: Hyperpigmentation with hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia and hypotension in a woman with autoimmune thyroid disease is primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison) in crisis; empirical hydrocortisone before biochemical confirmation is life-saving.

explanation.summary: Primary adrenal insufficiency in crisis presents with hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia and hyperpigmentation from ACTH excess. Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome (with Hashimoto thyroiditis) is a classical association. Immediate management is IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat then 200 mg over 24 hours infusion, IV normal saline for volume, dextrose for hypoglycaemia and treat any precipitant. Levothyroxine is held until glucocorticoid replacement is established to prevent worsening the crisis.
key_points: Hyperpigmentation + hyponatraemia + hyperkalaemia = primary adrenal insufficiency
IV hydrocortisone stat then 24 hr infusion is life-saving
Normal saline not Hartmann; dextrose for hypoglycaemia
Hold levothyroxine until glucocorticoid replacement established
explanation.pearls: Short synacthen test (250 microgram synthetic ACTH with cortisol at 0 and 30 min, expecting a peak above 500 nmol/L) confirms the diagnosis when done at least 24 hours after any hydrocortisone dose or by using dexamethasone as bridging therapy in the interim to avoid interference.

subtopic_detail: Necrotising fasciitis recognition
stem: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents to your emergency department with 24 hours of severe left leg pain out of proportion to the visible skin appearance. He fell in the garden 3 days ago with a small abrasion to his left shin. Today the leg is swollen with a small area of erythema over the shin. His HR is 128, BP 96/60, temperature 39.2 C. He is confused and cold peripherally. On palpation there is crepitus over the calf and pain extending well beyond the visible erythema.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, BP 96/60, RR 26, SpO2 96 percent, temp 39.2 C, cap refill 4 seconds, GCS 13
data_table.Examination: Small erythematous patch over shin with a 5 mm scab; pain and swelling extending well beyond visible erythema; crepitus on palpation of calf; foot cool with intact pulses; no bullae yet
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22 x10^9/L (4 to 11), CRP 285 mg/L (<5), Na 128 mmol/L (135 to 145), creatinine 168 micromol/L (<110), glucose 15.6 mmol/L, Hb 118 g/L, lactate 4.2 mmol/L (<2), CK 890 U/L (<200)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Urgent surgical consultation for wide debridement in theatre within 1 hour, IV meropenem 1 g and IV clindamycin 900 mg empirically, IV fluid resuscitation and blood cultures without delaying surgery
options.rationale: Pain out of proportion, crepitus, systemic toxicity and LRINEC-high biochemistry (WCC, Na, CRP, glucose, creatinine, Hb) in a diabetic point strongly to necrotising fasciitis; surgery within an hour is the intervention that improves survival.

options.text: IV flucloxacillin 2 g every 6 hours for standard cellulitis, IV normal saline 500 mL bolus, elevate the leg and mark the erythema border for reassessment in 4 hours before deciding on any further imaging
options.rationale: Cellulitis regimen misses the surgical urgency of necrotising fasciitis; pain out of proportion, crepitus and systemic toxicity mandate immediate surgical exploration.

options.text: CT lower limb with IV contrast to confirm gas in tissue planes before surgical consultation, with commencement of vancomycin and cefepime broad-spectrum antibiotics once radiological confirmation is obtained
options.rationale: Imaging must not delay surgery in suspected necrotising fasciitis; clinical diagnosis warrants immediate theatre for debridement and empirical antibiotics simultaneously.

options.text: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy referral as adjunctive treatment before surgical debridement is performed, with IV benzylpenicillin monotherapy for suspected clostridial gas gangrene from the garden wound
options.rationale: HBOT is adjunctive after debridement, not before; delay of surgery to arrange HBOT costs lives, and monotherapy misses the polymicrobial nature of type I necrotising fasciitis.

options.text: IV ceftriaxone 2 g monotherapy with tetanus booster and topical mupirocin to the abrasion, planned admission to the medical ward for observation and outpatient surgical review within 48 hours if the pain persists
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone monotherapy does not cover the polymicrobial spectrum or provide clindamycin's antitoxin effect; and ward observation delays life-saving debridement.

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency: features include pain out of proportion to examination, systemic toxicity, crepitus and haemorrhagic bullae later. LRINEC scoring supports suspicion using CRP, WCC, sodium, creatinine, haemoglobin and glucose. Management is immediate surgical exploration and wide debridement within 1 hour, empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics (meropenem plus clindamycin for antitoxin effect), IV fluid resuscitation and ICU-level supportive care. Imaging must never delay surgery.
key_points: Pain out of proportion + crepitus + systemic toxicity = suspect necrotising fasciitis
Surgical debridement within 1 hour is the priority
Empirical meropenem + clindamycin (antitoxin)
Never delay surgery for imaging
explanation.pearls: Add IV vancomycin if MRSA is prevalent in the community or hospital, and IV benzylpenicillin plus clindamycin for suspected group A streptococcal cases (LRINEC does not distinguish types); definitive antibiotics narrow once operative cultures return.

subtopic_detail: Type A aortic dissection recognition and initial management
stem: A 64-year-old man with a history of poorly controlled hypertension presents to your emergency department with 45 minutes of sudden severe tearing chest pain radiating to his back. He is diaphoretic and looks unwell. On examination his right arm BP is 178/98 and left arm BP is 128/72. He has a soft early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge. ECG shows sinus rhythm with 1 mm ST depression in V4 to V6 without ST elevation. Bedside troponin is mildly elevated at 42 ng/L (<14).

data_table.Vital signs: HR 108, BP 178/98 right arm and 128/72 left arm, RR 22, SpO2 96 percent, temp 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, alert; soft early diastolic murmur at LSE; right radial pulse full, left radial reduced volume; symmetrical lower limb pulses; no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus rhythm, 1 mm ST depression V4 to V6, no STE; troponin 42 ng/L (<14); chest X-ray widened mediastinum >8 cm; VBG pH 7.34, lactate 2.4 mmol/L (<2); creatinine 108 micromol/L (<110)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: IV sodium nitroprusside infusion titrated to systolic BP 100 to 120 mmHg first, then IV metoprolol 5 mg boluses for rate control, plus IV aspirin 300 mg and heparin 5000 units for acute coronary syndrome
options.rationale: Vasodilator alone increases reflex tachycardia and worsens aortic wall shear stress; beta-blockade must be given first. Antiplatelet and anticoagulant are contraindicated in suspected dissection.

options.text: IV labetalol infusion titrated to HR 60 and systolic BP 100 to 120 mmHg first before any vasodilator, urgent CT aortogram, cardiothoracic surgical activation, and hold antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy for now
options.rationale: The tearing pain, inter-arm BP differential, aortic regurgitation murmur and widened mediastinum are classical type A aortic dissection; the AU order is negative chronotrope and beta-blockade before vasodilator to reduce shear (dP/dt), urgent CT and cardiothoracic activation.

options.text: Immediate cardiac catheterisation for suspected NSTEMI given the ST depression, elevated troponin and chest pain, deferring aortic imaging until angiography excludes an acute coronary syndrome first
options.rationale: Angiography and anticoagulation on this NSTE presentation would kill a dissection patient; a widened mediastinum and inter-arm BP differential warrant aortogram before cath.

options.text: IV hydralazine 20 mg bolus every 20 minutes for BP control, oral aspirin 300 mg loading, oral clopidogrel 300 mg loading and admit to the coronary care unit for continuous cardiac monitoring overnight
options.rationale: Hydralazine increases reflex tachycardia and shear stress in dissection; and antiplatelet loading is contraindicated. Beta-blockade first, not hydralazine.

options.text: Thrombolysis with alteplase 100 mg IV over 90 minutes for suspected STEMI equivalent posterior wall infarction given the persistent ST depression V4 to V6 in this high risk chest pain presentation today
options.rationale: Thrombolysis in an unrecognised dissection is invariably fatal; the ST depression here reflects demand ischaemia from coronary compromise or dissection propagation, not STEMI equivalent that meets criteria.

explanation.summary: Type A aortic dissection presents with abrupt tearing chest and back pain, inter-arm blood pressure differential, aortic regurgitation from proximal extension, widened mediastinum on chest X-ray and pulse deficits. Immediate management is IV beta-blockade (labetalol or esmolol) titrated to HR 60 and systolic BP 100 to 120 mmHg before any vasodilator to minimise dP/dt and aortic wall shear stress; urgent CT aortogram and cardiothoracic surgical activation. Antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy is held pending imaging. Definitive management of type A is emergency open surgical repair.
key_points: Tearing pain + inter-arm BP differential + widened mediastinum = suspect dissection
Beta-blockade FIRST (target HR 60), then vasodilator (target SBP 100 to 120)
Urgent CT aortogram and cardiothoracic activation
Withhold antiplatelet and anticoagulant pending diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Type A dissection (involving the ascending aorta) is a surgical emergency with mortality rising 1 percent per hour; type B (descending only, distal to left subclavian) is managed medically unless complicated by malperfusion, rupture or refractory pain and hypertension, when thoracic endovascular aortic repair is considered.

subtopic_detail: Community-acquired pneumonia
stem: You are the medical registrar in an Australian metropolitan emergency department reviewing a 62-year-old man with 4 days of productive cough, right-sided pleuritic chest pain, fever and progressive breathlessness. He has type 2 diabetes and hypertension. His medications are metformin, perindopril and atorvastatin. He is not immunocompromised. He lives independently and has had no recent hospital admissions or overseas travel. He is up to date with pneumococcal and influenza vaccination. On examination he has bronchial breathing in the right mid-zone and dullness to percussion. Chest radiograph shows dense right middle-lobe consolidation without effusion.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 108, blood pressure 108/64, respiratory rate 28, SpO2 91% on room air, temperature 38.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: white cells 15.6 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), CRP 168 mg/L (<5), sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), urea 9.1 mmol/L (2.5-7.5), creatinine 88 micromol/L (60-110), lactate 2.4 mmol/L (<2), albumin 34 g/L (35-50), venous pH 7.36 (7.35-7.45), chest radiograph right middle-lobe consolidation without effusion
data_table.History: T2DM, hypertension, up to date pneumococcal and influenza, lives independently, no recent hospitalisation, no travel, no immunosuppression

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial antibiotic regimen and disposition?

options.text: Discharge home on oral amoxicillin 1 g every 8 hours for 5 days with general practitioner review at 48 hours
options.rationale: SMART-COP score is at least 3 (S=0 systolic 108, M=1 multilobar, A=1 albumin 34, R=1 respiratory rate 28, T=0, C=0, O=1 SpO2 91%, P=1 pH not <7.35 so 0) placing him in moderate to high risk. Discharging home understates severity. (Source: eTG Antibiotic CAP)

options.text: Admit to ward on intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily as monotherapy
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone monotherapy at 1 g daily is used for uncomplicated moderate CAP requiring admission in some Australian guidelines, but the correct benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline combination is the Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic recommendation for moderate CAP without severe features. Ceftriaxone is reserved for severe CAP or when benzylpenicillin is contraindicated. (Source: eTG Antibiotic CAP)

options.text: Admit to intensive care on intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam plus intravenous vancomycin loading dose
options.rationale: Broad-spectrum coverage is reserved for severe CAP requiring ICU support (SMART-COP >=5) or high-risk features such as recent hospitalisation, aspiration risk with structural lung disease, or bronchiectasis. This patient does not meet these criteria. (Source: eTG Antibiotic CAP)

options.text: Admit to ward on oral clarithromycin 500 mg every 12 hours as macrolide monotherapy for 5 days total
options.rationale: Macrolide monotherapy is inadequate for moderate CAP in Australia because of high pneumococcal resistance. Australian guidance uses beta-lactam plus atypical cover. (Source: eTG Antibiotic CAP)

options.text: Admit to ward on intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 6 hours plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily
options.rationale: Australian Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic first-line therapy for moderate CAP requiring admission is IV benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg BD (or oral clarithromycin) to cover atypicals. SMART-COP score of at least 3 places him in the moderate-to-high risk group warranting admission and IV therapy with switch to oral after 48 hours if improving. (Source: eTG Antibiotic CAP)

explanation.summary: Moderate community-acquired pneumonia in Australia (SMART-COP 3 to 4) requires hospital admission and combination antibiotic therapy targeting pneumococcus and atypical organisms. IV benzylpenicillin plus oral doxycycline is the Therapeutic Guidelines first-line regimen. Ceftriaxone is reserved for severe CAP or beta-lactam alternatives; broader-spectrum agents for ICU-level severity or specific risk factors.
key_points: SMART-COP >=3 = moderate; >=5 = severe warranting ICU consideration
Moderate CAP: IV benzylpenicillin 1.2 g q6h + doxycycline 100 mg BD
Severe CAP or ICU: IV ceftriaxone 1 g daily + azithromycin 500 mg IV daily (moxifloxacin if pen allergy)
Switch to oral after 48 hours of clinical improvement; total 5-7 days
explanation.pearls: SMART-COP awards 2 points each for systolic <90 mmHg, SpO2 <=90%, and pH <7.35 (all considered severe features), 1 point each for the other criteria. Score >=3 predicts intensive respiratory or vasopressor support.

subtopic_detail: Provoked DVT anticoagulation duration
stem: You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 54-year-old man 3 months after diagnosis of a right proximal femoral vein deep vein thrombosis. The DVT occurred 4 weeks after right total knee replacement with a 6-week postoperative period of significantly reduced mobility. He has no family history of thrombosis, no prior VTE, no active malignancy, no antiphospholipid syndrome, and no ongoing prothrombotic risk factors. He has completed 3 months of apixaban 5 mg twice daily without bleeding, has walked without ongoing swelling for the past 6 weeks, and has returned to normal daily activity. He asks how long he needs to remain on anticoagulation.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 72, blood pressure 128/78, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 138 g/L (135-170), platelets 240 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 78 micromol/L (60-110), eGFR >90 mL/min/1.73 m2, LFTs within normal limits, D-dimer not indicated at this time
data_table.History: 3 months of apixaban 5 mg BD after post-arthroplasty proximal DVT, no ongoing bleeding, no residual swelling for 6 weeks, no personal or family thrombotic history, no cancer or APS

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation plan from today?

options.text: Stop apixaban now and provide written advice on venous thromboembolism prevention for future surgery
options.rationale: This is a proximal DVT clearly provoked by a major transient risk factor (total knee replacement with post-operative immobility). Australian and international haematology guidance (Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand; ASH 2020) recommend cessation of anticoagulation at 3 months in this scenario because the annual recurrence risk after stopping is under 3%, similar to the annual major bleeding risk on ongoing therapy. Patient counselling about recognition of recurrence and future perioperative prophylaxis is essential. (Source: THANZ VTE guidelines)

options.text: Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily indefinitely as extended anticoagulation for the proximal deep vein thrombosis
options.rationale: Indefinite anticoagulation is reserved for unprovoked DVT, active cancer-associated VTE, or recurrent VTE. A proximal DVT provoked by a major transient risk factor does not meet indefinite therapy criteria and exposes the patient to unnecessary bleeding risk. (Source: THANZ VTE guidelines)

options.text: Reduce apixaban to 2.5 mg twice daily and continue indefinitely as extended prophylactic anticoagulation
options.rationale: The extended low-dose apixaban regimen (2.5 mg BD after initial 6 months) is used for unprovoked VTE where the decision is to continue anticoagulation but reduce bleeding risk. It does not apply to a clearly provoked VTE where cessation is preferred at 3 months. (Source: THANZ VTE guidelines)

options.text: Switch to aspirin 100 mg daily indefinitely as extended venous thromboembolism recurrence prevention
options.rationale: Aspirin has been studied for extended VTE prevention (ASPIRE, WARFASA) with only modest recurrence reduction and is inferior to DOAC continuation. It is not the standard approach after cessation of anticoagulation for a provoked DVT and adds bleeding risk without clear benefit here. (Source: THANZ VTE guidelines)

options.text: Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily for a further 3 months then stop and provide written VTE advice
options.rationale: Extending anticoagulation to 6 months for a proximal DVT provoked by a major transient risk factor confers no reduction in long-term recurrence relative to 3 months and adds bleeding exposure. Total therapy of 3 months is the standard duration. (Source: THANZ VTE guidelines)

explanation.summary: Anticoagulation duration for VTE depends on whether the event was provoked by a major transient factor (surgery, hospitalisation, trauma), a persistent factor, cancer, or unprovoked. Proximal DVT provoked by a major transient factor is treated for 3 months and stopped. Unprovoked or persistent-risk-factor VTE is considered for indefinite therapy weighing bleeding risk. Cancer-associated VTE typically receives extended DOAC or LMWH while the cancer is active.
key_points: Proximal DVT with major transient provoking factor -> 3 months anticoagulation then stop
Unprovoked proximal DVT -> at least 3 months then consider indefinite with periodic bleed-risk review
Cancer-associated VTE -> extended DOAC (edoxaban or apixaban) or LMWH while cancer active
Extended-phase apixaban dose is 2.5 mg twice daily; rivaroxaban 10 mg daily
explanation.pearls: For provoked distal (calf) DVT, 3 months of anticoagulation is often adequate but shorter courses (6 weeks) may suffice for isolated calf DVT with a clear provoking factor and reliable serial imaging follow-up.

subtopic_detail: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes
stem: You are the emergency department registrar. A 71-year-old man with chronic kidney disease stage 4 (baseline creatinine 260 micromol/L, eGFR 20 mL/min/1.73 m2) is brought in by paramedics for progressive weakness over 2 days. He takes perindopril, spironolactone and slow-K supplementation for prior hypokalaemia (last review 6 months ago). ECG on arrival shows peaked T waves in V2 to V5 and a prolonged PR interval of 240 ms. He is awake, chest is clear, no ischaemic chest pain, blood pressure and heart rate are stable. Point-of-care venous gas gives potassium 7.4 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 68, blood pressure 138/78, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: potassium 7.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0) on VBG, sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), bicarbonate 18 mmol/L (22-32), creatinine 340 micromol/L (60-110) vs baseline 260, glucose 6.8 mmol/L (3.5-6.0), pH 7.28 (7.35-7.45), ECG peaked T waves V2-V5 and PR 240 ms
data_table.History: CKD stage 4 baseline creatinine 260, medications perindopril, spironolactone, slow-K, no chest pain, no diabetes-related hypoglycaemia risk

lead_in: Which intervention should you perform FIRST?

options.text: Give intravenous insulin 10 units in 50 mL of 50% glucose over 20 minutes as the initial hyperkalaemia therapy
options.rationale: Insulin-glucose shifts potassium intracellularly and is a subsequent step, but does not immediately stabilise the myocardium. In the presence of ECG changes, calcium is given first because cardiac stabilisation cannot wait for the 20-30 minute onset of insulin-driven shift. (Source: eTG Fluids and Electrolytes: Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: Give intravenous calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL over 2 to 5 minutes with continuous cardiac rhythm monitoring
options.rationale: With hyperkalaemia and ECG changes (peaked T waves, PR prolongation), calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL over 2 to 5 minutes is the first-line intervention to stabilise the cardiac membrane. Onset is within 2 to 3 minutes and duration is 30 to 60 minutes. Subsequent steps shift and remove potassium. Cease perindopril, spironolactone and slow-K; consider renal replacement early in dialysis-eligible CKD stage 4. (Source: eTG Fluids and Electrolytes: Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: Give nebulised salbutamol 10 mg over 10 minutes as the initial intracellular potassium-shift therapy
options.rationale: Salbutamol shifts potassium intracellularly and can reduce serum potassium by 0.5 to 1 mmol/L, but the onset is 15 to 30 minutes and it does not stabilise the myocardium during that window. It is adjunctive after calcium and insulin-glucose. (Source: eTG Fluids and Electrolytes: Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: Give oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate 30 g with sorbitol as the initial potassium-removal therapy
options.rationale: Cation-exchange resins remove potassium slowly over hours and do not address acute myocardial risk. Their efficacy and safety are also debated (colonic necrosis) and they are not the first step in acute hyperkalaemia with ECG changes. (Source: eTG Fluids and Electrolytes: Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: Call renal services for urgent haemodialysis today and defer any other therapy until dialysis can start
options.rationale: Dialysis is often the definitive treatment for CKD stage 4 with symptomatic hyperkalaemia unresponsive to medical management, but arranging dialysis takes time. Immediate myocardial stabilisation with calcium cannot be deferred. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyperkalaemia)

explanation.summary: In hyperkalaemia with ECG changes, calcium gluconate is given first to stabilise the cardiac membrane. Insulin-glucose (with or without salbutamol) then shifts potassium into cells. Definitive removal is achieved by cessation of contributing agents, potassium-binding resins or haemodialysis. In CKD stage 4 or 5 with severe or refractory hyperkalaemia, early nephrology involvement for haemodialysis is essential.
key_points: Any hyperkalaemia with ECG changes -> calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL IV first
Then insulin 10 units IV with 50 mL 50% glucose over 20 min (monitor BSL 1-2 hourly for 6 h)
Adjunct salbutamol 10-20 mg nebulised for additional potassium shift
Definitive removal: cease offending drugs, potassium binders, haemodialysis if refractory or CKD
explanation.pearls: Insulin-glucose hypoglycaemia risk peaks 1-2 hours post-dose; monitor blood glucose for at least 6 hours after administration.

subtopic_detail: Sepsis hour-1 bundle and vasopressor initiation
stem: You are the medical registrar in an Australian emergency department. A 68-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and moderate CKD (baseline creatinine 130 micromol/L) is brought in with rigors, dysuria, right-flank pain and confusion. She is quickly recognised as having urosepsis. Within 30 minutes she has received IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg and IV amoxicillin-clavulanate. She has received 30 mL/kg of balanced crystalloid over 90 minutes. Her repeat lactate 60 minutes after starting fluids has risen from 4.2 to 5.1 mmol/L. She remains hypotensive with mean arterial pressure of 58 mmHg despite the completed bolus. Blood cultures were drawn before antibiotics.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 118, blood pressure 82/44 (MAP 58), respiratory rate 26, SpO2 96% on 4 L nasal prongs, temperature 39.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: white cells 22.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), CRP 316 mg/L (<5), lactate 5.1 mmol/L (was 4.2), sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 240 micromol/L (baseline 130), venous pH 7.28 (7.35-7.45), bicarbonate 16 mmol/L, urinalysis heavy nitrites and blood
data_table.History: T2DM, CKD baseline creatinine 130, urosepsis on antibiotics for 45 minutes, 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid completed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give a further 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus over 60 minutes and reassess lactate and blood pressure in one hour
options.rationale: The Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 bundle recommends initial crystalloid 30 mL/kg. Repeat 30 mL/kg fluid boluses beyond the initial resuscitation risk pulmonary oedema without addressing MAP. When MAP <65 after adequate initial fluid, vasopressor initiation is preferred rather than repeated boluses. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Commence peripheral noradrenaline infusion via a large-bore antecubital vein while central access is being established
options.rationale: The SSC and ANZICS guidance is to start noradrenaline early when MAP remains under 65 despite adequate initial crystalloid (30 mL/kg). Peripheral noradrenaline infusion through a large-bore proximal vein (antecubital or larger) is now supported for up to 24 hours or bridging to central access, and delays from waiting for central access are associated with worse outcomes. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Give intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg loading dose before starting vasopressor therapy for septic shock
options.rationale: Hydrocortisone is added when noradrenaline requirement exceeds 0.25 microgram/kg/min or when shock is refractory. It is not routinely given before vasopressor initiation. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Escalate to intravenous meropenem 1 g plus vancomycin loading dose 25 mg/kg for likely resistant urosepsis coverage
options.rationale: For community-acquired urosepsis, gentamicin plus amoxicillin-clavulanate provides adequate empiric coverage per Australian Therapeutic Guidelines. Escalation to broader spectrum with MRSA cover is not indicated in this scenario and does not address the immediate perfusion failure. (Source: eTG Antibiotic Urosepsis)

options.text: Delay commencing vasopressor therapy until the mean arterial pressure falls below 55 mmHg despite ongoing fluids
options.rationale: Delaying vasopressor risks prolonged tissue hypoperfusion. MAP target is 65 mmHg or above after initial fluid resuscitation; failure to meet this triggers noradrenaline. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

explanation.summary: Rising lactate 60 minutes after adequate initial crystalloid resuscitation with persistent MAP under 65 mmHg indicates fluid-refractory septic shock. The Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 bundle then calls for noradrenaline titrated to MAP at least 65 mmHg. Peripheral noradrenaline through a large-bore proximal vein is acceptable as a bridge to central access. Hydrocortisone is added if vasopressor requirement is high (typically noradrenaline >=0.25 microgram/kg/min).
key_points: Hour-1 sepsis bundle: measure lactate, blood cultures before antibiotics, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, 30 mL/kg crystalloid, vasopressor if MAP <65 after fluid
Noradrenaline is first-line vasopressor; peripheral use safe as bridge to central access
MAP target 65 mmHg or above (higher in chronic hypertension may be considered)
Add hydrocortisone 200 mg/day if noradrenaline >=0.25 mcg/kg/min or refractory
explanation.pearls: The 30 mL/kg initial fluid bolus is calculated on actual body weight in most Australian ED protocols; use ideal body weight in class III obesity to avoid over-resuscitation.

subtopic_detail: First demyelinating event and McDonald criteria
stem: You are the neurology registrar reviewing a 28-year-old woman referred by her general practitioner. Over the last 10 days she has developed progressive vision loss in her right eye with pain on eye movement. Ten months ago she had a 3-week episode of numbness across the right hemibody that resolved fully and she attributed it to stress and did not seek medical review at the time. She has no other medical history and takes no medications. On examination today her right visual acuity is 6/24 with a right relative afferent pupillary defect and a subtle red desaturation on the right; left eye 6/6. Neurological examination is otherwise normal. Fundoscopy shows a mildly swollen right optic disc.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 76, blood pressure 122/78, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, TSH within normal limits, HIV and syphilis serology negative, ANA negative, vitamin B12 380 pmol/L (>200), MRI brain and spine shows one enhancing right optic nerve lesion plus 4 non-enhancing periventricular T2 lesions plus 1 spinal cord T2 lesion at C4 plus 1 juxtacortical T2 lesion, no infratentorial lesion, CSF oligoclonal bands positive (not present in serum), aquaporin-4 antibody negative, MOG-IgG negative
data_table.History: 10 months ago transient right hemibody numbness for 3 weeks, now right optic neuritis, no other medical history, no medications

lead_in: What is the most appropriate diagnostic conclusion and next step?

options.text: Clinically isolated syndrome with insufficient evidence for a multiple sclerosis diagnosis; repeat magnetic resonance imaging in 3 months
options.rationale: The prior transient hemibody numbness followed by optic neuritis today represents two clinical attacks in different sites, and MRI demonstrates lesions in more than one typical MS location. Dissemination in space and time is met, so a diagnosis of multiple sclerosis can be made now rather than deferring to CIS. (Source: RACP Multiple Sclerosis Diagnosis)

options.text: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder based on optic and spinal cord involvement; commence rituximab this admission
options.rationale: Aquaporin-4 antibody negative, MOG-IgG negative, the MRI pattern (multiple typical MS locations without long spinal cord lesions >=3 vertebral segments), and CSF pattern all favour MS over NMOSD. Rituximab is not first-line without a NMOSD diagnosis. (Source: RACP Multiple Sclerosis Diagnosis)

options.text: Relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis meeting 2017 McDonald criteria; give IV methylprednisolone and refer for DMT
options.rationale: This patient has two clinical attacks (prior hemibody sensory episode plus current optic neuritis) with objective clinical evidence for the current attack (relative afferent pupillary defect, reduced acuity, red desaturation, swollen disc). MRI shows lesions in at least two of the four typical MS locations (periventricular, juxtacortical, cortical, infratentorial, spinal cord), satisfying dissemination in space. CSF-specific oligoclonal bands provide additional support and can substitute for dissemination in time under 2017 criteria. Acute optic neuritis is treated with IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 to 5 days; DMT selection is a neurologist-led decision. (Source: RACP Multiple Sclerosis Diagnosis)

options.text: Myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein-antibody-associated disease; commence high-dose oral prednisone taper only today
options.rationale: MOG-IgG is negative in this patient and the MRI does not show characteristic MOG features (long spinal cord or bilateral optic nerve lesions). Steroid monotherapy alone is not the appropriate long-term approach for MS. (Source: RACP Multiple Sclerosis Diagnosis)

options.text: Anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor encephalitis; refer for ovarian teratoma workup and plasmapheresis this admission
options.rationale: Anti-NMDA encephalitis presents with subacute psychiatric symptoms, seizures, movement disorders and autonomic instability rather than optic neuritis with typical MS MRI findings and MS-pattern oligoclonal bands. (Source: RACP Multiple Sclerosis Diagnosis)

explanation.summary: Two clinical attacks with objective evidence for at least one and MRI dissemination in space (lesions in at least two typical MS locations) satisfy the 2017 McDonald criteria for relapsing-remitting MS at first neurology contact. CSF-specific oligoclonal bands can substitute for dissemination in time. Acute optic neuritis is treated with IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 to 5 days. Disease-modifying therapy selection is neurologist-led and depends on disease activity, comorbidities and pregnancy plans.
key_points: 2017 McDonald criteria: DIS = lesion in >=2 of 4 typical MS regions (periventricular, juxtacortical/cortical, infratentorial, spinal); DIT = simultaneous asymptomatic + symptomatic lesion or new lesion on follow-up MRI or CSF-specific OCBs
Acute optic neuritis: IV methylprednisolone 1 g/day for 3-5 days; hastens recovery but does not change final visual outcome (ONTT)
DMT choice ranges from teriflunomide/glatiramer/interferon to natalizumab, ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, cladribine
Negative AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG plus positive OCBs supports MS over NMOSD/MOGAD
explanation.pearls: The Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial showed IV methylprednisolone accelerates visual recovery in first 2 weeks but does not affect final visual acuity at 12 months; oral prednisone alone showed higher relapse rate.

subtopic_detail: Haemodynamically unstable pulmonary embolism
stem: You are the medical registrar in the emergency department resuscitation cubicle. A 62-year-old man presented 20 minutes ago with sudden onset dyspnoea and syncope 40 minutes after arriving from an interstate flight. He is now clammy, breathless and confused. Point-of-care ultrasound shows a dilated right ventricle with poor contractility. Bedside troponin is 380 ng/L (upper reference 30) and NT-proBNP is 3400 pg/mL. He weighs 92 kg. His IV access is patent. He has no active bleeding, no recent surgery, no stroke, no known intracranial pathology, no bleeding disorder, no anticoagulation, no allergy. His wife confirms no head injury and no gastrointestinal bleeding in the last month.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 76/42, respiratory rate 34, SpO2 88% on 15 L non-rebreather, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: troponin 380 ng/L (<30), NT-proBNP 3400 pg/mL (<450), lactate 3.8 mmol/L (<2), venous pH 7.30 (7.35-7.45), full blood count within normal limits, INR 1.1, creatinine 96 micromol/L (60-110), point-of-care ultrasound dilated hypokinetic right ventricle with septal flattening; CT pulmonary angiogram unavailable in the next 10 minutes
data_table.History: Long-haul flight, sudden dyspnoea and syncope, no bleeding, no surgery, no stroke, no intracranial pathology, no anticoagulation, no allergy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Commence unfractionated heparin infusion at 80 units per kilogram bolus and await computed tomography pulmonary angiography
options.rationale: In high-risk (haemodynamically unstable) suspected pulmonary embolism where imaging is not immediately available, empiric systemic thrombolysis is recommended after weighing bleeding risk; delaying to await confirmatory imaging risks death from ongoing right ventricular failure. (Source: ANZ Society for Vascular Medicine PE guidance)

options.text: Commence intravenous adrenaline infusion, intubate for airway control, and defer thrombolysis until CT head done
options.rationale: There are no clinical features of intracranial haemorrhage. Delaying thrombolysis for a routine CT head in the absence of neurological signs adds mortality. Intubation may further compromise haemodynamics in massive PE due to loss of intrinsic sympathetic drive and worsening venous return. (Source: ANZ Society for Vascular Medicine PE guidance)

options.text: Give an intravenous 20 mL/kg fluid bolus and add dobutamine infusion for right ventricular support without thrombolysis
options.rationale: Aggressive volume loading in RV failure worsens septal displacement and reduces LV filling further. Small volume challenges (250-500 mL) may be considered, but ionotropic support alone without addressing the clot is insufficient for high-risk PE. (Source: ANZ Society for Vascular Medicine PE guidance)

options.text: Administer systemic alteplase 100 mg intravenously over 2 hours with concurrent unfractionated heparin per protocol
options.rationale: This is high-risk (massive) pulmonary embolism (sustained hypotension with RV dysfunction and biomarker elevation). ESC and ANZ guidance recommend systemic thrombolysis with alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 hours (or 0.6 mg/kg over 15 minutes up to 50 mg in cardiac arrest) with no absolute contraindications present. Anticoagulation is continued around the infusion per local protocol. Noradrenaline is preferred as vasoactive support in RV failure. (Source: ESC PE Guidelines 2019)

options.text: Refer for emergency surgical pulmonary embolectomy without giving any medical thrombolysis first this admission
options.rationale: Surgical embolectomy is reserved for patients with absolute contraindications to thrombolysis or failed thrombolysis, and access is limited to specialised centres. It is not first-line when systemic thrombolysis is available and safe. (Source: ESC PE Guidelines 2019)

explanation.summary: High-risk pulmonary embolism (persistent hypotension with right ventricular dysfunction and biomarker elevation) has 30-day mortality of 20 to 30% without reperfusion. Systemic thrombolysis with alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours (or 0.6 mg/kg over 15 minutes in cardiac arrest) is the ESC first-line therapy when no absolute contraindications are present. Noradrenaline supports RV perfusion; dobutamine adds inotropy if inotropic failure predominates. Catheter-directed thrombolysis or surgical embolectomy are alternatives in centres where systemic lysis fails or is contraindicated.
key_points: High-risk PE (persistent hypotension + RV dysfunction + elevated biomarkers) requires immediate reperfusion
Systemic alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 hours is first-line if no absolute contraindication
Absolute contraindications: haemorrhagic stroke ever, ischaemic stroke <6 mo, active bleeding, intracranial neoplasm, recent major surgery or head trauma <3 weeks
Noradrenaline preferred vasopressor in acute RV failure; avoid aggressive fluid loading
explanation.pearls: Alteplase reduced-dose regimen (0.6 mg/kg IV over 15 minutes, max 50 mg) is used during cardiac arrest with suspected PE, per ANZCOR guidance.

subtopic_detail: Cardiogenic shock post-STEMI mechanical circulatory support
stem: You are the cardiology registrar in the coronary care unit. A 64-year-old man had a large anterior STEMI 6 hours ago treated with primary PCI to the proximal LAD with successful stent deployment and TIMI 3 flow. Since return from the catheter laboratory he has developed cardiogenic shock: MAP 55 mmHg despite noradrenaline at 0.4 microgram/kg/min plus adrenaline at 0.15 microgram/kg/min, lactate 5.8 mmol/L rising from 4.4, urine output 5 mL/h, and mottled peripheries. Bedside echocardiogram shows LV EF 20% with global anterior akinesis, no mechanical complication (no VSD, no papillary muscle rupture, no free wall rupture), no pericardial effusion. Right ventricular function is preserved. Coronary anatomy confirms complete revascularisation. He has been intubated 30 minutes ago and remains on high FiO2.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 112 (sinus tachycardia), blood pressure 92/38 with MAP 55, respiratory rate 22 (ventilated), SpO2 92% on FiO2 0.8, temperature 36.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: troponin 25000 ng/L (<30), lactate 5.8 mmol/L rising from 4.4 (<2), creatinine 168 micromol/L (60-110) rising from 90, mixed venous saturation 45%, echocardiogram LV EF 20%, global anterior akinesis, no mechanical complication, RV preserved, no effusion; ECG anterior Q waves with residual ST elevation
data_table.History: Anterior STEMI 6 hours ago, primary PCI proximal LAD with TIMI 3 flow, complete revascularisation, intubated 30 min ago

lead_in: According to the most contemporary Australian and international evidence, what is the most appropriate mechanical circulatory support decision?

options.text: Insert an intra-aortic balloon pump now and continue the current noradrenaline plus adrenaline vasoactive support
options.rationale: IABP-SHOCK II demonstrated no 30-day, 6-month or 12-month mortality benefit for IABP in post-STEMI cardiogenic shock, and current ESC guidelines downgraded IABP for this indication. It is not the correct escalation. (Source: ESC AMI/Cardiogenic Shock 2023)

options.text: Increase noradrenaline to 0.6 microgram/kg/min and add a vasopressin infusion at 0.03 units per minute together
options.rationale: Escalating vasoactive support in the presence of rising lactate, falling MAP despite maximal doses, and refractory shock will not restore end-organ perfusion; escalation of mechanical support is required. (Source: ESC AMI/Cardiogenic Shock 2023)

options.text: Commence a dobutamine infusion at 5 microgram/kg/min in addition to the current noradrenaline and adrenaline
options.rationale: Adding an ionodilator in refractory shock at high catecholamine burden with hypotension is unlikely to restore adequate cardiac output and may worsen hypotension; MCS is the required step at this level of refractory shock. (Source: ESC AMI/Cardiogenic Shock 2023)

options.text: Initiate emergency haemodialysis today for lactate clearance and continue current vasoactive support otherwise
options.rationale: Haemodialysis does not treat cardiogenic shock. Lactate clearance follows from restored perfusion; dialysis alone does not address the underlying pump failure and delays effective escalation. (Source: ESC AMI/Cardiogenic Shock 2023)

options.text: Initiate veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation as bridge to recovery with concurrent LV venting strategy
options.rationale: Post-STEMI cardiogenic shock refractory to maximal vasoactive and inotropic support with rising lactate, low mixed venous saturation, oliguria and severe LV dysfunction meets criteria for VA-ECMO bridge to recovery or decision. Australian tertiary centres provide this via ECMO retrieval services (Alfred, RPA, PA). VA-ECMO raises LV afterload and can precipitate pulmonary oedema through LV distension, so a concurrent LV venting strategy (Impella, IABP or atrial septostomy) is standard alongside VA-ECMO. Neither ECLS-SHOCK (2023) nor EURO-SHOCK confirmed mortality benefit in unselected populations, but selected refractory post-STEMI shock at high-volume centres remains an accepted indication. (Source: ESC AMI/Cardiogenic Shock 2023)

explanation.summary: Refractory post-STEMI cardiogenic shock (rising lactate, falling MAP despite maximal vasoactive plus inotropic therapy, low mixed venous saturation, oliguria) meets criteria for consideration of VA-ECMO bridge to recovery or decision. IABP alone has no evidence for benefit (IABP-SHOCK II) and has been downgraded. VA-ECMO raises LV afterload; concurrent venting via Impella, IABP or septostomy is standard to prevent pulmonary oedema. ECLS-SHOCK 2023 did not confirm benefit in unselected populations, but selected refractory cases at high-volume centres still receive VA-ECMO.
key_points: IABP in post-STEMI cardiogenic shock: no 30-day, 6-mo, 12-mo mortality benefit (IABP-SHOCK II); ESC downgraded
VA-ECMO for refractory shock: bridge to recovery or decision at high-volume centres despite neutral ECLS-SHOCK results
VA-ECMO raises LV afterload -> concurrent LV vent (Impella, IABP, septostomy) is standard
Australian centres accessed via state ECMO retrieval services
explanation.pearls: SCAI Shock stage E (refractory shock on high-dose vasoactives with rising lactate) has 30-day mortality >75% without MCS in some cohorts; early consultation with ECMO retrieval service improves candidate selection.

subtopic_detail: Atrial fibrillation stroke prevention
stem: You are the GP seeing a 68-year-old woman with new persistent atrial fibrillation confirmed on 12-lead ECG and Holter. She has hypertension (on perindopril), type 2 diabetes (on metformin, HbA1c 7.0 percent), and no history of stroke, heart failure, vascular disease, or bleeding. Her BP today is 132/82, weight 78 kg, and creatinine 82 umol/L (eGFR 68 mL/min/1.73 m^2). She has no significant valvular heart disease on echo. She is symptomatic with palpitations but rate is controlled at 88 bpm on bisoprolol.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 88 irregular, blood pressure 132/82, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 98% on room air
data_table.History: New persistent AF, HTN, T2DM, no stroke/HF/vascular disease, no bleeding history
data_table.Bloods: creatinine 82 umol/L (45-90), eGFR 68 mL/min/1.73 m^2, HbA1c 7.0 percent, weight 78 kg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate stroke prevention strategy?

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg orally daily as antithrombotic therapy for atrial fibrillation with the score less than four total
options.rationale: Aspirin does not provide adequate stroke prevention in AF and is no longer recommended. It carries bleeding risk without stroke reduction benefit. (Source: NHFA CSANZ AF)

options.text: Start apixaban 5 mg orally twice daily long-term unless a specific contraindication develops during ongoing review
options.rationale: CHA2DS2-VA score is 3 (age 65 to 74 = 1, HTN = 1, DM = 1) indicating clear anticoagulation benefit. NOAC (apixaban, dabigatran, rivaroxaban) is first choice over warfarin in non-valvular AF. Apixaban 5 mg BD is standard unless dose reduction criteria (age >=80, weight <=60 kg, creatinine >=133 umol/L, with at least 2 of 3) are met. (Source: NHFA CSANZ AF)

options.text: No antithrombotic therapy since the annual stroke risk is low enough to permit conservative management strategy
options.rationale: CHA2DS2-VA of 3 confers an annual stroke risk of approximately 3.2 percent; anticoagulation reduces this substantially and is clearly indicated. (Source: NHFA CSANZ AF)

options.text: Warfarin targeting INR 2.5 with weekly monitoring by community pathology and pharmacist-led dose adjustment
options.rationale: Warfarin is second choice in non-valvular AF; NOACs are preferred for equivalent or superior efficacy, lower intracranial haemorrhage risk, and no INR monitoring. Warfarin remains first choice in mechanical valves and moderate to severe mitral stenosis. (Source: NHFA CSANZ AF)

options.text: Dual antiplatelet clopidogrel plus aspirin as an alternative to anticoagulation in patients with adequate rate control
options.rationale: Dual antiplatelet therapy is inferior to anticoagulation for stroke prevention in AF and carries substantial bleeding risk. It is not a substitute for anticoagulation. (Source: NHFA CSANZ AF)

explanation.summary: Non-valvular AF stroke prevention is guided by CHA2DS2-VA (Australia dropped the sex category in the 2018 NHFA/CSANZ update, now called CHA2DS2-VA). Score >=2 indicates NOAC therapy: apixaban 5 mg BD (2.5 BD if 2 of age >=80, weight <=60 kg, creatinine >=133), dabigatran 150 mg BD (110 BD if age >=75 or renal impairment), rivaroxaban 20 mg daily (15 mg if CrCl 30 to 49). Warfarin remains first line in mechanical valves and moderate to severe mitral stenosis. Aspirin and dual antiplatelet are not effective substitutes.
key_points: CHA2DS2-VA >=2: NOAC first line in non-valvular AF
Apixaban 5 mg BD; reduce to 2.5 BD if 2 of (age >=80, weight <=60 kg, creatinine >=133)
Warfarin only for mechanical valves or moderate to severe mitral stenosis
Aspirin not recommended for AF stroke prevention
explanation.pearls: For elective procedures on apixaban, hold 24 hours before low bleeding-risk procedures and 48 hours before high bleeding-risk procedures with normal renal function; no bridging with LMWH is required.

subtopic_detail: Acute ischaemic stroke thrombolysis
stem: You are the ED registrar seeing a 68-year-old man brought in 2 hours after sudden right-sided weakness and dysphasia witnessed by his wife. NIHSS is 12 (right hemiparesis, expressive aphasia, gaze preference). He has hypertension (on ramipril) and is on aspirin 100 mg daily. He has no recent surgery, no head injury, no bleeding, no anticoagulation, and no seizure with onset. His INR is 1.0. BP is currently 168/94. CT brain shows no haemorrhage and no established infarct; CTA shows a proximal M1 occlusion on the left MCA.

data_table.Vital signs: blood pressure 168/94, pulse 82 regular, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98% on room air
data_table.Investigations: CT brain no haemorrhage or established infarct; CTA left M1 occlusion; BSL 6.8 mmol/L; INR 1.0; platelets 245 x10^9/L (150-400)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give aspirin 300 mg orally now, admit to stroke unit, arrange elective thrombectomy tomorrow morning after MRI
options.rationale: Delaying thrombectomy in a patient with proximal LVO within the treatment window costs salvageable brain. Aspirin is not a substitute for thrombolysis or thrombectomy when both are indicated. (Source: Stroke Foundation)

options.text: Give IV labetalol 20 mg to lower blood pressure to below 140/80 before considering any reperfusion therapy option
options.rationale: Target BP before alteplase is <185/110, not <140/80. Aggressive BP lowering can worsen infarct extension by reducing collateral flow. (Source: Stroke Foundation)

options.text: Give IV alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (10 percent bolus, remainder over 60 min) plus arrange endovascular thrombectomy now
options.rationale: Within 4.5 hours of witnessed onset and no contraindications, IV alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (max 90 mg, 10 percent as bolus over 1 minute, remainder over 60 minutes) is standard. Proximal M1 occlusion with NIHSS 12 and imaging showing salvageable brain warrants concurrent endovascular thrombectomy (up to 6 hours from onset routinely; up to 24 hours with perfusion imaging showing mismatch). BP is treated to <185/110 before alteplase. (Source: Stroke Foundation)

options.text: Give IV heparin infusion to prevent clot propagation and reassess in 24 hours for further reperfusion candidacy
options.rationale: Early therapeutic anticoagulation is not beneficial and increases haemorrhage risk. Alteplase and thrombectomy are the reperfusion strategies. (Source: Stroke Foundation)

options.text: Withhold thrombolysis due to prior aspirin use and instead administer IV nimodipine and admit for expectant care
options.rationale: Aspirin use is not a contraindication to alteplase. Nimodipine is for subarachnoid haemorrhage vasospasm, not ischaemic stroke. (Source: Stroke Foundation)

explanation.summary: Acute ischaemic stroke reperfusion combines IV alteplase (within 4.5 hours; tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg is now guideline-endorsed as equivalent or superior in Australia) with endovascular thrombectomy for anterior circulation large vessel occlusion (within 6 hours routinely, up to 24 hours with favourable perfusion imaging). BP is treated to <185/110 before alteplase. Contraindications include haemorrhage, recent major surgery, prior intracerebral haemorrhage, active bleeding, INR >1.7 or NOAC use within window, platelets <100.
key_points: IV alteplase 0.9 mg/kg within 4.5 hours (tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg equivalent in Australia)
Endovascular thrombectomy for anterior circulation LVO up to 6 hours (24 hours with imaging)
BP target <185/110 before thrombolysis; <180/105 during and 24 hours after
Aspirin use is NOT a contraindication to alteplase
explanation.pearls: Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg as single IV bolus has replaced alteplase in many Australian stroke units; it is faster to administer (single bolus vs 60 minute infusion), does not delay transfer for thrombectomy, and shows equivalent or better outcomes in AcT and EXTEND-IA TNK trials.

subtopic_detail: Acute severe asthma exacerbation
stem: You are the ED registrar seeing a 26-year-old woman with a known history of asthma presenting with 6 hours of worsening breathlessness. She can speak in short phrases only. She has been using her salbutamol MDI hourly with minimal improvement. She has no fever, no chest pain, no haemoptysis, and no recent COVID or influenza-like illness. She has never been intubated for asthma. She takes budesonide/formoterol 200/6 mcg twice daily but admits variable adherence. She has no allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 128, respiratory rate 30, blood pressure 122/76, SpO2 90% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Widespread wheeze, prolonged expiratory phase, accessory muscle use, no cyanosis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Non-invasive ventilation with BiPAP settings 12/6 as first-line management before any bronchodilator escalation attempted
options.rationale: NIV in acute asthma has limited evidence and can worsen air trapping and hyperinflation. Bronchodilator therapy, oxygen, and steroids are first line. Intubation is considered for exhaustion or CO2 rise. (Source: NAC AAMH)

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 500 mg TDS for 5 days plus a salbutamol MDI with spacer 4 puffs 4-hourly and outpatient GP follow-up
options.rationale: Antibiotics are not routinely indicated unless there is evidence of bacterial infection. Discharge is unsafe in acute severe asthma; the patient requires immediate escalated bronchodilator therapy and steroids. (Source: NAC AAMH)

options.text: IV theophylline 250 mg loading dose over 20 min as first-line bronchodilator before nebulised salbutamol trial
options.rationale: Theophylline is not first line and has a narrow therapeutic index. Nebulised salbutamol plus ipratropium, oxygen, and systemic corticosteroid are the first-line management. (Source: NAC AAMH)

options.text: Salbutamol 5 mg plus ipratropium 500 mcg nebulised, oxygen to target 93 to 95 percent, and oral prednisolone 50 mg
