options.rationale: Acute severe asthma (unable to complete sentences, RR >=25, HR >=110, SpO2 <92 percent, PEF 33 to 50 percent) is treated with continuous or back-to-back nebulised salbutamol plus ipratropium, controlled oxygen to target SpO2 93 to 95 percent, oral prednisolone 50 mg (or IV hydrocortisone 100 mg if oral not tolerated), and IV magnesium sulfate 2 g if no rapid improvement. (Source: NAC AAMH)

options.text: Adrenaline 0.5 mg IM to lateral thigh as initial bronchodilator therapy before nebulised beta-agonist administration
options.rationale: IM adrenaline is reserved for anaphylaxis or life-threatening asthma with imminent arrest. It is not first line in acute severe asthma when nebulised salbutamol can be delivered. (Source: NAC AAMH)

explanation.summary: Acute severe asthma is treated with continuous or back-to-back nebulised salbutamol 5 mg (or MDI plus spacer 4 to 12 puffs) with ipratropium 500 mcg added for severe exacerbations, controlled oxygen to target SpO2 93 to 95 percent (avoid hyperoxia), and systemic corticosteroid (prednisolone 50 mg oral or hydrocortisone 100 mg IV) within 1 hour. IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 minutes is added if no rapid improvement. Life-threatening features (silent chest, cyanosis, bradycardia, exhaustion, altered LOC, PEF <33 percent) prompt ICU escalation and consideration of intubation.
key_points: Salbutamol 5 mg + ipratropium 500 mcg nebulised, controlled O2 to SpO2 93 to 95 percent
Prednisolone 50 mg oral (or hydrocortisone 100 mg IV) within 1 hour
IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 min if no rapid improvement
ICU review for life-threatening features (silent chest, exhaustion, altered LOC, PEF <33 percent)
explanation.pearls: Discharge criteria after acute asthma: PEF >=75 percent predicted or personal best, stable on 4-hourly bronchodilator, review of technique and adherence, prednisolone 50 mg daily for 5 to 7 days total, written action plan, and follow-up within 2 to 7 days.

subtopic_detail: Type 2 diabetes second-line pharmacotherapy
stem: You are the GP seeing a 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 8 years, on metformin 1 g twice daily, with an HbA1c of 8.4 percent (target <7 percent). He has hypertension (on perindopril), stable ischaemic heart disease with prior MI 3 years ago (on aspirin, atorvastatin, bisoprolol), and eGFR 62 mL/min/1.73 m^2. His weight is 94 kg (BMI 31), BP 128/78, and there is no diabetic ketoacidosis, no recurrent UTI or genital infection, and no history of DKA-precipitating illness. He has good renal function and no diabetic foot ulcers.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 72, blood pressure 128/78, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 98% on room air, weight 94 kg
data_table.Bloods: HbA1c 8.4 percent, eGFR 62 mL/min/1.73 m^2, creatinine 92 umol/L (60-110), LDL 1.8 mmol/L on statin
data_table.Comorbidity: Prior MI 3 years ago, HTN, no DKA history, no recurrent GU infections, no foot ulcers

lead_in: What is the most appropriate add-on to metformin?

options.text: Add gliclazide MR 60 mg oral daily titrated up over 6 weeks and continue metformin for glycaemic control only
options.rationale: Sulfonylureas do not provide cardiovascular benefit and carry hypoglycaemia and weight gain risks. In a patient with established ASCVD, SGLT2i or GLP-1 RA is preferred as second line. (Source: RACGP Diabetes)

options.text: Add basal insulin glargine 10 units subcutaneously nocte titrated by 2 units every 3 days for glycaemic control
options.rationale: Insulin is added when other options have failed or in specific circumstances (severe hyperglycaemia, symptomatic). It causes hypoglycaemia and weight gain without cardiovascular benefit. Cardioprotective agent first. (Source: RACGP Diabetes)

options.text: Add pioglitazone 30 mg oral daily to improve insulin sensitivity and continue metformin for durable glycaemic control
options.rationale: Pioglitazone carries risks of heart failure, weight gain, fractures, and bladder cancer signal. It is not preferred over SGLT2i or GLP-1 RA in patients with ASCVD. (Source: RACGP Diabetes)

options.text: Add sitagliptin 100 mg oral daily as weight-neutral therapy with low hypoglycaemia risk and continue metformin fully
options.rationale: DPP-4 inhibitors are weight neutral with low hypoglycaemia but do not provide cardiovascular protection. In ASCVD, SGLT2i or GLP-1 RA is preferred as second line. (Source: RACGP Diabetes)

options.text: Add empagliflozin 10 mg oral daily and continue metformin for combined cardiovascular and glycaemic benefit
options.rationale: In T2DM with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, an SGLT2 inhibitor (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin) or GLP-1 receptor agonist (semaglutide, dulaglutide, liraglutide) with proven cardiovascular benefit is added regardless of HbA1c. Empagliflozin reduces cardiovascular death, MI, stroke, and heart failure hospitalisation (EMPA-REG). (Source: RACGP Diabetes)

explanation.summary: In type 2 diabetes with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, heart failure, or chronic kidney disease, an SGLT2 inhibitor (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin) or GLP-1 receptor agonist (semaglutide, dulaglutide, liraglutide) with proven cardiovascular or renal benefit is added regardless of HbA1c. SGLT2 inhibitors are preferred in heart failure and CKD; GLP-1 RA give greater HbA1c and weight reduction. Both reduce major adverse cardiovascular events. Sulfonylureas, DPP-4 inhibitors, and insulin remain useful for glycaemic control without cardioprotective benefit.
key_points: T2DM + ASCVD: add SGLT2i or GLP-1 RA regardless of HbA1c
SGLT2i preferred in heart failure and CKD (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin)
GLP-1 RA give greater HbA1c and weight reduction (semaglutide, dulaglutide)
Sulfonylureas cause hypoglycaemia and weight gain, no CV benefit
explanation.pearls: SGLT2 inhibitor sick day rules: withhold during acute illness, dehydration, fasting, and surgery to reduce euglycaemic DKA risk. Warn about mycotic genital infections (approximately 5 to 10 percent, more in women) and rare Fournier's gangrene.

subtopic_detail: Pheochromocytoma pre-operative preparation
stem:
You are the endocrinology registrar reviewing a 44-year-old woman referred for episodic hypertension with headaches, palpitations, and diaphoresis lasting 15 to 20 minutes several times weekly. Her home blood pressures range 148/92 to 210/126. She has lost 5 kg unintentionally over 3 months.

Investigations show plasma metanephrines: normetanephrine 4.8 nmol/L (below 0.9), metanephrine 3.1 nmol/L (below 0.5). 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines are also elevated at 4 times the upper limit. CT abdomen shows a 4.2 cm right adrenal mass with unenhanced attenuation of 32 Hounsfield units and heterogenous enhancement. The endocrine surgeon is planning laparoscopic adrenalectomy in 3 weeks. Her ECG shows normal sinus rhythm at 96 bpm with LVH by voltage criteria.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 96, blood pressure 178/108, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: plasma normetanephrine 4.8 nmol/L (<0.9), metanephrine 3.1 nmol/L (<0.5), potassium 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 68 umol/L
data_table.Imaging: right adrenal mass 4.2 cm, 32 HU unenhanced, heterogenous enhancement, no metastases

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first step in preoperative preparation?

options.text: Commence intravenous magnesium sulfate infusion and admit for continuous BP monitoring until surgery is performed
options.rationale: Magnesium infusion is used intraoperatively as an adjunct; it is not the standard preoperative preparation, which is oral alpha blockade over 10 to 14 days plus salt loading. (Source: eTG Endocrinology)

options.text: Commence metoprolol 50 mg twice daily immediately to control heart rate and blood pressure ahead of surgery
options.rationale: Starting beta blockade before alpha blockade leaves alpha1 vasoconstriction unopposed, precipitating hypertensive crisis; alpha blockade must come first. (Source: eTG Endocrinology)

options.text: Commence ramipril 10 mg daily and amlodipine 5 mg daily for blood pressure control before surgery
options.rationale: ACE inhibitors and calcium channel blockers are not the preferred first-line preoperative preparation because they do not blunt catecholamine surges during tumour manipulation. Alpha blockade is the standard. (Source: eTG Endocrinology)

options.text: Proceed to laparoscopic adrenalectomy urgently without prior medical blockade to avoid drug side effects
options.rationale: Operating without preoperative alpha blockade causes intraoperative hypertensive crisis from catecholamine release with high risk of stroke, myocardial infarction and death. (Source: eTG Endocrinology)

options.text: Commence phenoxybenzamine 10 mg BD for at least 10 to 14 days, adding metoprolol closer to surgery only if tachycardia develops
options.rationale: Non-selective alpha blockade (phenoxybenzamine) for a minimum of 10 to 14 days before surgery is standard; beta blockade may be added only AFTER adequate alpha blockade to control reflex tachycardia. Beta blockade first would leave unopposed alpha stimulation and can precipitate hypertensive crisis. (Source: eTG Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Preoperative preparation for pheochromocytoma requires alpha blockade before beta blockade to prevent hypertensive crisis from unopposed alpha stimulation during tumour manipulation. Phenoxybenzamine is the standard non-selective alpha blocker, started at 10 mg twice daily and titrated up. Adequate blockade is achieved with target seated BP below 130/80, standing BP above 90 systolic, mild orthostatic drop, and Hb rise reflecting plasma volume expansion. Beta blockade is added only if reflex tachycardia develops.
key_points: Alpha blockade FIRST (phenoxybenzamine 10 to 14 days minimum)
Beta blockade ONLY after alpha blockade if tachycardia
Liberal salt intake to counter volume contraction
Intraoperative watch for BP swings and post-resection hypotension
explanation.pearls: Roizen criteria for adequate alpha blockade: seated BP <130/80, standing SBP >90, mild orthostasis, no ECG ST-T changes for 2 weeks; phenoxybenzamine typical dose 20 to 100 mg/day divided doses.

subtopic_detail: Guillain-Barré syndrome ascending weakness with respiratory watch
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar admitting a 58-year-old man with 5 days of ascending symmetric weakness starting in his feet and now involving his thighs and hands. He had a diarrhoeal illness 3 weeks ago that self-resolved. On examination he has bilateral facial weakness. Power is 3/5 in lower limbs, 4/5 in upper limbs. Reflexes are absent throughout. Sensation shows mild distal glove-and-stocking paraesthesiae. His forced vital capacity at the bedside is 1.6 L (predicted 4.0 L). His maximum negative inspiratory force is minus 30 cmH2O. He has no bulbar symptoms today but coughed weakly.

CSF shows protein 1.2 g/L (below 0.45), cell count 3 x10^6/L (below 5), glucose normal. Nerve conduction studies are pending.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 96, blood pressure 138/86, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Neuro: power LL 3/5, UL 4/5, areflexic throughout, bilateral LMN facial weakness, mild sensory loss
data_table.Respiratory: FVC 1.6 L (40% predicted), NIF -30 cmH2O, weak cough

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Admit monitored, start IVIG 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days, and escalate to ICU if FVC falls below 1 litre or 20 mL/kg or NIF worsens
options.rationale: Guillain-Barré syndrome with FVC 40 percent predicted and weak cough warrants monitored admission, prompt IVIG 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days (equivalent efficacy to plasma exchange but easier logistically), and clear ICU triggers for intubation before crisis. (Source: eTG Neurology)

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 60 mg daily and admit for observation until nerve conduction studies confirm the diagnosis
options.rationale: Corticosteroids alone are ineffective in Guillain-Barré syndrome and delay definitive treatment; IVIG or plasma exchange is standard. (Source: eTG Neurology)

options.text: Discharge with outpatient neurology review because absence of bulbar symptoms and stable saturations reassure against near-term deterioration
options.rationale: FVC 40 percent predicted with weak cough is a red flag for impending respiratory failure; outpatient management is unsafe until progression has clearly plateaued. (Source: eTG Neurology)

options.text: Start plasma exchange and immediately follow with IVIG for combined effect, admitting to ICU regardless of respiratory parameters
options.rationale: Combined IVIG plus plasma exchange offers no benefit over either alone and adds cost and risk; choose one modality. Blanket ICU admission without triggers is not the standard. (Source: eTG Neurology)

options.text: Arrange urgent MRI whole spine to exclude cord compression before initiating any specific therapy for Guillain-Barré syndrome
options.rationale: Cord compression is unlikely given areflexia, facial weakness, and albuminocytological dissociation on CSF; delaying treatment for MRI is inappropriate although imaging may still be arranged in parallel if red flags exist. (Source: eTG Neurology)

explanation.summary: Guillain-Barré syndrome is an acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy typically preceded by a diarrhoeal or respiratory illness. It causes ascending symmetric weakness with areflexia and albuminocytological CSF dissociation. Respiratory failure is the main killer; regular FVC and NIF are required, with intubation if FVC below 20 mL/kg (roughly 1 litre for average adults) or NIF above minus 25 cmH2O or rapid decline. Treatment is IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days or 5-session plasma exchange, both equally effective.
key_points: IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day x 5 days OR plasma exchange, NOT both
FVC less than 20 mL/kg (~1 L) or NIF less than -25 cmH2O equals ICU intubation
Steroids alone are NOT effective
VTE prophylaxis with LMWH, autonomic monitoring for dysrhythmia and BP swings
explanation.pearls: 20/30/40 rule for respiratory triage: FVC <20 mL/kg, NIF <-30, or MEP <40 cmH2O predict need for mechanical ventilation. Serial 4-hourly bedside spirometry in first 48 hours.

subtopic_detail: Acute type A aortic dissection
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar assessing a 62-year-old man with sudden onset ripping interscapular chest pain radiating to the back and neck 90 minutes ago. He has hypertension on ramipril, poorly adherent. On examination his right arm blood pressure is 168/98, left arm 118/72 (differential 50 mmHg). There is a new early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge. Pulses in both radial arteries are palpable but unequal.

ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 108 with no acute ST changes. Chest X-ray shows a widened mediastinum. CT aortogram is being reported now: the radiologist rings to tell you there is an intimal flap extending from the aortic root through the ascending aorta and into the aortic arch with false lumen involving the origin of the innominate artery. There is a small pericardial effusion but no tamponade physiology.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 108, blood pressure 168/98 right arm and 118/72 left arm, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Exam: diastolic murmur LSE, BP differential 50 mmHg, unequal radials
data_table.Imaging: widened mediastinum on CXR, CT aortogram intimal flap aortic root to arch, small pericardial effusion, no tamponade

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Administer aspirin 300 mg, ticagrelor 180 mg loading, and IV heparin, then transfer for urgent coronary angiography
options.rationale: Antiplatelet and anticoagulant loading is contraindicated in dissection because they increase haemorrhage risk; treatment is surgical, not ACS-directed. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular)

options.text: Commence intravenous nitroprusside infusion to lower BP rapidly then arrange transfer for endovascular stent grafting
options.rationale: Nitroprusside before beta blockade causes reflex tachycardia that worsens shear stress and dissection propagation; beta blockade must come first. Endovascular repair is for type B dissection, not type A. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular)

options.text: Commence IV esmolol targeting heart rate 60 and systolic BP 100 to 120, then immediately transfer to a cardiothoracic centre for repair
options.rationale: Type A (ascending) aortic dissection requires urgent surgical repair; medical therapy targets heart rate 60 and SBP 100 to 120 (beta blocker FIRST to reduce dP/dt then vasodilator if needed) while arranging immediate transfer. Untreated Stanford type A has 1 to 2 percent per hour mortality. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular)

options.text: Admit to the cardiology ward for observation with oral beta blocker and analgesia, book non-urgent CT surveillance
options.rationale: Ward-level observation is inadequate for type A dissection; delayed surgery increases mortality by 1 to 2 percent per hour, so immediate cardiothoracic transfer is required. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular)

options.text: Perform urgent pericardiocentesis in the ED before transfer to address the small pericardial effusion
options.rationale: Pericardiocentesis is contraindicated in dissection with pericardial effusion because decompression can restart bleeding into the pericardium and precipitate death; drain in theatre only if in tamponade arrest during surgery. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Acute aortic dissection is classified as Stanford type A (ascending, requires urgent surgery) or type B (descending, medical unless malperfusion). Immediate management is aggressive control of heart rate then blood pressure to reduce aortic wall shear stress: beta blocker infusion (esmolol or labetalol) targeting heart rate 60, then vasodilator (nitroprusside or GTN) for BP 100 to 120 systolic. Type A patients need emergency cardiothoracic surgical repair. Pericardiocentesis for tamponade is avoided outside theatre.
key_points: Type A (ascending) equals emergency surgery; type B (descending) usually medical
Heart rate control (beta blocker) FIRST to reduce dP/dt, then BP control
Target HR 60, SBP 100 to 120
Avoid pericardiocentesis in type A with effusion (bleeding risk)
explanation.pearls: Untreated Stanford type A dissection mortality: 1 to 2 percent per hour in the first 48 hours; 50 percent by 48 hours. IRAD registry confirms surgery reduces in-hospital mortality from 58 percent (medical) to 27 percent (surgical).

subtopic_detail: Hypertensive emergency with acute pulmonary oedema
stem:
You are the ED registrar called for a 64-year-old woman with 2 hours of severe dyspnoea. She has a history of hypertension on ramipril, has stopped taking it for a fortnight because of a chest infection. On arrival she is speaking in single words, sitting upright, using accessory muscles. Blood pressure is 232/126, pulse 118, respiratory rate 34, SpO2 82 percent on room air improving to 92 percent on 15 L/min via non-rebreather. Auscultation reveals bibasal crackles to mid-zones and an audible S3.

ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 118, LVH with strain. Chest X-ray shows bilateral perihilar interstitial oedema, no consolidation, no pneumothorax. Point-of-care troponin is mildly elevated at 42 ng/L (below 14). Bedside echocardiogram shows preserved LV ejection fraction of 60 percent, marked concentric hypertrophy, and B-lines throughout both lung fields.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 118, blood pressure 232/126, respiratory rate 34, SpO2 92% on 15 L/min NRB, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: troponin 42 ng/L (<14), creatinine 108 umol/L (45-90), potassium 4.1 mmol/L, BNP 812 pg/mL (<100)
data_table.Imaging: CXR bilateral interstitial oedema, echo LVEF 60% with concentric LVH, diffuse B-lines

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management combination?

options.text: Restart oral ramipril 10 mg immediately, give oral frusemide 40 mg, and reassess in an hour
options.rationale: Oral therapy is too slow for hypertensive pulmonary oedema; IV afterload reduction with GTN and IV frusemide is required alongside non-invasive ventilation. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular)

options.text: Administer intravenous labetalol 20 mg bolus and titrate to systolic BP below 140 mmHg within 30 minutes
options.rationale: Rapid target BP below 140 within 30 minutes risks under-perfusion of vital organs; the standard target is 20 to 25 percent MAP reduction in the first hour. GTN is preferred over labetalol in acute pulmonary oedema because beta blockade may worsen decompensated failure. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular)

options.text: Give intravenous morphine 5 mg and start heparin infusion for suspected coronary ischaemia given the troponin rise
options.rationale: Morphine in acute pulmonary oedema is associated with increased mortality and does not treat the underlying hypertensive afterload; troponin rise here is demand-related and does not indicate acute plaque rupture. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular)

options.text: Apply non-invasive positive pressure ventilation, start IV glyceryl trinitrate infusion, and give IV frusemide 40 mg
options.rationale: Hypertensive acute pulmonary oedema (SCAPE) responds to non-invasive positive pressure ventilation to reduce work of breathing and afterload, IV GTN as first-line afterload reduction (target MAP fall 20 to 25 percent in the first hour), and diuresis. This addresses both blood pressure and pulmonary oedema. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular)

options.text: Intubate immediately and initiate mandatory mechanical ventilation before starting any vasoactive therapy
options.rationale: Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation is first-line and often avoids intubation in SCAPE; intubation should be reserved for NIV failure, exhaustion, or altered consciousness. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Sympathetic crashing acute pulmonary oedema (SCAPE) is a hypertensive emergency with acute afterload mismatch and flash pulmonary oedema. First-line treatment is non-invasive positive pressure ventilation, IV nitrate (GTN infusion), and diuresis. Target 20 to 25 percent reduction in mean arterial pressure over the first hour, then further gradual reduction. Morphine is avoided because of mortality signal. Rapid supra-physiological reduction risks stroke and organ ischaemia.
key_points: SCAPE (hypertensive APO): NIV + IV GTN + IV diuretic
Target MAP fall 20 to 25% in first hour, NOT rapid to normal
Morphine avoided (mortality signal)
Intubation only if NIV fails or altered consciousness
explanation.pearls: IV GTN dose in SCAPE: start 5 to 10 mcg/min, uptitrate every 3 to 5 min to effect (up to 200 mcg/min). Rapid afterload reduction resolves oedema within 30 to 60 min in most cases.

subtopic_detail: Adult community-acquired bacterial meningitis
stem:
You are the ED registrar assessing a 58-year-old man brought in by ambulance with 8 hours of severe headache, fever, and vomiting. His wife reports he became confused in the last hour. He has no known drug allergies, has a history of ischaemic heart disease, and is not immunocompromised. On examination he has a temperature of 39.4, GCS 13 (E3V4M6), photophobia, and neck stiffness. Kernig sign is positive. There is a small non-blanching petechial rash over his shins. He has no focal neurological deficit. There are no papilloedema on fundoscopy.

His observations are pulse 118, blood pressure 108/62, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 96 percent on room air. Bedside glucose is 6.1 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 118, blood pressure 108/62, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Neuro: GCS 13 (E3V4M6), photophobia, neck stiffness, Kernig positive, no focal deficit, no papilloedema

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Start IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg 8-hourly first for suspected HSV encephalitis pending imaging and CSF results
options.rationale: The picture is classic bacterial meningitis (petechiae, neck stiffness, rapid onset); HSV encephalitis presents with focal deficit, seizure, or personality change. Aciclovir may be added if encephalitis is suspected but is not the first single agent. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

options.text: Perform an urgent lumbar puncture immediately in ED for CSF analysis before giving antibiotics to preserve culture yield
options.rationale: Antibiotics must not be delayed for LP in suspected bacterial meningitis; blood cultures first, then empiric antibiotics with dexamethasone, and LP as soon as safe. CSF culture yield is reduced by pre-LP antibiotics but the risk of delaying treatment far outweighs this. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

options.text: Give IV ceftriaxone 2 g alone and defer benzylpenicillin because it adds no coverage beyond ceftriaxone in an adult
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone does not cover Listeria monocytogenes; adults 50 years and older, immunocompromised, or with chronic illness need added benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin for Listeria empirically. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

options.text: Withhold dexamethasone until CSF confirms pneumococcal meningitis to avoid immunosuppression during viral or aseptic causes
options.rationale: Dexamethasone must be given with or just before the first antibiotic dose to be effective; deferring it until culture results loses the survival and hearing preservation benefit shown in pneumococcal meningitis. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

options.text: Take blood cultures, give IV dexamethasone 10 mg then IV ceftriaxone 2 g and benzylpenicillin 2.4 g together, then arrange CT and LP
options.rationale: Adult community-acquired bacterial meningitis is treated with empiric IV ceftriaxone plus benzylpenicillin (for Listeria cover if over 50 years) after blood cultures; dexamethasone 10 mg IV is given just before or with the first antibiotic dose to reduce hearing loss and mortality in pneumococcal meningitis. LP follows if not contraindicated. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Empiric therapy for adult community-acquired bacterial meningitis is IV ceftriaxone 2 g plus IV benzylpenicillin 2.4 g (Listeria cover for age 50 or older, immunocompromised, pregnant, alcohol use disorder). Dexamethasone 10 mg IV 6-hourly is given with or just before the first antibiotic dose because it reduces mortality and hearing loss in pneumococcal meningitis. LP should not delay antibiotics; CT before LP is required if depressed consciousness, focal deficit, seizure, immunocompromised, or papilloedema.
key_points: Blood cultures first, then dex 10 mg IV, then ceftriaxone 2 g + benzylpenicillin 2.4 g
Benzylpenicillin adds Listeria cover for age >=50, immunocompromised, chronic illness
Do not delay antibiotics for LP or CT
CT before LP if reduced GCS, focal signs, seizure, immunocompromised, papilloedema
explanation.pearls: Aciclovir 10 mg/kg IV 8-hourly added if encephalitis features (focal deficit, seizure, personality change). Contact precautions and PEP for close contacts of confirmed meningococcal disease (ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO single dose).

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis in patient on chronic corticosteroids with intercurrent sepsis
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 54-year-old woman with 2 days of fever and productive cough. She has rheumatoid arthritis and has been on prednisolone 7.5 mg daily for 6 years, plus methotrexate. On arrival she is drowsy (GCS 13), pale, and diaphoretic. Blood pressure is 82/44, pulse 128, temperature 38.9, respiratory rate 26, SpO2 91 percent on room air. Chest exam reveals right basal crackles. Blood glucose is 3.2 mmol/L.

Bloods show sodium 128 mmol/L, potassium 5.2 mmol/L, urea 12.4 mmol/L, creatinine 148 umol/L, CRP 220 mg/L, WCC 18.4 x10^9/L with left shift, lactate 4.2 mmol/L. Chest X-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation. She has been given 500 mL Hartmann's, still hypotensive.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 82/44, respiratory rate 26, SpO2 91% on room air, temperature 38.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 148 umol/L (45-90), glucose 3.2 mmol/L, lactate 4.2 mmol/L, CRP 220 mg/L (<5)
data_table.Chronic Rx: prednisolone 7.5 mg daily for 6 years, methotrexate 15 mg weekly

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial priority alongside fluid resuscitation and antibiotics?

options.text: Double her usual oral prednisolone dose to 15 mg once she is able to swallow, and reassess in 6 hours
options.rationale: Oral steroids are inadequate for adrenal crisis in a shocked, drowsy patient with likely absorption compromise; parenteral hydrocortisone is required immediately. (Source: eTG Endocrinology)

options.text: Administer hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus immediately, then 200 mg over 24 hours by infusion (or 50 mg IV 6-hourly)
options.rationale: Chronic prednisolone at 7.5 mg for years suppresses the HPA axis; septic shock is a major physiological stressor causing adrenal crisis. IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus then 200 mg/24 h (or 50 mg 6-hourly) is empirical and life-saving; hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia support the diagnosis. (Source: eTG Endocrinology)

options.text: Perform a short synacthen test now before giving any steroid to establish the diagnosis and guide long-term therapy
options.rationale: Diagnostic testing must not delay steroid replacement in suspected adrenal crisis; treat empirically, test later once stabilised (and note that recent hydrocortisone will affect cortisol assay). (Source: eTG Endocrinology)

options.text: Give IV fludrocortisone 100 micrograms daily to address the hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone has slow onset and is not standard acute therapy for adrenal crisis; hydrocortisone at stress doses provides sufficient mineralocorticoid activity acutely. (Source: eTG Endocrinology)

options.text: Withhold any additional corticosteroid pending blood cortisol result to avoid steroid-induced immunosuppression in sepsis
options.rationale: Withholding stress-dose hydrocortisone in adrenal crisis is fatal; the benefit far outweighs any additional infection risk, and antibiotics address the sepsis in parallel. (Source: eTG Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Chronic corticosteroid therapy at doses of 5 mg prednisolone or higher for more than 3 to 4 weeks suppresses the HPA axis and predisposes to adrenal crisis under stress (sepsis, surgery, trauma). Empirical hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus then 200 mg over 24 hours by infusion (or 50 mg IV 6-hourly) is life-saving and given before diagnostic testing. Classical biochemistry includes hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, and hypotension refractory to fluid alone.
key_points: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus then 200 mg/24 h infusion (or 50 mg IV 6h)
Treat empirically; do NOT delay for synacthen test
Hyponatraemia + hyperkalaemia + hypoglycaemia + shock triad
Long-term on 5+ mg prednisolone requires stress-dose steroid education
explanation.pearls: All patients on prednisolone 5 mg/day for >4 weeks need MedicAlert and stress dose plan: double oral steroid for minor illness, hydrocortisone 100 mg IM (Emerpen or SoluCortef) for vomiting or surgery.

subtopic_detail: Suspected necrotising fasciitis lower limb
stem:
You are the surgical registrar called to ED for a 52-year-old man with 36 hours of a rapidly expanding painful red lower leg. He has type 2 diabetes on metformin. On arrival he is grey and diaphoretic. The affected leg has a poorly demarcated area of dusky discoloration extending from mid-shin to knee, with two 2 cm haemorrhagic bullae over the shin, and a small area of skin necrosis. He reports pain out of proportion to the visible signs. There is crepitus on palpation. He is confused.

Observations: pulse 132, blood pressure 92/54, respiratory rate 26, SpO2 94 percent on room air, temperature 39.2. Bloods show white cell count 21.6 x10^9/L, CRP 356 mg/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, glucose 15.4 mmol/L, creatinine 168 umol/L, lactate 4.8 mmol/L. LRINEC score is calculated at 9.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 132, blood pressure 92/54, respiratory rate 26, SpO2 94% on room air, temperature 39.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: WCC 21.6 x10^9/L, CRP 356 mg/L (<5), sodium 132 mmol/L, glucose 15.4 mmol/L, creatinine 168 umol/L, lactate 4.8 mmol/L
data_table.Exam: dusky lower leg, haemorrhagic bullae, crepitus, pain out of proportion, LRINEC 9

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Immediate surgical debridement in theatre with empiric IV meropenem, vancomycin, and clindamycin plus resuscitation en route
options.rationale: Necrotising fasciitis (LRINEC 9 with pain out of proportion, crepitus, and haemorrhagic bullae) is a surgical emergency; source control by wide debridement in theatre is the definitive treatment and must not be delayed for imaging. Empiric broad-spectrum plus clindamycin (for toxin suppression) is standard. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange urgent MRI leg to confirm fascial involvement before proceeding with surgical debridement in theatre
options.rationale: Imaging must not delay operative debridement in high-probability necrotising fasciitis; MRI or CT may be used only when the diagnosis is uncertain and clinical picture allows. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

options.text: Commence IV flucloxacillin 2 g 6-hourly for presumed cellulitis and observe for clinical response over 6 to 12 hours
options.rationale: Flucloxacillin monotherapy is inadequate for necrotising fasciitis, which is often polymicrobial or streptococcal with toxin production; treating this as cellulitis loses the surgical window. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

options.text: Give IV vancomycin monotherapy, hyperbaric oxygen therapy, and defer any surgery until fully stabilised
options.rationale: Hyperbaric oxygen has an unproven role and should not delay surgical source control; vancomycin alone lacks Gram-negative and anaerobic cover. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

options.text: Perform bedside skin biopsy for frozen section histology in the ED before theatre to confirm the diagnosis
options.rationale: Bedside biopsy is not standard and delays definitive theatre debridement; the clinical picture and LRINEC score are sufficient to proceed. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis is a rapidly progressive soft tissue infection with high mortality if surgery is delayed. Clinical clues include pain out of proportion, dusky or bullous skin change, crepitus, and systemic sepsis. LRINEC score of 6 or more raises suspicion; 8 or more is high risk. Immediate management is aggressive resuscitation, empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics including clindamycin for toxin suppression, and urgent surgical debridement in theatre. Imaging must not delay theatre.
key_points: Surgical debridement is the primary and time-critical intervention
Empiric: meropenem + vancomycin + clindamycin (toxin suppression)
LRINEC score >=6 raises suspicion; clinical judgement outranks the score
Do NOT delay theatre for MRI in a septic patient with classic features
explanation.pearls: LRINEC variables: CRP, WCC, Hb, sodium, creatinine, glucose. Score >=8 has PPV around 90% for NF; however sensitivity is imperfect so a lower score does not exclude the diagnosis clinically.

subtopic_detail: Acute gout flare in a patient with chronic kidney disease
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 68-year-old man in the acute medical clinic with 24 hours of a very painful, red, swollen right first metatarsophalangeal joint. He has had two similar episodes previously that self-resolved with paracetamol over 5 to 7 days. He has stage 4 CKD with eGFR 24 mL/min/1.73 m2 (baseline 22 to 26), hypertension on amlodipine, ischaemic heart disease on aspirin, and takes no other regular medications. He is not on urate-lowering therapy.

On examination the right first MTP joint is warm, tender, erythematous with overlying skin taut and shiny, and range of motion is severely restricted by pain. There is a small tophaceous nodule on the right olecranon. He is afebrile, blood pressure 132/78, pulse 88. Serum urate today is 0.52 mmol/L (upper limit 0.42), creatinine 236 umol/L, CRP 68 mg/L.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 88, blood pressure 132/78, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: creatinine 236 umol/L (baseline 220-240), eGFR 24 mL/min/1.73 m2, urate 0.52 mmol/L (<0.42), CRP 68 mg/L (<5)
data_table.Exam: right first MTP joint warm, erythematous, swollen, tender, right olecranon tophus

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line therapy for the acute flare?

options.text: Commence oral naproxen 500 mg BD for 5 days with a proton pump inhibitor for gastroprotection during acute treatment
options.rationale: NSAIDs are contraindicated in stage 4 CKD because of the risk of further renal impairment and hyperkalaemia; steroids or intra-articular therapy are safer alternatives. (Source: eTG Rheumatology)

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 25 mg daily for 5 days and discuss commencing allopurinol at low dose after the acute flare has resolved
options.rationale: In stage 4 CKD, NSAIDs are contraindicated and colchicine risks accumulation and toxicity; oral prednisolone 25 to 30 mg daily for 3 to 5 days is a preferred first-line acute anti-inflammatory choice in CKD. Urate-lowering therapy is discussed after the acute flare with allopurinol started low and titrated. (Source: eTG Rheumatology)

options.text: Commence oral colchicine 1 mg then 500 micrograms 1 hour later, then 500 micrograms 12-hourly for a full 3 days
options.rationale: Colchicine accumulates in stage 4 CKD (eGFR under 30) with high toxicity risk (neuromyopathy, cytopenias); dose reduction to 500 micrograms daily is possible but steroid is generally preferred. (Source: eTG Rheumatology)

options.text: Commence allopurinol 300 mg daily now to reduce serum urate and treat the acute flare simultaneously in one visit
options.rationale: Starting allopurinol during an acute flare can prolong or worsen it; also 300 mg is too high a start dose in stage 4 CKD (start 50 mg and titrate). Urate-lowering therapy is discussed after the flare settles. (Source: eTG Rheumatology)

options.text: Perform bedside joint aspiration for intra-articular corticosteroid injection and send synovial fluid for gram stain and crystals
options.rationale: Intra-articular steroid is reasonable for a single joint when infection is excluded, but oral prednisolone is simpler and equally effective in this context; aspirating a first MTP is technically difficult and injection risks contamination. (Source: eTG Rheumatology)

explanation.summary: Acute gout in CKD is treated with oral or intra-articular corticosteroid as first-line because NSAIDs are contraindicated and colchicine accumulates. Oral prednisolone 25 to 30 mg for 3 to 5 days is effective and generally well tolerated. Urate-lowering therapy (allopurinol) is initiated after the acute flare settles, starting at low dose (50 mg in eGFR under 30) and uptitrated to a serum urate target of 0.36 mmol/L (or 0.30 with tophi), with colchicine or NSAID cover as flare prophylaxis where safe.
key_points: NSAIDs contraindicated in CKD; colchicine accumulates in eGFR <30
Oral prednisolone 25 to 30 mg for 3 to 5 days is first-line in CKD
Allopurinol start dose in eGFR <30: 50 mg, titrate every 4 weeks
Target serum urate <0.36 mmol/L (<0.30 with tophi)
explanation.pearls: HLA-B*5801 screening pre-allopurinol reduces SJS/TEN risk (particularly Han Chinese, Korean, Thai populations). Febuxostat is an alternative XO inhibitor but has cardiovascular safety concerns and is second-line.

subtopic_detail: Haemodynamic instability with echocardiographic RV strain
stem:
You are the medical registrar in ED reviewing a 58-year-old man with sudden dyspnoea and collapse 2 days after a long haul flight from Los Angeles. He has a heart rate of 132, blood pressure 82/48 despite 2 litres of crystalloid, and cool peripheries. Oxygen saturation is 88 percent on 15 litres via non-rebreather. Bedside echocardiogram shows a dilated hypokinetic right ventricle with paradoxical septal motion. CT pulmonary angiogram confirms bilateral saddle embolus. He is on no anticoagulant and has no bleeding contraindications.

The intensivist has intubation prepared and asks about definitive reperfusion.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 132, blood pressure 82/48, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 88% on 15 L NRB, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: Hb 138 g/L (135-175), platelets 232 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 92 umol/L (60-110), lactate 4.8 mmol/L (under 2.0), high sensitivity troponin 480 ng/L (under 26)
data_table.Imaging: CTPA bilateral saddle embolus with RV/LV ratio 1.6, bedside echo dilated hypokinetic RV

lead_in: What is the most appropriate reperfusion strategy?

options.text: Catheter directed thrombolysis with reduced dose alteplase 24 mg over 12 hours plus IV heparin infusion
options.rationale: Catheter directed thrombolysis is considered for submassive PE where bleeding risk from full dose systemic tPA is high; in massive PE with shock, systemic tPA is faster and first line. (Source: ANZ Society of Cardiology PE Statement)
source_refs: ANZ Society of Cardiology PE Statement

options.text: Therapeutic enoxaparin 1 mg per kg twice daily alone with careful volume replacement and inotrope support
options.rationale: Anticoagulation alone does not reperfuse and is insufficient in massive PE with obstructive shock; reperfusion by thrombolysis or embolectomy is required. (Source: ANZ Society of Cardiology PE Statement)
source_refs: ANZ Society of Cardiology PE Statement

options.text: Immediate surgical embolectomy on cardiopulmonary bypass without first attempting systemic thrombolysis
options.rationale: Surgical embolectomy is second line if thrombolysis fails or is contraindicated; first line for massive PE without contraindication is systemic tPA. (Source: ANZ Society of Cardiology PE Statement)
source_refs: ANZ Society of Cardiology PE Statement

options.text: Systemic alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 hours plus therapeutic unfractionated heparin infusion targeted to APTT
options.rationale: Massive PE with sustained hypotension and RV dysfunction is a class I indication for systemic thrombolysis with alteplase; concurrent unfractionated heparin is titrated to APTT after tPA. (Source: ANZ Society of Cardiology PE Statement)
source_refs: ANZ Society of Cardiology PE Statement

options.text: Insert an IVC filter first, then start therapeutic heparin infusion and reassess for tPA at 24 hours
options.rationale: IVC filters do not treat the existing clot causing shock and delaying tPA is dangerous in massive PE; filters are reserved for anticoagulation contraindication or recurrence on therapy. (Source: ANZ Society of Cardiology PE Statement)
source_refs: ANZ Society of Cardiology PE Statement

explanation.summary: Massive (high risk) pulmonary embolism is defined by sustained hypotension or shock from acute PE. Systemic thrombolysis with alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 hours plus concurrent unfractionated heparin is first line when there are no absolute bleeding contraindications. Surgical embolectomy or catheter directed thrombolysis are reserved for failed or contraindicated systemic tPA. Anticoagulation alone or IVC filter placement do not treat the obstruction.
key_points: Massive PE: shock or hypotension plus PE, immediate reperfusion needed
Alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 hours plus UFH infusion is first line
Surgical embolectomy or CDT if tPA fails or contraindicated
IVC filter only when anticoagulation is contraindicated
explanation.pearls: PE mortality with shock is around 30 to 50 percent untreated and falls to 10 to 20 percent with prompt tPA; alteplase 0.6 mg per kg over 15 minutes bolus is used in cardiac arrest from suspected PE, standard 100 mg over 2 hours in sustained shock without arrest.

sources.label: ANZ Society of Cardiology PE Statement

subtopic_detail: pH 6.90 with severe hypokalaemia and altered conscious level
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 24-year-old woman with new type 1 diabetes presenting with 24 hours of vomiting and abdominal pain. Glasgow Coma Scale is 13. She is Kussmaul breathing at 32 per minute. Blood pressure is 96/58 with pulse 128. Weight is 60 kg. Venous blood gas pH is 6.90 with a bicarbonate of 4 and anion gap of 34. Plasma glucose is 32 mmol/L, potassium is 3.0, and creatinine 132. She has no urinary ketone strip but capillary ketones are 6.8.

Her initial 500 mL crystalloid bolus is running. You must set the initial insulin and potassium plan.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 100% on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius, GCS 13
data_table.Bloods: sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.0 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), bicarbonate 4 mmol/L (22-32), creatinine 132 umol/L (45-90), glucose 32 mmol/L (3.5-8.0), pH 6.90, ketones 6.8 mmol/L (under 0.6), lactate 2.4 mmol/L (under 2.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Start dextrose 10 percent infusion and normal insulin infusion together to avoid rapid glucose fall over 2 hours
options.rationale: Dextrose is added when glucose falls under 14 mmol/L on insulin, not initially at glucose 32; and insulin cannot start until K over 3.3 mmol/L is corrected. (Source: ADS DKA Guideline)

options.text: Start fixed rate insulin infusion at 0.1 units per kg per hour immediately alongside crystalloid resuscitation
options.rationale: Starting insulin with potassium under 3.3 mmol/L causes dangerous intracellular potassium shift and arrhythmia; correct K to 3.5 first. (Source: ADS DKA Guideline)

options.text: Give IV sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol infusion over 30 minutes because pH is under 7.00 with cardiovascular risk
options.rationale: Bicarbonate does not improve outcomes in DKA and can worsen hypokalaemia and cerebral oedema risk; it is not routinely indicated even at pH under 7.00 unless refractory shock is present. (Source: ADS DKA Guideline)

options.text: Give a subcutaneous rapid acting insulin bolus of 10 units and then commence oral fluids and delay IV insulin
options.rationale: SC insulin is unreliable in shock or dehydration and is not first line in severe DKA; IV infusion is standard, and hypokalaemia must be corrected before starting insulin. (Source: ADS DKA Guideline)

options.text: Continue crystalloid resuscitation and replace potassium to over 3.5 mmol/L before starting insulin infusion
options.rationale: Potassium under 3.3 mmol/L is a contraindication to starting insulin because insulin drives further intracellular shift and precipitates arrhythmia; correct K first, then start insulin at 0.1 units per kg per hour. (Source: ADS DKA Guideline)

explanation.summary: Severe DKA with initial potassium under 3.3 mmol/L is a contraindication to starting insulin because insulin drives potassium intracellularly and precipitates arrhythmia. The priority is fluid resuscitation and potassium replacement to above 3.5 mmol/L before commencing IV insulin infusion at 0.1 units per kg per hour. Bicarbonate is not routine even at pH under 7.00. Add dextrose when glucose falls under 14 mmol/L on insulin infusion.
key_points: Potassium under 3.3 mmol/L: hold insulin until corrected to above 3.5
Standard fixed rate insulin: 0.1 units per kg per hour IV
Bicarbonate not routinely indicated in DKA even at pH under 7.00
Add dextrose 10 percent when glucose falls under 14 mmol/L on insulin
explanation.pearls: ADS thresholds: hold insulin K under 3.3, add KCl 40 mmol per litre if K 3.3 to 5.3; cerebral oedema risk in adults is low but reduce fluid rate if child, symptoms occur usually 4 to 12 hours in, treat with mannitol 0.5 to 1 g per kg or 3 percent saline 5 mL per kg.

subtopic_detail: M1 middle cerebral artery occlusion at 4 hours from onset
stem:
You are the stroke registrar in a metropolitan ED reviewing a 68-year-old right-handed man who developed sudden left hemiparesis and neglect 4 hours ago on a family car trip. NIHSS is 18 with dense left arm weakness, forced right gaze deviation, and hemispatial neglect. He is on aspirin 100 mg for coronary disease. Non-contrast CT shows no haemorrhage and no established infarct; ASPECTS is 9. CT angiogram confirms a right M1 occlusion. CT perfusion shows a mismatch ratio of 2.1 with core 18 mL and penumbra 58 mL. He has no thrombolysis contraindications and weighs 82 kg.

Interventional neuroradiology is available in-house.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 86, blood pressure 168/94, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, GCS 14
data_table.Bloods: Hb 148 g/L (135-175), platelets 232 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 96 umol/L (60-110), INR 1.0, glucose 6.2 mmol/L (3.5-8.0)
data_table.Imaging: NCCT ASPECTS 9 no bleed, CTA right M1 occlusion, CTP core 18 mL penumbra 58 mL mismatch 2.1

lead_in: What is the most appropriate reperfusion strategy?

options.text: IV tenecteplase 0.25 mg per kg bolus now followed by endovascular thrombectomy for the M1 occlusion
options.rationale: Within 4.5 hours of onset with no contraindication, IV thrombolysis (tenecteplase or alteplase) plus endovascular thrombectomy for a large vessel occlusion is first line and outperforms either alone. (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines Australia)

options.text: Endovascular thrombectomy alone without IV thrombolysis because he is on aspirin already
options.rationale: Antiplatelet use is not a contraindication to IV thrombolysis; skipping tPA loses the benefit of pre-thrombectomy reperfusion and small vessel clot clearance. (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines Australia)

options.text: IV thrombolysis only without thrombectomy because the CT ASPECTS score is 9 and core is small
options.rationale: Large vessel occlusion with disabling deficit benefits from thrombectomy even after tPA; withholding it wastes proven mortality and functional benefit. (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines Australia)

options.text: Loading dose clopidogrel 300 mg plus aspirin 300 mg and admit to the stroke unit without reperfusion
options.rationale: Dual antiplatelet loading is not reperfusion and is not appropriate as sole therapy in disabling stroke with LVO within the reperfusion window. (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines Australia)

options.text: Delay reperfusion until 24 hours to allow perfusion imaging repeat and reduce haemorrhagic transformation risk
options.rationale: Delay of reperfusion loses time-dependent benefit; the mismatch profile at 4 hours already supports urgent tPA plus thrombectomy. (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines Australia)

explanation.summary: Acute ischaemic stroke with a disabling deficit and confirmed anterior circulation large vessel occlusion should receive IV thrombolysis within 4.5 hours if no contraindication, plus endovascular thrombectomy up to 24 hours with favourable imaging. Tenecteplase 0.25 mg per kg has non-inferior evidence to alteplase and is now often first line in Australia. Combined therapy is better than either alone.
key_points: IV tenecteplase 0.25 mg per kg within 4.5 hours of onset for eligible patients
Endovascular thrombectomy for anterior circulation LVO up to 24 hours with mismatch
Antiplatelet use is not a contraindication to IV thrombolysis
Blood pressure target under 185/110 before tPA, under 180/105 for 24 hours after
explanation.pearls: Australian Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines now recommend tenecteplase 0.25 mg per kg IV single bolus as an alternative to alteplase within 4.5 hours; thrombectomy has NNT around 4 to 5 for functional independence in LVO stroke within 6 hours.

subtopic_detail: Anterior STEMI with pulmonary oedema and hypotension after primary PCI
stem:
You are the coronary care unit registrar 4 hours after successful primary PCI to the LAD in a 62-year-old man with anterior STEMI. He is now hypotensive with blood pressure 78/52 despite noradrenaline at 0.4 mcg per kg per minute. He has bibasal crackles, JVP raised to angle, and cool peripheries. Echocardiogram shows LV ejection fraction 20 percent with anterior akinesis, moderate mitral regurgitation, and no mechanical complication. Lactate is 4.2. He is intubated and sedated. Cardiac output monitoring shows CI 1.6.

The interventional cardiologist has confirmed no residual coronary lesion.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 118, blood pressure 78/52 on noradrenaline 0.4, respiratory rate 22 ventilated, SpO2 92% on 60% FiO2, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: Hb 128 g/L (135-175), platelets 224 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 138 umol/L (60-110), lactate 4.2 mmol/L (under 2.0), high sensitivity troponin 42000 ng/L (under 26)
data_table.Imaging: echo LVEF 20% anterior akinesis moderate MR no VSD no tamponade, chest X-ray bilateral alveolar oedema

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in circulatory support?

options.text: Add dobutamine 5 mcg per kg per minute to noradrenaline and continue medical therapy with diuretics
options.rationale: Adding an inotrope on top of high dose vasopressor in worsening shock is unlikely to reverse hypoperfusion and delays escalation to mechanical support with proven benefit. (Source: ANZ Society of Cardiology STEMI Statement)
source_refs: ANZ Society of Cardiology STEMI Statement

options.text: Insert an Impella CP percutaneous LV assist device and wean noradrenaline as cardiac output improves
options.rationale: In cardiogenic shock after STEMI unresponsive to inotropes with escalating lactate, mechanical circulatory support (Impella or VA-ECMO in some centres) is indicated; the DanGer Shock trial showed Impella CP mortality benefit in selected STEMI shock. (Source: ANZ Society of Cardiology STEMI Statement)
source_refs: ANZ Society of Cardiology STEMI Statement

options.text: Give IV nitroglycerin infusion at 20 mcg per minute to reduce afterload and improve pulmonary oedema now
options.rationale: Nitroglycerin lowers preload and can precipitate profound hypotension in cardiogenic shock with SBP under 90; it is inappropriate as an escalation step here. (Source: ANZ Society of Cardiology STEMI Statement)
source_refs: ANZ Society of Cardiology STEMI Statement

options.text: Give IV levosimendan 0.1 mcg per kg per minute over 24 hours and continue current vasopressor support
options.rationale: Levosimendan can worsen hypotension in fixed cardiogenic shock and has not shown mortality benefit; it is not the priority when mechanical support is available. (Source: ANZ Society of Cardiology STEMI Statement)
source_refs: ANZ Society of Cardiology STEMI Statement

options.text: Insert an intra-aortic balloon pump because IABP has proven mortality benefit in cardiogenic shock post-MI
options.rationale: IABP-SHOCK II showed no mortality benefit for IABP in post-MI cardiogenic shock; contemporary practice favours Impella or VA-ECMO for refractory shock. (Source: ANZ Society of Cardiology STEMI Statement)
source_refs: ANZ Society of Cardiology STEMI Statement

explanation.summary: Refractory cardiogenic shock after STEMI with escalating vasopressor need and rising lactate is an indication for mechanical circulatory support, with recent evidence (DanGer Shock 2024) supporting Impella CP over IABP or medical therapy alone in selected STEMI shock. IABP has no mortality benefit. Adding more inotropes or preload reducers can worsen outcomes. Early escalation before multi-organ failure is key.
key_points: Refractory STEMI cardiogenic shock: escalate to mechanical support early
DanGer Shock trial: Impella CP mortality benefit in STEMI shock
IABP-SHOCK II: no mortality benefit for IABP in post-MI shock
Avoid vasodilators like GTN when SBP under 90 mmHg
explanation.pearls: DanGer Shock 2024 NEJM showed 6 month mortality 45.8 percent Impella CP vs 58.5 percent standard care in STEMI shock, at cost of more bleeding and limb ischaemia; VA-ECMO used when biventricular failure or Impella insufficient.

sources.label: ANZ Society of Cardiology STEMI Statement

subtopic_detail: Type 2 respiratory failure on maximal medical therapy
stem:
You are the medical registrar in ED with a 26-year-old woman with severe asthma who has not improved after continuous nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium, IV hydrocortisone 100 mg, and IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 minutes. She is diaphoretic, unable to speak in words, and has a silent chest. Peak flow was 90 L/min on arrival (best 420) and now cannot be recorded. Arterial gas 30 minutes into treatment shows pH 7.21, pCO2 68, pO2 62 on 15 L via non-rebreather. Heart rate is 148. She has a prior ICU admission for asthma.

The ICU consultant is at bedside for airway management.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 148, blood pressure 132/86, respiratory rate 42, SpO2 88% on 15 L NRB, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), lactate 4.6 mmol/L (under 2.0), pH 7.21, pCO2 68 mmHg (35-45), pO2 62 mmHg (80-100)
data_table.Imaging: chest X-ray hyperinflation no pneumothorax no consolidation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: IV aminophylline 5 mg per kg loading dose over 20 minutes then continuous infusion 0.5 mg per kg per hour
options.rationale: Aminophylline has limited additional benefit over maximal beta-agonist plus magnesium and adds arrhythmia risk in a patient already needing intubation. (Source: TSANZ/ANZSA Severe Asthma Guideline)

options.text: Continuous BiPAP 12/6 cmH2O with pressure support titration and repeat gas in 30 minutes before intubation
options.rationale: NIV in severe asthma with silent chest, exhaustion, and rising CO2 delays definitive airway and risks arrest; intubation is indicated now, not further NIV. (Source: TSANZ/ANZSA Severe Asthma Guideline)

options.text: Rapid sequence intubation with ketamine 1.5 mg per kg IV and rocuronium then lung protective ventilation
options.rationale: Life threatening asthma with rising CO2 and exhaustion after maximal therapy requires intubation; ketamine is preferred induction agent for bronchodilator effect and cardiovascular stability, with permissive hypercapnia thereafter. (Source: TSANZ/ANZSA Severe Asthma Guideline)

options.text: Repeat IV magnesium sulfate 2 g bolus and add second dose IV hydrocortisone before considering intubation
options.rationale: Repeating magnesium is not evidence supported and steroid effect takes hours; the patient needs an airway now, not another delayed pharmacological trial. (Source: TSANZ/ANZSA Severe Asthma Guideline)

options.text: IV adrenaline infusion 0.05 mcg per kg per minute and continue nebulised beta-agonist without airway plan
options.rationale: Systemic adrenaline is reserved for peri-arrest anaphylaxis or shock; it does not replace intubation in exhausted asthma with rising CO2 and silent chest. (Source: TSANZ/ANZSA Severe Asthma Guideline)

explanation.summary: Severe or near-fatal asthma with exhaustion, silent chest, and rising CO2 despite maximal medical therapy requires intubation. Ketamine is the preferred induction agent for its bronchodilator effect. Post-intubation ventilation uses low tidal volumes, low rate, long expiratory time, and permissive hypercapnia to avoid dynamic hyperinflation. NIV is not first line in this deteriorating scenario.
key_points: Life threatening asthma with rising CO2 or silent chest: intubate
Ketamine 1 to 2 mg per kg IV is preferred induction agent
Permissive hypercapnia and prolonged expiratory time post intubation
Watch for dynamic hyperinflation and pneumothorax during ventilation
explanation.pearls: TSANZ suggests tidal volume 5 to 6 mL per kg, RR 8 to 10, I:E 1:4, plateau pressure under 30, allow pCO2 up to 80 mmHg with pH over 7.15; ketamine dose 1 to 2 mg per kg IV, with rocuronium 1.2 mg per kg for RSI.

subtopic_detail: Na 110 mmol/L with seizure and altered conscious state
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 74-year-old woman brought to ED after a witnessed 2 minute generalised seizure at home. She has been vomiting for 3 days and is on hydrochlorothiazide and citalopram. GCS is 12 now, no localising signs, no meningism. Sodium is 110, potassium 3.4, urea 6.4, creatinine 92, glucose 5.2. Serum osmolality is 240 and urine sodium 62. She is not clinically dehydrated. Airway is patent and BP is 122/74.

The intensivist is present and asks about immediate fluid strategy.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 88, blood pressure 122/74, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, GCS 12
data_table.Bloods: sodium 110 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), urea 6.4 mmol/L (2.5-8.0), creatinine 92 umol/L (45-90), glucose 5.2 mmol/L (3.5-8.0), serum osmolality 240 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 380 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 62 mmol/L
data_table.Imaging: CT brain unremarkable, chest X-ray clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate fluid management?

options.text: Give tolvaptan 15 mg orally now and start 0.9 percent saline at 100 mL per hour after loading dose is given
options.rationale: Tolvaptan risks over-rapid correction and osmotic demyelination and is not first line in acute symptomatic severe hyponatraemia; hypertonic saline in controlled boluses is standard. (Source: European Hyponatraemia Guideline)

options.text: Start 0.9 percent saline infusion at 500 mL per hour and reassess sodium in 4 hours before other action
options.rationale: Isotonic saline can worsen hyponatraemia by adding to intake in SIAD physiology; symptomatic severe hyponatraemia needs hypertonic saline, not isotonic infusion, to raise sodium quickly. (Source: European Hyponatraemia Guideline)

options.text: Fluid restrict to 800 mL per day and observe on the ward without giving any bolus of saline for 24 hours
options.rationale: Fluid restriction alone is far too slow for a patient with active seizure and Na 110; hypertonic saline is needed to stop cerebral symptoms rapidly. (Source: European Hyponatraemia Guideline)

options.text: Give 150 mL 3 percent saline bolus IV over 10 minutes and repeat once or twice to a maximum rise of 6 mmol/L in 24 hours
options.rationale: Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizure, coma) is treated with hypertonic saline boluses to raise sodium by 4 to 6 mmol/L rapidly to stop symptoms, capped at 8 to 10 mmol/L in 24 hours to prevent osmotic demyelination. (Source: European Hyponatraemia Guideline)

options.text: Give IV frusemide 40 mg and 0.9 percent saline together to remove free water and raise sodium concentration
options.rationale: Frusemide plus isotonic saline can be used cautiously in some volume overload chronic cases but is inappropriate in acute symptomatic severe hyponatraemia; hypertonic bolus stops cerebral symptoms fastest. (Source: European Hyponatraemia Guideline)

explanation.summary: Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia with seizure or reduced GCS is treated with 150 mL 3 percent saline IV over 10 minutes, repeated once or twice, targeting a rise of 4 to 6 mmol/L to abort cerebral symptoms, then capped at 8 to 10 mmol/L in 24 hours to prevent osmotic demyelination syndrome. Isotonic saline can worsen the picture in SIAD-type physiology. Tolvaptan and free water restriction are for chronic settings.
key_points: Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia: 150 mL 3% saline bolus over 10 minutes
Repeat once or twice to raise Na 4 to 6 mmol/L to abort symptoms
Cap correction at 8 to 10 mmol/L per 24 hours to prevent ODS
Do not use tolvaptan in acute symptomatic phase
explanation.pearls: European guideline (2014) and Aussie NKF: 150 mL 3% saline IV over 10 minutes as bolus; if over-correction occurs, give 5% dextrose 10 mL per kg over 1 hour plus DDAVP 2 to 4 mcg subcut to reverse.

subtopic_detail: Adult with subacute meningism and CSF lymphocytosis with low glucose
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 42-year-old man from a high TB prevalence country with 3 weeks of headache, fever, and progressive drowsiness. He has right sixth nerve palsy and mild neck stiffness. HIV serology is pending. CT brain shows basal meningeal enhancement and mild hydrocephalus with open ventricles. Lumbar puncture opening pressure is 32 cm CSF, protein 2.2 g/L, glucose 1.4 mmol/L with paired plasma 6.4, and 240 lymphocytes with 20 neutrophils. GeneXpert MTB/RIF positive on CSF is available in 2 hours.

He is stable but drowsy. You must initiate treatment now.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 92, blood pressure 124/78, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.1 degrees Celsius, GCS 13
data_table.Bloods: Hb 118 g/L (135-175), white cells 9.4 x10^9/L (4-11), sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 86 umol/L (60-110), ALT 32 U/L (5-40), CRP 68 mg/L (under 5)
data_table.Imaging: CT brain basal meningeal enhancement mild hydrocephalus, chest X-ray upper lobe infiltrates and small right hilar node

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Start rifampicin and isoniazid only for 12 months with pyridoxine and defer pyrazinamide until sputum is available
options.rationale: Two-drug induction is inadequate for TB meningitis and risks resistance and treatment failure; standard four-drug induction with steroids is indicated even before sputum results. (Source: WHO TB Consolidated Guidelines)

options.text: Empirical ceftriaxone 2 g IV twice daily plus benzylpenicillin 2.4 g IV 4 hourly awaiting culture data
options.rationale: Bacterial meningitis cover alone misses TB, and the CSF profile (lymphocytic pleocytosis, very low glucose, high protein, opening pressure 32) is classic for TB, especially with positive GeneXpert pending. (Source: WHO TB Consolidated Guidelines)

options.text: Give IV aciclovir 10 mg per kg 8 hourly for possible herpes encephalitis and await MRI brain imaging
options.rationale: HSV encephalitis produces temporal lobe changes and PCR-positive CSF, not basal meningeal enhancement with markedly low glucose; aciclovir alone misses the treatable TB. (Source: WHO TB Consolidated Guidelines)

options.text: Start RIPE anti-tubercular therapy alone without corticosteroids because steroids risk TB dissemination
options.rationale: Adjunctive dexamethasone reduces mortality in TB meningitis and is standard alongside RIPE; withholding steroids loses a proven mortality benefit. (Source: WHO TB Consolidated Guidelines)

options.text: Start rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol plus IV dexamethasone 0.4 mg per kg per day tapered over 8 weeks
options.rationale: TB meningitis is treated with standard RIPE quadruple therapy plus adjunctive dexamethasone (Thwaites regimen), which reduces mortality across HIV-negative and HIV-positive adults. (Source: WHO TB Consolidated Guidelines)

explanation.summary: TB meningitis is treated with a 2 month intensive phase of rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, then a 7 to 10 month continuation phase of rifampicin and isoniazid, alongside adjunctive dexamethasone tapered over 6 to 8 weeks. Steroids reduce mortality by around 30 percent. CSF classically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis, high protein, very low glucose, and high opening pressure. GeneXpert MTB/RIF Ultra on CSF is the first-line rapid test.
key_points: TBM treatment: 2 months RIPE plus 7 to 10 months RH, with dexamethasone taper
Dexamethasone reduces mortality across HIV-negative and HIV-positive adults
CSF: lymphocytic pleocytosis, protein over 1 g/L, glucose under 40% serum
GeneXpert MTB/RIF Ultra on CSF is preferred rapid diagnostic
explanation.pearls: Thwaites steroid regimen: dexamethasone 0.4 mg per kg per day IV for 1 week, 0.3 for week 2, 0.2 for week 3, 0.1 for week 4, then 4 mg orally reducing over 4 weeks; add pyridoxine 25 mg daily with isoniazid to prevent neuropathy.

subtopic_detail: Persistent shock despite repeat IM adrenaline in a patient on beta-blocker
stem:
You are the medical registrar in ED with a 58-year-old man 15 minutes after peanut ingestion. He has facial swelling, widespread urticaria, wheeze, and stridor. He has received IM adrenaline 500 mcg twice at 5 minute intervals, IV fluid 2 litres crystalloid, IV hydrocortisone 200 mg, and IV chlorphenamine 10 mg, but remains hypotensive at 78/44 with pulse 62. He is on bisoprolol 5 mg for atrial fibrillation and rivaroxaban 20 mg. The airway is patent for now but stridor is worsening.

The anaesthetist is preparing for intubation.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 62, blood pressure 78/44, respiratory rate 30, SpO2 90% on 15 L NRB, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, GCS 14
data_table.Bloods: Hb 138 g/L (135-175), platelets 220 x10^9/L (150-400), lactate 3.6 mmol/L (under 2.0), tryptase pending
data_table.Imaging: chest X-ray hyperinflation no oedema no pneumothorax

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start IV adrenaline infusion at 0.05 to 0.5 mcg per kg per minute and give IV glucagon 1 mg for beta-blocker effect
options.rationale: Refractory anaphylaxis after two IM adrenaline doses requires an IV adrenaline infusion; in beta-blocker refractoriness, IV glucagon 1 to 5 mg bolus bypasses the beta-receptor block via cAMP. (Source: ANZAAG Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Continue further IM adrenaline every 5 minutes and add nebulised salbutamol without changing route or dose
options.rationale: IM boluses have a ceiling and delayed absorption in shock; IV infusion is required in refractory anaphylaxis with sustained hypotension after two IM doses. (Source: ANZAAG Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Give IV noradrenaline 0.1 mcg per kg per minute as first line vasopressor instead of adrenaline in this case
options.rationale: Adrenaline is the first line vasoactive drug in anaphylaxis (alpha and beta effects, mast cell stabilisation); noradrenaline is a second line adjunct only if adrenaline is insufficient. (Source: ANZAAG Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Give IV hydrocortisone 500 mg further and repeat IV chlorphenamine 10 mg without additional vasopressor therapy
options.rationale: Corticosteroids and antihistamines are adjunctive and do not treat acute shock; withholding IV adrenaline infusion in refractory anaphylaxis is unsafe. (Source: ANZAAG Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Give IV dopamine 5 mcg per kg per minute infusion and delay intubation because airway may improve with fluids
options.rationale: Dopamine is not first line in anaphylaxis; worsening stridor with sustained shock mandates prompt airway management, not delay. (Source: ANZAAG Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Refractory anaphylaxis after two doses of IM adrenaline needs escalation to an IV adrenaline infusion. In patients on beta-blockers who fail to respond, IV glucagon 1 to 5 mg bolus can bypass the beta-block via cAMP. Adjunctive steroids and antihistamines do not treat shock. Airway must be secured urgently if stridor is worsening.
key_points: Refractory anaphylaxis: escalate to IV adrenaline infusion
IV glucagon 1 to 5 mg for beta-blocker refractoriness
Adrenaline is first line, noradrenaline second line adjunct
Steroids and antihistamines are adjunctive, not shock therapy
explanation.pearls: ANZAAG lists IV adrenaline 1 mg in 1000 mL saline = 1 mcg per mL, start at 5 mL per minute in an adult; glucagon 1 to 5 mg IV bolus over 5 minutes for beta-blocker refractoriness, may repeat and follow with infusion 5 to 15 mcg per minute.

subtopic_detail: Wells score with age-adjusted D-dimer threshold
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 78 year old woman with 24 hours of pleuritic chest pain and mild dyspnoea. She had a total knee replacement 3 weeks ago and is mobilising with a frame at home. She has no haemoptysis, no leg swelling, and no history of malignancy. On examination she is haemodynamically stable with clear chest and no calf swelling or tenderness. Her chest X-ray is unremarkable. Her Wells score is 4.5 (surgery in last 4 weeks 1.5, PE as likely as alternative 3). An age-adjusted D-dimer using the 500 x age formula returns a value of 700 micrograms/L (age-adjusted cut-off 780).

Her creatinine is 92 micromol/L and eGFR is 62.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 88, blood pressure 132/78, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.8

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform CT pulmonary angiography as the Wells score of 4.5 places her in the PE-likely group requiring imaging
options.rationale: Two-level Wells >4 places the patient in the PE-likely group where CTPA is indicated regardless of D-dimer; her Wells of 4.5 with normal renal function makes CTPA the imaging of choice. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society ANZ 2021)

options.text: Discharge with reassurance because the age-adjusted D-dimer is below the cut-off for her age at 780 today value
options.rationale: D-dimer strategies (standard or age-adjusted) are only validated in PE-unlikely groups (Wells <=4); a moderate to high probability Wells score requires imaging regardless of D-dimer. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society ANZ 2021)

options.text: CT pulmonary angiogram given the moderate Wells probability, notwithstanding the negative age-adjusted D-dimer today
options.rationale: With a Wells score of 4.5 (PE likely, >4) the age-adjusted D-dimer strategy is NOT applicable; D-dimer testing is reserved for Wells <=4 (PE unlikely); imaging is required regardless of D-dimer in Wells >4. However Wells 4.5 puts patient in the PE-likely group so CTPA is warranted. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society ANZ 2021)

options.text: Ventilation-perfusion scan first-line as the initial imaging modality due to her age and preserved renal function level
options.rationale: V/Q scan is an alternative when CTPA is contraindicated (contrast allergy, severe renal impairment, pregnancy); with eGFR 62 CTPA is safer and faster for interpretation. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society ANZ 2021)

options.text: Bilateral lower limb Doppler ultrasound as a proxy investigation to avoid contrast exposure with age-related nephropathy risk
options.rationale: Doppler ultrasound of legs is used to detect DVT when PE is suspected and imaging is not immediately available; a positive DVT plus clinical PE suspicion treats as PE, but with eGFR 62 CTPA is not contraindicated and is the definitive investigation. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society ANZ 2021)

explanation.summary: PE diagnostic strategy uses Wells score to stratify patients into PE-unlikely (Wells <=4) or PE-likely (Wells >4). In PE-unlikely, D-dimer (age-adjusted for over 50 using age x 10 in micrograms/L) rules out PE when below cut-off. In PE-likely, D-dimer is bypassed and imaging is performed regardless. CT pulmonary angiography is first-line unless contrast contraindicated (severe renal impairment eGFR <30, contrast allergy, pregnancy) when V/Q scan is preferred. Doppler of legs supports diagnosis if positive but does not exclude PE if negative.
key_points: Wells >4 = PE-likely: image regardless of D-dimer
Wells <=4 plus age-adjusted D-dimer below cut-off rules out PE
CTPA first-line if renal function adequate
V/Q scan when CTPA contraindicated
explanation.pearls: Age-adjusted D-dimer cut-off (age x 10 mcg/L) reduces false positives in >50s from around 40 to 25 percent without affecting negative predictive value; adopted in AU and European guidelines but the standard 500 mcg/L cut-off remains used in some centres.

subtopic_detail: Membrane stabilisation and shift plus removal choices
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 68 year old man on haemodialysis who missed his last two sessions because he was interstate for a family bereavement. He presents with generalised weakness, palpitations, and nausea. He is on perindopril and spironolactone for cardiomyopathy. His observations show bradycardia and normotension. His ECG shows peaked T waves throughout, PR prolongation to 240 ms, and a QRS complex 130 ms without loss of P waves. Serum potassium is markedly raised. He has functioning tunnelled dialysis catheter access already in situ.

Nephrology is arranging urgent dialysis to run within the next 45 minutes.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 48, blood pressure 128/72, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.ECG: peaked T waves, PR 240 ms, QRS 130 ms, no loss of P waves, no arrhythmia
data_table.Bloods: potassium 7.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), sodium 138 mmol/L, urea 32 mmol/L, creatinine 720 micromol/L, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, glucose 6.4 mmol/L
data_table.Medications: perindopril 10 mg daily, spironolactone 25 mg daily, carvedilol 6.25 mg BD

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management step?

options.text: Withhold treatment until formal potassium result is repeated to rule out haemolysis and dialysis is ready to commence
options.rationale: The ECG changes confirm the biochemical hyperkalaemia; awaiting repeat testing risks cardiac arrest during the wait. (Source: eTG Complete Acute Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: Oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate 30 g stat with repeat 8 hourly while awaiting haemodialysis for potassium removal today
options.rationale: Resonium is a slow-acting cation exchange resin with modest effect and does not address life-threatening ECG changes; membrane stabilisation with calcium is the immediate step. (Source: eTG Complete Acute Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 10 mg alone with cessation of perindopril and spironolactone while awaiting the dialysis session
options.rationale: Salbutamol lowers potassium modestly by around 0.5-1.0 mmol/L but does not stabilise the myocardium; calcium is the immediate priority in ECG changes of this severity. (Source: eTG Complete Acute Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: IV sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol over 10 minutes as first-line treatment for the wide complex and metabolic acidosis today
options.rationale: Bicarbonate has role in severe metabolic acidosis but does not stabilise the myocardium acutely; calcium precedes bicarbonate and shift strategies in acute hyperkalaemia with ECG changes. (Source: eTG Complete Acute Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: IV calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10 percent solution followed by insulin-dextrose shift and immediate haemodialysis when available
options.rationale: Hyperkalaemia with peaked T waves, PR prolongation, and QRS widening requires immediate IV calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10 percent for membrane stabilisation, then insulin-dextrose (10 units actrapid with 50 mL of 50 percent glucose) for shift, and dialysis for definitive removal in this ESRD patient. (Source: eTG Complete Acute Hyperkalaemia)

explanation.summary: Severe hyperkalaemia (>=6.5 mmol/L or ECG changes) is a medical emergency treated in three parallel steps: membrane stabilisation with IV calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10 percent (or calcium chloride 5-10 mL of 10 percent via central line) repeated as needed; potassium shift with insulin-dextrose (10 units actrapid with 50 mL of 50 percent glucose) and nebulised salbutamol 10-20 mg; and definitive removal with haemodialysis in ESRD, or resonium and diuretics in preserved renal function. Cease contributing drugs (ACE inhibitor, ARB, spironolactone, NSAID). Continuous cardiac monitoring is essential.
key_points: IV calcium first for ECG changes (membrane stabilisation)
Insulin-dextrose plus salbutamol for shift
Haemodialysis for definitive removal in ESRD
Cease ACEI, ARB, spironolactone, NSAID
